records.name: 5-Amino-1MQ
records.description: 5-Amino-1MQ (5-amino-1-methylquinolinium) is a small molecule inhibitor of Nicotinamide N-Methyltransferase (NNMT) — an enzyme expressed primarily in adipose tissue and the liver that catalyzes the methylation and inactivation of nicotinamide (vitamin B3). NNMT's primary substrate is nicotinamide, which it converts to 1-methylnicotinamide using S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. This reaction simultaneously depletes the cellular pool of nicotinamide available for NAD+ biosynthesis and consumes SAM that would otherwise be used in critical epigenetic methylation reactions. In metabolic disease states and obesity, NNMT is dramatically upregulated in white adipose tissue — this upregulation serves as a metabolic brake that suppresses NAD+ levels, reduces mitochondrial biogenesis, impairs fat oxidation, and locks white adipocytes in an energy-storing, lipogenic state. By inhibiting NNMT, 5-Amino-1MQ removes this metabolic brake: nicotinamide is redirected into the Preiss-Handler pathway for NAD+ synthesis, intracellular NAD+ levels rise, SAM is conserved for epigenetic regulation, SIRT1 (NAD+-dependent deacetylase) activity increases, mitochondrial biogenesis is upregulated via PGC-1α, and white adipocytes shift toward a metabolically active, fat-burning phenotype that resembles beige/brown adipose tissue. Preclinical research in diet-induced obese mice demonstrates that NNMT inhibition with 5-Amino-1MQ reduces fat mass without reductions in food intake, lean mass, or activity — indicating a direct metabolic reprogramming effect rather than appetite suppression. Blood glucose, insulin, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol improve in these models. Importantly, 5-Amino-1MQ achieves NAD+ restoration through a mechanistically different pathway than direct NAD+ supplementation (injected NAD+) or NAD+ precursor supplementation (NMN, NR). It does not add exogenous NAD+ substrate — it preserves and redirects the endogenous nicotinamide pool by preventing its methylation and excretion. This makes 5-Amino-1MQ and NAD+ injection mechanistically complementary: 5-Amino-1MQ prevents depletion while injectable NAD+ directly restores the pool, producing additive intracellular NAD+ elevation when stacked. The "With Meals" dosing window distinguishes 5-Amino-1MQ from nearly every other compound in this database. NNMT activity peaks during active metabolic states, and the small molecule's oral/injectable bioavailability is best utilized when the metabolic pathways it influences are actively engaged. The stimulant-adjacent side effects (insomnia, jitteriness in sensitive subjects) are mechanistically consistent with the increase in cellular energy production and sympathomimetic-like upregulation of metabolic rate — not from direct adrenergic receptor activation, but from the downstream cascade of increased mitochondrial activity. As the most experimental compound in Category IV alongside SLU-PP-332, 5-Amino-1MQ lacks human clinical trial data, and all mechanism-based claims extrapolate from in vitro and rodent studies conducted primarily between 2018–2022.

contraindications: Active malignancy — NNMT inhibition increases intracellular NAD+ and SIRT1 activity, which in normal cells promotes health and longevity; in cancer cells, elevated NAD+ can fuel tumor metabolic demands and enhance DNA repair capacity that helps cancer cells evade treatment.

Concurrent use with MAO inhibitors (MAOIs) — 5-Amino-1MQ contains a quinolinium structure; potential pharmacological interaction with monoamine oxidase inhibition pathways is not characterized but warrants caution.

Breastfeeding — no safety data.

Pediatric use — no data.

sideEffects: Insomnia or sleep disruption — the most commonly reported side effect; increased cellular energy production and metabolic rate elevation interfere with sleep onset; mitigated by strict morning or with-meal dosing, never in the evening.
Mild anxiety and jitteriness — sympathomimetic-like stimulation from metabolic rate increase; not from direct adrenergic receptor agonism but from downstream mitochondrial activation; dose-dependent.
Injection site irritation — redness, soreness at the subcutaneous site; standard peptide injection response.
Mild headache — reported in early weeks; likely related to cellular metabolic shifts and NAD+ pathway activation.
Gastrointestinal discomfort — mild nausea or GI upset; more common if taken without food (hence the "With Meals" dosing requirement).
Transient fatigue in the post-dose window — paradoxical; as cells shift metabolic programs, a short window of fatigue may precede the sustained energy improvement.
Potential overstimulation of NAD+ production — theoretical; excessive SIRT1 activation could alter epigenetic regulation in ways not fully characterized in long-term human research.
No endocrine disruption — 5-Amino-1MQ has no known activity at hormone receptors; does not affect cortisol, testosterone, estrogen, or thyroid hormone pathways.

records.name: ACE-031
records.description: ACE-031 (ramatercept, ACVR2B-Fc) is not a traditional peptide but a soluble fusion protein — the extracellular domain of the activin type IIB receptor (ActRIIB) fused to an IgG1 Fc antibody fragment. This architecture makes it a ligand trap rather than a receptor agonist: it circulates freely in the bloodstream and sequesters the ligands that would normally bind membrane-bound ActRIIB, preventing them from delivering their signaling. The critical ligands it traps include myostatin (GDF-8), activin A, activin B, and GDF-11 — all of which are endogenous negative regulators of skeletal muscle mass. Myostatin is the most pharmacologically relevant of these: it is expressed specifically in skeletal muscle and functions to cap muscle fiber growth, acting as a biological governor on hypertrophy. By trapping myostatin and the related activins before they reach their membrane receptors, ACE-031 removes the inhibitory brake on muscle protein synthesis and satellite cell activity, producing rapid, pronounced skeletal muscle hypertrophy that is independent of training stimulus or androgen signaling. Clinical development of ACE-031 was led by Acceleron Pharma and progressed through Phase 1 (healthy postmenopausal women) and Phase 2 trials (boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy). The Phase 1 data confirmed robust pharmacological activity — a single 3 mg/kg dose produced statistically significant 3.3% increases in total lean mass and 5.1% increases in thigh muscle volume at day 29 by DXA and MRI respectively, with a mean half-life of 10–15 days. The Phase 2 DMD trial demonstrated trends for lean mass increase and maintenance of the six-minute walk test. However, the Phase 2 trial was halted in 2011 and the entire development program was discontinued in 2013 following safety signals: subjects in the DMD trial developed spontaneous epistaxis (nosebleeds) and telangiectasias (dilated superficial blood vessels), leading Acceleron and Shire to conclude that the vascular side effect profile was not acceptable for the target population. The vascular adverse effects are mechanistically explained by ACE-031's off-target trapping of BMP9 and BMP10 — two bone morphogenetic proteins that bind ActRIIB and are required for vascular endothelial homeostasis, particularly in the maintenance of arteriovenous differentiation and capillary integrity. When BMP9/BMP10 signaling is disrupted, vessels lose structural tone and capillaries dilate abnormally — which is the biological mechanism behind both the epistaxis and telangiectasias observed in the trials. This is the defining safety characteristic of ACE-031 that separates it from all other muscle-building compounds in this database: its risks are vascular, not hormonal, and they are directly caused by its mechanism of action rather than being an incidental pharmacological side effect. Research protocols must account for this by keeping doses conservative, cycle lengths extremely short (2–4 weeks maximum), and excluding any subject with pre-existing vascular fragility or bleeding disorders.

rows.notes: Due to vascular side effects, research doses are kept conservative.

Washout: Minimum 4 weeks off to prevent severe vascular issues.
contraindications: Bleeding disorders of any type — epistaxis and vascular fragility are direct pharmacological consequences of ACE-031's mechanism; any pre-existing coagulation disorder dramatically amplifies hemorrhagic risk.
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy — warfarin, heparin, aspirin, clopidogrel, NOACs; additive bleeding risk with BMP9/BMP10 pathway disruption.
Uncontrolled hypertension — elevated blood pressure combined with compromised vascular wall integrity from BMP9/BMP10 blockade increases risk of spontaneous vessel rupture.
Known hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) or family history of vascular malformations — BMP9 is the primary genetic driver of HHT; ACE-031 mechanistically recapitulates HHT pathology.
Active malignancy — ActRIIB ligand trapping removes activin A suppression, which may release growth restraints on tumor cells.
History of cancer — exercise caution; myostatin/activin pathway manipulation has theoretical tumor growth implications.
Pregnancy — fusion protein safety not established; avoid.
Breastfeeding — safety not established.
Known hypersensitivity to ACE-031, IgG1 Fc fusion proteins, or any formulation components.
Cardiovascular disease or history of stroke — vascular integrity compromise from BMP9/BMP10 blockade in subjects with pre-existing vascular disease is high risk.
Severe anemia — epistaxis-related blood loss may worsen anemia.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension — BMP9 and BMP10 are critical regulators of pulmonary vascular tone; blocking them may worsen PAH.
Pediatric use — the DMD trial that drove program discontinuation was in pediatric subjects; the vascular risk is not offset by muscle benefit in children.
History of hereditary angioedema or vascular fragility syndromes.
sideEffects: Epistaxis (spontaneous nosebleeds) — the primary and program-terminating adverse effect from clinical trials; directly caused by BMP9/BMP10 trapping disrupting nasal mucosal vascular integrity; onset typically within the first 2–4 weeks; severity ranges from minor to persistent bleeding requiring intervention.

Telangiectasias (dilated superficial blood vessels) — small, visible dilated capillaries on the skin and mucosal surfaces; a direct consequence of BMP9/BMP10 pathway disruption; may persist after cessation of ACE-031.
Injection site erythema and local reactions — redness, swelling, induration at subcutaneous injection site; reported in Phase 1 trials as the most common injection-related adverse event.
Headache — common; likely related to vasodilation from BMP9/BMP10 disruption and changes in cerebral vascular tone.
Elevated blood pressure or blood pressure variability — secondary to disrupted vascular endothelial signaling.
Nausea — mild; reported in Phase 1 data.
Fatigue — mild; self-resolving.
Dizziness — vasodilation-mediated; transient.

Theoretical long-term vascular remodeling — chronic BMP9/BMP10 blockade in animal models produces arteriovenous malformation-like lesions; human clinical exposure was too short to assess this risk fully.
Immunogenicity — ACE-031 is a fusion protein; anti-drug antibodies are possible with repeated administration, potentially reducing efficacy and causing hypersensitivity reactions.
Gum bleeding — oral mucosal vascular fragility from BMP9/BMP10 disruption.
Risk of pathological vascular shunting — theoretical; loss of arteriovenous boundary signaling.

records.name: Adamax
records.description: Adamax is a next-generation synthetic neuropeptide derivative of Semax created by substituting the standard N-terminal methionine residue with an adamantane-modified amino acid group — a bulky, highly lipophilic tricyclic carbon cage structure (adamantane) that profoundly increases CNS penetrance by dramatically improving blood-brain barrier permeability. Standard Semax, while active on peripheral TrkB receptors and capable of CNS effects through circumventricular organ entry, has limited direct BBB penetration due to its hydrophilic peptide character. The adamantane modification converts Adamax into an exceptionally lipophilic molecule that crosses the BBB freely, achieving CNS concentrations of the active pharmacophore that are estimated to be several-fold higher than equivalent doses of parent Semax. At these concentrations, Adamax drives BDNF gene transcription and TrkB receptor activation in cortical and hippocampal neurons with a magnitude that produces measurable neurogenesis, synaptic density increases, and CREB-mediated long-term potentiation gene expression at doses where Semax would produce only modest BDNF elevation. The MC4R melanocortin receptor activation that provides Semax's acute dopaminergic and attentional effects is similarly amplified by the improved CNS delivery — producing a more intense, faster-onset cognitive enhancement effect that is qualitatively described as substantially more potent than the parent compound. The neurogenic and cognitive-enhancing activity profile of Adamax makes it the highest-ceiling compound in the Category V neural group. The standard protocol doses (100–200mcg/day) are deliberately conservative, and the alternative escalation to 1,000mcg reflects the dose range at which the BDNF and neuroplasticity effects become most pronounced based on research use experience. BDNF elevation at these doses is not merely modulatory — it is robustly neurotrophic, activating the full downstream cascade from TrkB autophosphorylation through PI3K/Akt (neuronal survival), MAPK/ERK (synaptic plasticity), and PLCγ (Ca²⁺-mediated synaptic strength). The synergy with Cerebrolysin is mechanistically complementary rather than redundant: Adamax drives endogenous BDNF production and TrkB signaling from within the neuron, while Cerebrolysin delivers exogenous neuropeptide fragments including BDNF-like, NGF-like, GDNF-like, and CNTF-like bioactive components that activate the same downstream survival and plasticity cascades from outside the cell. Together they create a convergent neurotrophic signal that neither compound achieves alone — which is the mechanistic basis for their synergistic pairing. The contraindication with Semax is absolute and requires clear understanding. Semax and Adamax are not merely similar compounds — Adamax is a pharmacokinetically superior version of Semax acting on precisely the same receptors with greater potency and CNS access. Co-administering them provides no additional benefit across any target receptor while stacking the stimulant-adjacent adverse effects (MC4R-driven anxiety, cardiovascular activation, insomnia) and driving the TrkB receptor toward downregulation through sustained supraphysiological agonism. The half-life of approximately 1–2 hours means the acute CNS effects are relatively short-lived, requiring morning administration to prevent evening insomnia from residual MC4R activation. The 4-week washout after the 8-week cycle is essential: BDNF receptor downregulation at TrkB following prolonged high-dose agonism reduces subsequent cycle response, and the washout period allows receptor density to recover to baseline.

Late-day administration (after noon) — the half-life of 1–2 hours means direct receptor activity clears reasonably quickly, but the BDNF transcription and MC4R-driven arousal effects persist several hours; evening administration reliably causes insomnia.

Concurrent MAOI use — dopaminergic and serotonergic potentiation via MC4R creates serotonin/dopamine excess risk in the presence of monoamine oxidase inhibition.
Pregnancy — no safety data; BDNF signaling plays critical roles in fetal neural development; exogenous supraphysiological BDNF stimulation in utero is not established as safe.
Breastfeeding — no safety data.
sideEffects: Overstimulation — the most expected and dose-dependent adverse effect; characterized by racing thoughts, mental hyperactivity, inability to relax, mild euphoria at higher doses; a direct consequence of amplified MC4R-driven dopaminergic and noradrenergic tone from high CNS-penetrant delivery; managed with dose reduction or Selank co-administration.

Insomnia — MC4R arousal activation persists several hours beyond the short plasma half-life; any administration after noon or at doses above individual tolerance reliably produces sleep onset difficulty; morning-only strict dosing is the primary management.
Increased resting heart rate — mild tachycardia from adrenergic-adjacent MC4R activation; generally 5–10 BPM above baseline; typically well-tolerated but warrants monitoring.
Anxiety and irritability — common at doses above individual tolerance; mechanistically identical to Semax anxiety but with greater intensity due to enhanced CNS delivery.
Headache — reported in the initiation phase; possibly related to rapid changes in BDNF-driven cerebrovascular tone; typically self-limiting within the first week.

Hair shedding (rare) — BDNF elevation from Adamax, amplified relative to Semax, can accelerate hair follicle cycling and produce transient telogen effluvium; same mechanism as documented with Semax but potentially more pronounced.

TrkB receptor downregulation — the primary long-term risk of sustained high-dose administration without adequate washout; results in diminished response to subsequent Adamax or Semax cycles; the 4-week washout protocol is the mitigation strategy.
Nasal irritation — with intranasal administration specifically; not applicable to subcutaneous route.

Mild blood pressure elevation — from adrenergic-adjacent MC4R/dopaminergic activation; rarely clinically significant at standard doses but warrants monitoring in subjects with cardiovascular risk factors.

records.name: Adipotide (FTPP)
records.description: Adipotide, also known as FTPP (Fat-Targeted Proapoptotic Peptide) or Prohibitin-TP01, represents a fundamentally different category of fat loss compound than anything else in this database. Every other metabolic compound here works through appetite suppression, metabolic rate elevation, or lipolytic signaling — they make your body use fat differently. Adipotide physically destroys the blood supply to white adipose tissue, causing fat cells to die from ischemia. Its architecture is a dual-domain peptide: the N-terminal CKGGRAKDC homing domain binds specifically to prohibitin-1 and annexin A2 (ANXA2) receptors that are highly expressed on the endothelial cells of blood vessels supplying white adipose tissue. Once bound, the compound is internalized into those endothelial cells, where the C-terminal D(KLAKLAK)₂ proapoptotic domain disrupts mitochondrial membranes, triggers cytochrome c release, and initiates caspase-dependent apoptosis. The blood vessels collapse. The fat cells downstream die from lack of oxygen and nutrients. The dead tissue is cleared by the body's immune cleanup systems. This process is physically irreversible — fat tissue that is ablated does not regenerate those vascular structures. The landmark research data comes from a 2011 Science Translational Medicine study by Barnhart et al. using obese rhesus monkeys — one of the closest metabolic models to humans. Treated animals lost up to 38.7% of total body fat over the study period and demonstrated rapid, weight-independent improvements in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity — improvements that appeared before significant weight loss had occurred, suggesting direct metabolic signaling effects beyond simple fat removal. Subsequent mouse studies confirmed the fat loss results and identified an unexpected secondary effect: reduction in food intake, possibly secondary to disrupted adipokine signaling as fat mass is rapidly eliminated. Despite these impressive preclinical results, clinical development was formally discontinued as of 2019. The reason is the kidney. The fundamental challenge with adipotide is that renal tubular endothelial cells express sufficient prohibitin-1 receptors to allow off-target binding and internalization of the proapoptotic domain — meaning the same mechanism that kills fat cell vasculature also causes dose-dependent renal tubular injury. In the primate studies, all treated animals showed predictable, dose-related nephrotoxicity: elevated creatinine, proteinuria, and altered tubular function. The injury was described as largely reversible after treatment cessation, which is why the washout protocol includes mandatory equal time off to allow renal recovery. This is the defining safety constraint for any adipotide protocol: the kidneys are the limiting factor, not the fat loss efficacy. Aggressive hydration, baseline renal function labs, and strict cycle length enforcement are non-negotiable.

Mitigates severe renal stress while providing steady adipose tissue apoptosis.

Conditions requiring intact adipose tissue signaling — white adipose tissue is an endocrine organ; subjects with conditions dependent on leptin, adiponectin, or other adipokine homeostasis may experience severe metabolic disruption from rapid adipose ablation.

Severely underweight subjects or very low body fat — destruction of remaining adipose tissue may push subjects into ectopic fat deposition in organs (liver, muscle, pancreas) with paradoxically worse metabolic outcomes.
Diabetes mellitus on insulin or glucose-lowering agents without dose adjustment — rapid weight-independent improvements in insulin sensitivity may cause hypoglycemia without medication adjustment.
Pediatric use — safety and efficacy not established; absolutely contraindicated.
Dehydration or inability to maintain adequate fluid intake during protocol — dehydration dramatically amplifies nephrotoxicity.
sideEffects: Renal tubular injury — primary and most serious adverse effect; dose-dependent nephrotoxicity observed consistently across all treated animals in primate studies; off-target prohibitin binding in renal tubular endothelium triggers same apoptotic cascade as in adipose vasculature.
Elevated serum creatinine — direct marker of renal tubular injury; requires baseline labs and monitoring throughout cycle.
Proteinuria — increased protein excretion in urine indicating glomerular or tubular compromise; monitor via urinalysis.
Changes in urine output — decreased urine output may signal acute tubular injury; any sustained reduction warrants immediate cessation.
Severe dehydration — adipose tissue apoptosis and subsequent inflammation drive significant fluid shifts; aggressive hydration is mandatory throughout the protocol.

Excessive and potentially irreversible fat loss — the proapoptotic mechanism is not titrated precisely; subjects may lose more fat than intended, and destroyed adipose vasculature does not regenerate.

Ectopic fat deposition risk — if adipose storage capacity is significantly reduced without corresponding dietary changes, excess calories may be deposited in the liver, skeletal muscle, or pancreas, paradoxically worsening metabolic health.

Disrupted adipokine signaling — rapid destruction of white adipose tissue disrupts leptin, adiponectin, resistin, and other adipokine levels with unpredictable metabolic and appetite-regulating consequences.
Secondary appetite suppression — observed in mouse studies; possibly mediated by disrupted leptin signaling as fat mass is rapidly depleted; may result in inadequate caloric intake.
Rapid and unexpected improvements in insulin sensitivity — documented in primate studies independent of weight loss; may precipitate hypoglycemia in subjects on insulin or glucose-lowering agents.

Immune activation and inflammatory response — large-scale adipose tissue cell death releases cellular debris requiring immune clearance; potential for systemic inflammatory response in high-dose protocols.
Injection site reactions — localized inflammation at subcutaneous administration sites.
Fatigue — systemic inflammatory load from concurrent tissue apoptosis and immune cleanup.
No long-term human safety data exists — clinical development was discontinued; all safety information is derived from preclinical animal studies only.

records.name: AHK-Cu
records.description: AHK-Cu (alanyl-histidyl-lysyl copper complex, also known as Copper Tripeptide-3) is a synthetic copper-binding tripeptide structurally related to GHK-Cu but with a distinct amino acid sequence — alanine replaces glycine at the N-terminal position. This single substitution meaningfully shifts the compound's biological selectivity. While GHK-Cu operates as a broad-spectrum tissue regenerative signal, AHK-Cu is heavily biased toward endothelial cell activation and dermal papilla cell support, making it the preferred copper peptide for hair follicle regeneration and microvascular integrity. At the cellular level, AHK-Cu promotes dermal papilla cell (DPC) survival and proliferation, inhibits DHT-mediated follicle miniaturization by modulating androgen receptor sensitivity in follicular tissue, and stimulates angiogenesis around the hair bulb — the perifollicular vascular supply that determines follicle size and growth-phase duration. Research published in aesthetic dermatology journals shows AHK-Cu reduces apoptosis in dermal papilla cells by increasing anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 expression, reducing pro-apoptotic Bax, and decreasing cleaved caspase-3 and PARP fragmentation by 42.7% and 77.5% respectively — shifting the follicular environment decisively toward survival and active growth phase (anagen). The hair restoration mechanism of AHK-Cu is mechanistically complementary to but distinct from minoxidil and finasteride. Minoxidil extends the anagen phase via potassium channel opening and VEGF upregulation; finasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase to block DHT conversion. AHK-Cu operates upstream of both by directly supporting the structural biology of dermal papilla cells and improving the microvascular environment that determines follicle health, rather than manipulating hormonal or ion channel pathways. This means AHK-Cu can be stacked with minoxidil or finasteride protocols without mechanism competition or pharmacological conflict. The injectable form achieves systemic delivery to all follicle beds simultaneously — scalp, beard, and body hair — at a predictable plasma concentration, whereas topical AHK-Cu formulations are more localized but also well-documented in clinical aesthetics literature for scalp application. Like GHK-Cu, the injection site pain associated with subcutaneous AHK-Cu is significant and is caused by the copper ion component — described as burning, welting, and localized redness. The injected copper complex interacts with subcutaneous tissue in a manner that triggers a sharp inflammatory-sting response regardless of formulation or vehicle. Site rotation and co-injection with BPC-157 (borrowing the same GHK-Cu pain mitigation strategy) are the primary management approaches. The endothelial cell activation mechanism also provides general microvascular benefits beyond hair follicles — improved wound healing vascularity, cutaneous microcirculation support, and connective tissue repair — making AHK-Cu useful in broader aesthetic repair stacks alongside GHK-Cu and BPC-157.

rows.notes: Subcutaneous for systemic effect.

washout: Cycle Length: 8 weeks.
Washout: 4 weeks off.
contraindications: Wilson's disease or other genetic copper metabolism disorders — the injectable copper complex bypasses normal hepatic copper handling; contraindicated in any subject with impaired copper transport.
Known copper hypersensitivity or copper allergy — systemic injection may provoke significant immune/inflammatory reactions in copper-sensitive individuals.
Active malignancy — AHK-Cu promotes endothelial cell proliferation and angiogenesis; in the context of active cancer these mechanisms could support tumor vascularization.
Pregnancy — no human safety data; copper homeostasis is critical during fetal development.
Breastfeeding — no established safety data.
Known hypersensitivity to AHK-Cu or peptide excipients.
Concurrent use of copper-chelating agents (e.g., penicillamine, trientine, high-dose zinc) — will competitively neutralize the copper complex.
Elevated baseline serum copper levels or hemochromatosis — impaired metal homeostasis increases copper toxicity risk at injectable doses.
sideEffects: Severe Post-Injection Pain (PIP) and welting — the primary and expected adverse effect of subcutaneous AHK-Cu; burning, stinging, redness, and local welt formation at the injection site; copper ion-mediated; identical in mechanism to GHK-Cu PIP; mitigated by co-injection with BPC-157 and frequent site rotation.
Bruising and localized hematoma — common with daily administration; the 8-week cycle with rotation manages but does not eliminate this.
Local induration and redness — tissue copper deposition response; self-resolving between injections.
Copper toxicity at excessive doses — abdominal pain, metallic taste, nausea, vomiting, weakness, anemia; not expected at standard protocol doses but a risk with chronic accumulation.
Transient local hyperpigmentation — tyrosinase activation from copper delivery can produce pigment changes at injection sites; typically reversible.
Nausea — rare; copper-related at higher doses.
Headache — uncommon.
Mild systemic fatigue — reported in early weeks; related to angiogenic and remodeling signal activation.

records.name: AICAR
records.description: AICAR (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleoside, also known as acadesine) is a cell-permeable nucleoside analog that is phosphorylated intracellularly to ZMP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide) — a structural and functional mimetic of AMP (adenosine monophosphate). Because AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) is activated by elevated AMP:ATP ratios — the cellular signal of energy depletion — ZMP accumulation tricks AMPK into "believing" the cell is energy-depleted even in energy-replete conditions. The result is full activation of AMPK without the actual energy deficit that normally drives it. AMPK activation by AICAR produces a comprehensive metabolic shift: GLUT4 translocation to the muscle cell surface for enhanced glucose uptake, upregulation of fatty acid oxidation enzymes, suppression of mTOR (reducing protein synthesis but enhancing metabolic efficiency), activation of PGC-1α for mitochondrial biogenesis, and induction of the slow-twitch oxidative fiber gene expression program. This is the biological basis for AICAR being characterized as an exercise mimetic — it activates the molecular switch that exercise uses to produce its metabolic adaptations, independently of physical activity. The landmark 2008 studies by Evans and colleagues at the Salk Institute demonstrated that AICAR administration in mice increased their treadmill running capacity by 44% without any prior training — and that combining AICAR with the PPARδ agonist GW1516 produced a 77% increase in running endurance. These results, published in Cell, created significant attention to exercise mimetics as a therapeutic class and simultaneously placed AICAR on WADA's prohibited list for athletic competition. The clinical pharmacological background of AICAR extends well before peptide research interest: AICAR was originally developed by Gensia (later Fujisawa) as a cardioprotective agent for cardiac surgery — it reduces ischemia-reperfusion injury by adenosine mechanism and purine synthesis pathway modulation. This clinical history in cardiac surgery provides the safety data foundation for short-term human use that most compounds in this database lack: AICAR has been administered intravenously in multiple cardiology trials, giving a clinically validated safety profile at acute doses, though the subcutaneous research protocols used here are less formally characterized. The pharmacological distinction between AICAR and MOTS-c — both AMPK activators — is important for protocol design. AICAR activates AMPK directly through ZMP-AMP mimicry in a mechanistically upstream, cell-wide fashion. MOTS-c activates AMPK through a more targeted mitochondrial pathway (folate cycle AICAR accumulation) and also signals through nuclear translocation. The result is that while both compounds activate AMPK and produce complementary effects on fat oxidation, endurance, and glucose metabolism, they do so through different biochemical entry points — which is why their compatibility is synergistic rather than redundant. AICAR requires the largest raw dosing quantity of any compound in the database (10–25mg minimum effective dose vs. the microgram ranges of most peptides) because its mechanism requires intracellular phosphorylation to ZMP at concentrations sufficient to allosterically activate AMPK, which demands substantially higher extracellular loading.

rows.notes: Requires extremely large dosing protocols compared to standard peptides.
Initiation phase.
Escalation phase.
Peak phase.

washout: Cycle Length: 4 weeks max.
Washout: 4-8 weeks off. Short cycles recommended due to strain on metabolic pathways.
contraindications: Cardiovascular instability or active cardiac arrhythmia — AICAR affects cardiac adenosine metabolism and can influence heart rate and rhythm; contraindicated in subjects with unstable cardiac conditions.
Insulin therapy or sulfonylurea use without clinical supervision — AICAR's GLUT4 upregulation and glucose uptake enhancement creates additive hypoglycemia risk with insulin or insulin secretagogues.
Metformin use — both AICAR and metformin activate AMPK; overlapping activation intensifies the glucose-lowering and metabolic effects; monitor closely.

Gout or hyperuricemia — AICAR increases uric acid levels through purine catabolism pathway modulation; in subjects with gout, elevated baseline uric acid, or reduced renal uric acid clearance, AICAR may precipitate gout flares.
Renal impairment — AICAR and its metabolites are renally cleared; impaired elimination may cause accumulation and exaggerated pharmacological effects.

Active malignancy — AMPK activation has complex effects in cancer metabolism; AICAR's anti-proliferative effects have been noted in some cancer models, but its metabolic support of oxidative phosphorylation in other tumor types is not fully characterized.
Athletes competing under WADA anti-doping regulations — AICAR is explicitly listed on the WADA Prohibited List as an AMPK activator.
Known hypersensitivity to AICAR or nucleoside analog compounds.
Pregnancy — purine metabolism alteration is not established as safe in fetal development.
Breastfeeding — no safety data.
Severe hepatic impairment — AICAR metabolism and the downstream purine synthesis pathway changes may be unpredictable with impaired hepatic function.
sideEffects: Hypoglycemia — the most significant acute adverse effect; AICAR drives aggressive glucose uptake via GLUT4 in muscle tissue; risk is highest when dosed fasted without planned exercise; always pre-workout, always with subsequent energy expenditure.

Severe lethargy post-clearance — as AICAR washes out, the metabolic state driven by ZMP-induced AMPK activation resolves; a crash-like fatigue episode is reported by a majority of users after the dose clears, particularly with higher doses; this is a direct pharmacological consequence of the metabolic demand AICAR imposed.

Elevated uric acid (hyperuricemia) — a well-characterized adverse effect from clinical cardiology data; AICAR increases purine catabolism through its adenosine mechanism, elevating urate production; particularly relevant in subjects predisposed to gout.
Headache — commonly reported; possibly related to adenosine system activity and cerebral vasodilation effects.
Nausea — reported in clinical trial data at higher doses; dose-related.
Injection site irritation — redness, swelling, pain at subcutaneous injection site; the large doses required (10–25mg) mean larger injection volumes than most peptides.

Cardiac rhythm effects — AICAR modulates cardiac adenosine signaling, which has electrophysiological implications; generally mild at research doses but warrants monitoring in subjects with pre-existing arrhythmias.

Fatigue and muscle soreness — reported during the active dosing window as the metabolic program shifts; paradoxical given the "exercise mimetic" characterization but consistent with the metabolic reorganization.

Potential AMPK overstimulation impacting muscle protein synthesis — sustained mTOR suppression from prolonged AICAR use may impair muscle hypertrophy signaling; this is the mechanistic basis for the strict 4-week maximum cycle length.
Lactic acid accumulation at high doses — theoretical; AICAR at very high doses can saturate oxidative phosphorylation pathways and shift toward glycolytic energy production with lactate production.

records.name: Alprostadil
records.description: Alprostadil is synthetic prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) — a naturally occurring 20-carbon eicosanoid lipid mediator derived from dihomo-γ-linolenic acid through the cyclooxygenase pathway. Endogenous PGE1 is produced locally in penile vascular and cavernosal smooth muscle tissue where it acts on EP2 and EP4 prostaglandin receptors (Gs-coupled GPCRs) to activate adenylyl cyclase, increase intracellular cAMP, and activate protein kinase A — producing smooth muscle relaxation, vasodilation of the helicine arteries of the corpora cavernosa, and venous outflow restriction through sinusoidal dilation. This vascular mechanism produces erection through direct local hemodynamic control: blood flows into the corpora cavernosa faster than it drains, producing the intracorporeal pressure elevation that constitutes erection. Unlike PT-141 (central CNS arousal via MC4R) or PDE5 inhibitors (cGMP preservation via PDE5 blockade), alprostadil acts at the direct prostaglandin receptor level on the end-organ smooth muscle itself — making it effective in subjects where neither CNS arousal nor cGMP signaling are functional, including men with severe vascular disease, radical prostatectomy, spinal cord injury, and complete PDE5 inhibitor failure. This positioning as the final pharmacological tool for severe organic ED explains the "extreme intervention" language in the original description — alprostadil intracavernosal injection is FDA-approved (Caverject, Edex) for ED refractory to all other treatments and represents the standard of care before surgical penile prosthesis implantation. The administration route for alprostadil in the ED application is intracavernosal injection — direct injection into the corpus cavernosum of the penis — which is distinct from subcutaneous injection used for other compounds in this database. The intracavernosal route achieves immediate high local PGE1 concentrations at the target smooth muscle tissue without the systemic clearance that would attenuate the effect from peripheral subcutaneous administration. This route is highly effective but requires precise technique: the injection must be placed into the lateral aspect of the mid-shaft corpus cavernosum with a fine-gauge needle (27–30G), avoiding the midline dorsal vessels and urethra. The dose titration starting at 2.5mcg reflects the extreme potency of direct intracavernosal PGE1 — even a few micrograms in this tissue compartment produces full vasodilatory smooth muscle relaxation; dose escalation to 20mcg and beyond is done only in men with established vascular insufficiency where higher concentrations are needed to overcome the degree of smooth muscle fibrosis and vascular disease. The priapism risk with alprostadil is not rare or theoretical — it is the primary safety concern associated with every intracavernosal injection and the reason for the mandatory dose titration protocol starting at 2.5mcg. Prostaglandin E1 produces erection by sustaining corpus cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation; if the dose is too high, or if individual sensitivity is greater than expected, the venous outflow compression continues beyond the normal resolution window and the corpora cavernosa cannot re-empty. Ischemic priapism (high-pressure, low-flow) develops when erection duration exceeds 4 hours: without penile arterial inflow, cavernosal tissue becomes anoxic and acidotic, ultimately producing irreversible smooth muscle fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction if not treated within 6–8 hours. Emergency treatment consists of intracavernosal phenylephrine injection (alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction) or surgical shunting. This risk profile makes alprostadil the compound in this database with the highest consequence adverse event per dose — mandating the ultra-conservative starting dose and strict frequency limitations.

rows.notes: Extremely potent. Start at lowest possible dose (2.5mcg) and inject directly into the corpus cavernosum (intracavernosal).

washout: Cycle Length: Single use.
Washout: Do not exceed more than 3 times per week, with at least 24 hours between doses.
contraindications: Sickle cell anemia and sickle cell trait — the red blood cell sickling triggered by the hypoxic, acidotic environment of sustained erection dramatically increases the risk of ischemic priapism in sickle cell subjects; absolute contraindication.
Leukemia and other conditions with abnormal blood viscosity or hypercoagulability — abnormal blood cell populations obstructing cavernosal venous outflow create priapism risk independent of dose.
Multiple myeloma and polycythemia vera — hyperviscosity states increase intracavernosal stasis and priapism risk.
Thrombocytopenia or bleeding disorders — intracavernosal injection in subjects with impaired hemostasis creates risk of uncontrolled intracorporeal hematoma.
Concurrent anticoagulant therapy (warfarin, novel oral anticoagulants, therapeutic heparin) — same mechanism as bleeding disorder risk; must be weighed carefully.

Concurrent use with other vasoactive erectile agents (PDE5 inhibitors, PT-141 within 24 hours) — additive vasodilatory effects dramatically increase priapism risk; combination of intracavernosal alprostadil with oral PDE5 inhibitors is specifically warned against.

Penile anatomical abnormalities (severe Peyronie's disease with plaques, penile fibrosis, penile angulation) — intracavernosal injection into abnormal tissue carries injection complication risk and may not produce physiological erection.
Hypersensitivity to alprostadil, prostaglandin E1, or formulation excipients.
History of priapism — subjects who have previously had priapism (regardless of cause) are at substantially elevated risk of recurrence with alprostadil; use requires careful risk-benefit assessment.
Urethral stricture or conditions where urethral alprostadil is being used simultaneously — the intracavernosal and intraurethral routes must not be combined.
sideEffects: Penile pain at injection site — the most commonly reported adverse effect; occurs in approximately 30–50% of subjects with intracavernosal injection; caused by direct PGE1 nociceptor activation in cavernosal tissue (EP1 receptor stimulation); typically mild to moderate; the primary reason men discontinue intracavernosal therapy.

Priapism (prolonged erection > 4 hours) — the most serious adverse effect; ischemic priapism destroys cavernosal smooth muscle through hypoxia and acidosis; frequency approximately 1–5% per injection; higher with excessive doses; constitutes a urological emergency requiring immediate intervention; the driver of the mandatory starting dose of 2.5mcg.

Penile fibrosis and Peyronie's disease development — repeated intracavernosal injections at the same site cause chronic micro-trauma and fibrotic healing; produces penile curvature, plaques, and eventually impairs the erectile mechanism; site rotation and frequency limitation mitigate.
Hematoma at injection site — subcutaneous or intracorporeal bleeding from the injection; more common with poor technique or anticoagulation; managed with sustained pressure.

Hypotension — systemic absorption of PGE1 from intracavernosal administration produces peripheral vasodilation at higher doses; typically mild but symptomatic in subjects with cardiovascular disease or baseline hypotension.
Dizziness and lightheadedness — secondary to the mild hypotensive effect; positional changes during the active erection period should be managed carefully.
Urethral burning — if injection inadvertently contacts periurethral tissue; not characteristic of correct intracavernosal technique.

Prolonged or recurrent erection not reaching priapism threshold — erections lasting 2–4 hours that spontaneously resolve with activity, cold application, or mild exercise; a warning sign that dose reduction is warranted.
Penile ecchymosis — bruising along the penile shaft from extravasation of blood during injection; cosmetic; self-resolving.
Rare: systemic PGE1 effects (flushing, diaphoresis) at highest doses — more common with excessive doses or accidental intravascular injection.

records.name: Amino Lipotropic Complex (LC216)
records.description: The Amino Lipotropic Complex (product code LC216) is a broad-spectrum lipotropic and amino acid injection that expands on the basic MIC formula by adding performance and recovery aminos plus a fuller B-vitamin panel. It is a vitamin and amino acid blend rather than a peptide, working through nutritional and metabolic support pathways, and it is administered as a fixed direct dose without titration. Each milliliter contains L-Carnitine 20mg, L-Arginine 20mg, Methionine 25mg, Inositol 50mg, Choline 50mg, B6 (Pyridoxine) 25mg, B5 (Dexpanthenol) 25mg, and B12 (Methylcobalamin) 1mg. Carnitine, methionine, inositol, and choline provide the lipotropic fat-mobilization action, arginine supports nitric oxide production and blood flow, and the B6, B5, and B12 panel supports amino acid metabolism, energy production, and red blood cell formation. In practice, LC216 is used by people who want a more complete metabolic and recovery injection than a bare-bones MIC shot, combining fat-metabolism support with amino acids and a richer vitamin profile in a single administration. It appeals to users who are training hard and dieting simultaneously, since the arginine and B-vitamin content support circulation and energy while the lipotropic base supports fat processing. It is commonly run as a standing weekly injection during body-recomposition or fat-loss phases, and some users appreciate that the added inositol may also provide mild mood and stress-regulation benefits alongside its lipotropic role. As with all blends in this category, it is a support tool that performs best on top of a solid diet and training foundation. Mechanistically, LC216 layers four distinct actions into one shot: lipotropic fat transport (carnitine, methionine, choline, inositol), vasodilation and nutrient delivery (arginine via nitric oxide), coenzyme support for macronutrient metabolism (B5 and B6), and methylation plus energy support (B12). This combination is meant to support both fat loss and training recovery at once. Users should expect gradual, cumulative benefits rather than an acute effect, with the possible exception of the energy lift from B12. Morning administration is preferred because several components are mildly energizing. Injection sites should be rotated, and standard precautions for liver, kidney, and seizure history apply, with the added note that arginine can lower blood pressure and should be used cautiously by anyone on antihypertensive medication.

rows.notes: Direct-dose amino lipotropic injection with no titration required. A typical protocol is 0.5 to 1 mL administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly 2 to 3 times per week. Administer in the morning to avoid sleep disruption. Rotate injection sites each administration. Suitable for continuous use during recomposition or fat-loss phases.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to any component amino acid, vitamin, or formulation excipient.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding unless directed and supervised by a physician.
Active liver or kidney disease unless medically supervised.
History of seizures, as carnitine may lower the seizure threshold in susceptible individuals.
Uncontrolled low blood pressure or concurrent high-dose antihypertensive therapy, due to the arginine content.
sideEffects: Injection site irritation, redness, warmth, or tenderness.
Mild flushing or a warm sensation shortly after injection.
Lightheadedness from the vasodilatory effect of arginine.
Fishy body odor at higher choline intakes.
Nausea or mild gastrointestinal upset.
Increase in energy or restlessness if dosed late in the day.
Headache.

records.name: AOD-9604
records.description: AOD-9604 is a synthetic peptide derived from the C-terminal end of human growth hormone — specifically amino acids 177 through 191 of the full HGH molecule. The "AOD" stands for Anti-Obesity Drug, which reflects exactly what it was engineered to be. The rationale was straightforward: full HGH produces two types of effects — anabolic tissue-building effects driven by IGF-1 elevation, and lipolytic fat-burning effects driven by a specific region of the HGH molecule. AOD-9604 is that lipolytic region, isolated and slightly modified, stripped of all the anabolic and glycemic machinery that makes full HGH complicated to use. The result is a compound that stimulates fat breakdown (lipolysis) in adipocytes and inhibits new fat formation (lipogenesis) through beta-3 adrenergic receptor pathways, without meaningfully raising IGF-1, without affecting blood glucose or insulin sensitivity, and without the tissue growth effects of full HGH. Fasted administration is critical because insulin presence in the bloodstream directly competes with lipolytic signaling — eating before or shortly after pinning significantly blunts the compound's effect. AOD-9604 was taken through Phase 2 clinical trials for obesity in the 2000s, making it one of the few research peptides in this database with actual human trial data. Results showed meaningful reductions in body fat and triglycerides with an excellent tolerability profile comparable to placebo — the compound is genuinely well-tolerated by most subjects. However, it did not meet the commercial threshold for drug approval as a standalone obesity treatment, which is why it never reached Phase 3 as a pharmaceutical. Its effect size is modest compared to the GLP-1 class — researchers typically see incremental body composition improvements rather than dramatic weight loss numbers. This is important to set expectations correctly: AOD-9604 is a precision fat-burning tool, not a primary weight loss compound. It shines in the context of a broader protocol where its specific lipolytic mechanism adds a distinct layer that GLP-1 agonists and GH secretagogues do not directly provide. The practical niche for AOD-9604 is as a synergistic adjunct in GH axis and metabolic protocols. It stacks particularly well with CJC-1295 (No DAC) and Ipamorelin because those compounds stimulate natural GH pulses — which elevates systemic lipolytic activity — while AOD-9604 provides direct, receptor-level fat cell targeting simultaneously. When added to an active GLP-1 protocol, it contributes a fat-specific lipolytic mechanism that operates independently of GLP-1 receptor saturation. The reconstitution requirement is important: AOD-9604 requires an acidic pH environment to prevent gelation, which is why the recommended reconstitution is 1/3 acetic acid to 2/3 bacteriostatic water. Standard bacteriostatic water alone will cause the peptide to clump and become ineffective. Its short ~3-hour half-life means the fasted window post-injection matters more for this compound than for almost any other in this database.

rows.notes: AM upon waking preferred, do not eat 2-4 hrs post pinning.
AM upon waking preferred, do not eat 2-4 hrs post pinning.
AM upon waking preferred, do not eat 2-4 hrs post pinning.
AM upon waking and PM 1hr post meal, do not eat 2-4 hrs post pinning.

Concurrent use with Adipotide — both compounds target adipose tissue through distinct destructive or disruptive mechanisms; combined use creates unpredictable and potentially dangerous systemic fat cell stress.
Concurrent use with AOD-CJC-IPA blend — results in double-dosing of AOD-9604 within the same protocol.
Pregnancy — safety not established; potential fetal risk.
Breastfeeding — safety not established.
Known hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis to AOD-9604 or formulation excipients.
Severe hepatic impairment — limited metabolic clearance data.
Severe renal impairment — limited clearance data; dehydration risk.
Endocrine disorders involving active GH excess (e.g., acromegaly) — additive lipolytic GH pathway stimulation.

Diabetes mellitus requiring tight glycemic management — while AOD-9604 does not directly alter glucose, rapid systemic lipolysis releases free fatty acids that may transiently affect insulin sensitivity in brittle diabetics.

Nausea — reported in approximately 8.4% of subjects; typically mild and transient.
Headache — reported in approximately 6.7% of subjects; often dose-related and more common at the 500mcg dose.
Fatigue or lethargy during the adaptation period — reported in approximately 5.3% of subjects.
Dizziness — reported in approximately 3.8% of subjects.
Flushing — transient warmth or redness, particularly following injection; attributed to beta-3 adrenergic activation.
Transient changes in appetite — increased or decreased hunger during early protocol stages; inconsistent across subjects.
Gelation-related injection issues — failure to reconstitute with acetic acid/bacteriostatic water blend results in a gelled, ineffective solution that causes unnecessary injection site irritation.
Blunted efficacy from feeding — eating within 2 hours post-injection significantly reduces lipolytic effect; not a side effect per se but a primary protocol compliance risk.
Allergic reactions — rare; localized rash or itching at injection site.

records.name: Ara-290
records.description: ARA-290 is a synthetic 11-amino acid peptide engineered from the helix B region of erythropoietin (EPO) — the specific structural surface of the EPO protein that activates the Innate Repair Receptor (IRR), a heterodimeric receptor complex consisting of the EPO receptor (EPOR) and the beta-common receptor (βcR, also known as CD131). This receptor complex is fundamentally distinct from the classical homodimeric EPOR that drives erythropoiesis: the IRR is expressed on neurons, Schwann cells, immune cells, pancreatic beta cells, and other non-hematopoietic tissues where it mediates tissue protection, nerve repair, and anti-inflammatory signaling — completely independent of red blood cell production. ARA-290 was engineered with the specific design goal of separating EPO's tissue-protective activity from its erythropoietic activity: it binds the IRR with high affinity and activates its downstream cytoprotective and neural repair signals while having essentially no activity at the classical erythropoiesis-driving EPOR homodimer. This means ARA-290 achieves EPO's profound neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects without any of the blood-thickening, hematocrit-elevating, thrombotic risk that makes full EPO dangerous. The primary research application driving interest in ARA-290 is small fiber neuropathy (SFN) — a condition characterized by degeneration and loss of the small unmyelinated and thinly myelinated nerve fibers (C-fibers and Aδ-fibers) that carry pain, temperature, and autonomic signals in the skin and viscera. Small fiber neuropathy produces chronic neuropathic pain, burning, tingling, allodynia, and autonomic dysfunction, and has few effective treatments because most existing neuropathic agents only manage symptoms without addressing the underlying nerve degeneration. ARA-290 activates IRR on Schwann cells and dorsal root ganglion neurons, driving remyelination, axonal regeneration, and survival of the small fiber population through PI3K/Akt and MAPK signaling downstream of βcR activation. Clinical Phase 2 data from Heijenbrok et al. and Brines et al. in subjects with diabetic and sarcoidosis-associated SFN demonstrated statistically significant improvements in intraepidermal nerve fiber density (the gold-standard biopsy measure of small fiber integrity), pain scores, and autonomic function — providing the most direct human clinical evidence for nerve fiber regeneration from any peptide in this database. The IRR-mediated anti-inflammatory activity of ARA-290 parallels its neural repair mechanism: βcR activation on macrophages and dendritic cells suppresses NFκB-driven pro-inflammatory cytokine production (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-12) while promoting regulatory T-cell differentiation and IL-10 production, producing an anti-inflammatory phenotype shift similar to but mechanistically distinct from KPV. This dual neural repair/anti-inflammatory activity makes ARA-290 synergistically valuable alongside BPC-157 and TB-500: BPC-157 drives angiogenesis, collagen synthesis, and musculoskeletal repair through GABAergic and NO-signaling pathways; TB-500 mobilizes thymosin beta-4 for actin cytoskeletal cell migration and vascular repair; ARA-290 specifically addresses the neural component of tissue repair — Schwann cell function, nerve fiber regeneration, and the neuroinflammatory component of chronic neuropathic conditions — that neither BPC-157 nor TB-500 directly targets. The synergy designation reflects these orthogonal but complementary repair mechanisms converging on complete tissue restoration including the neural architecture.

Aggressive protocol. Maximum 4 weeks.

Active malignancy with EPO receptor expression — while ARA-290 does not drive erythropoiesis, certain tumors express IRR components (βcR) and could theoretically receive pro-survival IRR signaling; caution in oncological contexts.
Concurrent full-dose EPO administration — ARA-290 and EPO may compete at the EPOR/βcR receptor complex; combined use is not characterized.
Pregnancy — IRR signaling in fetal tissue development is not characterized; safety not established.
Breastfeeding — no safety data.
Pediatric use — no safety or dosing data established.
Autoimmune conditions currently treated with immunosuppressive biologics — ARA-290's immunomodulatory activity may interact unpredictably with concurrent biologic immunosuppression.

Mild transient fatigue — reported in a subset of subjects during the first week; possibly related to the acute neuroinflammatory modulation phase.
Mild headache — uncommon; transient; mechanism not characterized.
Transient dizziness — rare; mild; possibly related to βcR-mediated vasodilatory activity in some subjects.
Nausea — uncommon; mild; self-limiting.

No erythropoietic effects — ARA-290 has no meaningful activity at the classical EPOR homodimer that drives red blood cell production; hematocrit and hemoglobin are not elevated; there is no thrombotic or polycythemia risk.

records.name: BPC-157
records.description: BPC-157 (Body Protective Compound-157) is a synthetic pentadecapeptide — a 15 amino acid sequence derived from a larger protein found in human gastric juice. It is entirely lab-synthesized and does not exist at functional concentrations in endogenous physiology, but it is structurally derived from the native gastric protein BPC, which is part of the stomach's intrinsic cytoprotective system. BPC-157 has the largest preclinical research base of any compound in this database, with hundreds of published animal studies spanning musculoskeletal repair, gastrointestinal healing, neurological protection, and cardiovascular effects. Its primary mechanisms operate through two major pathways: upregulation of VEGF (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor) signaling via VEGFR2 receptor activation, which drives angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation) and accelerates microvascular repair; and activation of the Akt/eNOS pathway to increase endothelial nitric oxide production, which promotes vasodilation, reduces inflammation, and stabilizes endothelial integrity. Downstream from these two drivers, BPC-157 also markedly enhances fibroblast activity — the cells responsible for collagen synthesis in connective tissue — accelerating structural repair of tendons, ligaments, cartilage, and muscle at rates consistently 2–4x faster than control groups in tendon transection animal models. The scope of BPC-157's documented research effects is unusually broad for a single compound: tendon and ligament healing, intestinal permeability repair (leaky gut), gastric ulcer healing, bone fracture repair, nerve regeneration, systemic inflammation reduction, and dopamine system modulation (the "Dopamine Buffer" property reflects findings that BPC-157 normalizes dopamine activity in animal models of addiction and stress — reducing hyperdopaminergic states and preventing hypodopaminergic crashes). This last property has led to research interest in BPC-157 for post-stimulant recovery protocols and neurological stabilization. The gut-healing applications are mechanistically consistent with its gastric origin — BPC-157 repairs gastric and intestinal mucosal damage with remarkable speed in NSAID-injury, alcohol-injury, and inflammatory bowel models, and is uniquely stable in gastric acid, unlike most peptides. Despite the extraordinary depth of its preclinical data, BPC-157 has essentially no published randomized controlled clinical trial data in humans — it has not progressed through formal FDA clinical trials. This gap between the preclinical evidence base and clinical validation is the defining limitation of BPC-157. All human use exists in a regulatory grey area of clinical observation and patient-reported outcomes. The angiogenesis-promoting mechanism is the central safety concern: in a healthy context, new vessel formation accelerates healing; in a subject with subclinical or active cancer, the same angiogenic drive could promote tumor vascularization and growth. This makes cancer history the absolute contraindication it is.

records.name: BPC-157 + TB-500
records.description: The BPC-157 + TB-500 blend is the foundational systemic healing combination in the research peptide field — a 1:1 ratio co-lyophilized blend (available in 10mg and 20mg vials, both providing equal parts of each compound) that pairs two mechanistically distinct and complementary tissue repair compounds into a single injection event. BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound 157) is a synthetic 15-amino acid pentadecapeptide (Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val) derived from a cytoprotective protein isolated from human gastric juice; its primary healing mechanism operates through VEGFR2 (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2) activation to drive therapeutic angiogenesis — the growth of new capillary networks into hypoxic, ischemic, or damaged tissue beds, restoring the oxygen and nutrient delivery without which wound healing cannot progress beyond the inflammatory phase. BPC-157's angiogenic mechanism is complemented by: nitric oxide synthase (NOS) pathway normalization in injured endothelium (restoring endothelial NO production to re-establish vasodilatory capacity), potent NF-κB and STAT3 pathway suppression (producing anti-inflammatory effects that resolve the acute inflammatory phase and enable tissue regeneration), direct fibroblast proliferation stimulation, upregulation of growth factor receptor expression (EGFR, TGF-βR) in wound fibroblasts, and uniquely among healing peptides, a dopaminergic modulatory mechanism — BPC-157 normalizes dopamine D1/D2 receptor expression, DOPAC/HVA dopamine metabolite ratios, and dopamine turnover in striatal and mesolimbic circuits, which is the pharmacological basis for both its mood-regulating secondary effects and the "Dopamine Buffer" property tag. TB-500 acts through a distinct but functionally complementary mechanism: Thymosin Beta-4 (the full sequence; TB-500 is the research peptide fragment containing the active Ac-SDKP motif and surrounding sequence) sequesters G-actin monomers through its LKKTET actin-binding motif, modulating the G-actin/F-actin equilibrium in tissue repair cells (keratinocytes, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, cardiac repair cells) to promote directional cell migration — the active movement of repair cells from wound margins into the wound bed that is the rate-limiting step of the remodeling phase of wound healing after the initial inflammatory response subsides. The mechanistic complementarity of BPC-157 and TB-500 covers the complete sequence of tissue repair phases. Acute inflammatory phase: BPC-157's NF-κB suppression and prostaglandin-independent cytoprotective activity resolve excessive inflammation that would otherwise produce chronic wound states; TB-500's Ac-SDKP fragment has documented anti-inflammatory activity through NF-κB suppression via an independent pathway. Proliferative/granulation phase: BPC-157's VEGFR2-driven angiogenesis builds the vascular scaffold that new granulation tissue requires; TB-500's cell migration facilitation moves fibroblasts and keratinocytes into the vascular scaffold to begin matrix deposition. Remodeling phase: BPC-157's fibroblast EGFR and TGF-βR upregulation drives matrix deposition and cross-linking; TB-500's continued actin dynamics support maintains the contractile fibroblast (myofibroblast) phenotype required for wound contraction and scar maturation. The 1:1 ratio is empirically derived from the research community's extensive use experience — both compounds contribute equally essential mechanisms without one requiring a higher molar ratio than the other. The two available vial sizes (10mg and 20mg) represent different absolute dose pools with identical ratios; the standard protocol doses remain the same regardless of vial size, with the 20mg vial simply providing a longer supply at the same daily dose before reconstitution. The "Injury Protocol" alternative titration (1mg–3mg two to three times daily for 8+ weeks, injected as close to the injury site as safely possible) represents the highest-intensity application of BPC-TB — the maximum acute post-surgical or severe injury recovery protocol. The site-proximity injection guidance is based on BPC-157's demonstrated enhanced efficacy in animal models when injected in close proximity to the injury site versus systemic distal injection — local angiogenic and fibroblast activation effects are concentration-dependent and site-localized; while the systemic distribution of subcutaneous injection provides whole-body healing support, perilesional injection concentrates the VEGFR2 signaling at the tissue that most requires angiogenic support. This is a principle not applicable to most peptides in this database but specifically documented for BPC-157 given the VEGFR2-mediated angiogenic mechanism that is most potent at the local concentration achieved by proximity injection.

records.name: Bronchogen
records.description: Bronchogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu) Khavinson bioregulator derived from bronchial and lung tissue polypeptide extracts — identified as the bioactive core sequence responsible for the bronchial epithelial repair, respiratory mucosa regeneration, and pulmonary function-supporting activity of the native lung tissue extract. The respiratory epithelium that lines the bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli is among the most exposed and metabolically stressed epithelial surfaces in the body: it encounters approximately 10,000–20,000 liters of air per day containing particulates, pathogens, oxidants, pollutants, and allergens while simultaneously maintaining the gas exchange efficiency, mucociliary clearance, and barrier function that protect the entire respiratory tract. Bronchial epithelial cells — particularly ciliated columnar epithelial cells, Clara (Club) cells, and mucus-producing goblet cells — undergo accelerated functional decline with cumulative oxidative exposure, smoking, air pollution, recurrent infection, and normal aging. The age-related decline in bronchial tissue homeostasis manifests as reduced mucociliary clearance velocity, impaired epithelial barrier integrity, reduced secretory IgA production, decreased bronchial epithelial regenerative capacity following injury, and loss of the normal Clara cell secreted protein (CC16/CCSP) anti-inflammatory activity that protects the lower respiratory tract. Bronchogen acts as a bioregulator at the bronchial epithelial cell level — interacting with epithelial cell surface receptors and transcription factors to normalize the gene expression programs governing ciliary function, mucus composition, barrier integrity, and the anti-inflammatory secretory profile of the respiratory epithelium. The clinical research context for Bronchogen in the Khavinson literature demonstrates applications in two primary populations: aging subjects with declining respiratory reserve and subjects with chronic inflammatory respiratory disease. In aging subjects, Bronchogen administration produced improvements in spirometric lung function parameters (FEV1/FVC ratio, peak flow), enhanced mucociliary clearance as measured by saccharin transit time, normalization of bronchial epithelial cytology toward healthier regenerative profiles, and reduction in the frequency of respiratory infections — consistent with restored barrier function and mucociliary defense. In subjects with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and chronic bronchitis, Bronchogen cycles produced reductions in airway inflammation markers, improvements in exercise tolerance, reduction in exacerbation frequency, and improvement in quality-of-life respiratory symptom scores. The synergy designation with Chonluten reflects a complementary tissue-level relationship: Bronchogen targets the bronchial epithelium of the conducting airway (the tube walls, mucociliary apparatus, and barrier function), while Chonluten targets the alveolar epithelium and lung parenchyma where gas exchange occurs — together providing comprehensive coverage of the respiratory system from the large airways down to the alveolar gas exchange surface. The bedtime dosing window (2 hours after last meal) is the most specifically prescribed administration timing of any Khavinson bioregulator in this database. This timing reflects two factors: the respiratory system undergoes maximal parasympathetic-dominant repair activity during sleep (reduced respiratory rate, reduced airway inflammation, increased repair cytokine activity, maximal mucociliary clearance activity during slow-wave sleep), providing the ideal physiological context for bioregulator-driven gene program normalization; and the 2-hours-post-meal restriction ensures the peptide is absorbed in a non-competing digestive environment where gastric acid and proteolytic enzyme activity from the fed state have subsided, improving bioavailability through reduced peptide degradation in the gastrointestinal environment encountered during subcutaneous absorption.

records.name: Cagrilintide
records.description: Cagrilintide is a long-acting amylin analog — and amylin is a hormone most people have never heard of despite it being one of the body's most important satiety signals. Amylin is co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells every time you eat, and its job is to signal the brain that food has arrived: it slows gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon, and most critically, activates appetite-regulating centers in the area postrema and hindbrain to create a durable feeling of fullness. Cagrilintide is an engineered analog of this hormone — modified to last a full week on a single subcutaneous injection, versus native amylin which clears in minutes. What makes cagrilintide pharmacologically distinct from every other compound in the incretin category is that it does not touch the GLP-1 receptor at all. It operates on an entirely separate hormonal pathway, which means it produces satiety through a completely different mechanism than semaglutide, tirzepatide, or any other GLP-1 compound. This mechanistic independence is the entire reason cagrilintide is so valuable as a stacking agent. When you combine it with a GLP-1 agonist like semaglutide, you are not doubling up on the same pathway — you are hitting appetite suppression from two separate angles simultaneously, producing additive effects that neither compound achieves alone. The Phase 3 REDEFINE-1 trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025, confirmed this directly: CagriSema (the fixed co-formulation of cagrilintide 2.4mg + semaglutide 2.4mg) produced 20.4% mean body weight loss at 68 weeks versus 3% for placebo — results that meaningfully exceeded semaglutide alone. Cagrilintide also appears to work through leptin re-sensitization, which is particularly relevant for subjects with leptin resistance where GLP-1 agonists alone produce diminishing returns. As monotherapy, cagrilintide achieved weight loss comparable to semaglutide in head-to-head data, which is remarkable for a single-receptor amylin agent. The primary risk unique to cagrilintide is its gastric-slowing effect stacking on top of existing GLP-1 compound protocols. When used alone it is well-tolerated, but when layered onto an active semaglutide or tirzepatide protocol, the combined gastric emptying delay can become clinically significant — producing extreme fullness, inability to consume adequate calories, and in some cases near-complete gastric paralysis at higher doses of both compounds. This is why the micro-stacking protocol starting at 0.125mg to 0.25mg weekly is so important when combining it with any GLP-1 agonist: the doses need to be titrated together carefully, not each at their standalone maximum. The CagriSema fixed combination is listed as contraindicated with standalone cagrilintide specifically to prevent accidental dual-dosing of the same compound.

records.name: CagriSema (Cagrilintide + Semaglutide)
records.description: CagriSema is a co-lyophilized fixed-ratio combination of Cagrilintide (a long-acting amylin analog) and Semaglutide (a GLP-1 receptor agonist) at a 1:1 ratio — in this database, a 10mg vial providing 5mg of each compound. The dual-receptor mechanism is pharmacologically distinct from any single-agent metabolic compound: Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors (GLP-1R) in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus and brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), producing POMC/CART neuron activation that reduces appetite, increases satiety signaling, and slows gastric emptying through vagal afferent suppression; Cagrilintide activates amylin receptors (AMY1, AMY2, AMY3 — heterodimers of calcitonin receptor with receptor activity-modifying proteins RAMP1-3) primarily in the area postrema and NTS, producing satiety signaling, nutrient sensing enhancement, and further gastric emptying delay through a completely independent neuroanatomical pathway. The additive and potentially synergistic satiety effect from two non-overlapping receptor systems targeting the same downstream endpoints (appetite reduction, reduced caloric intake, metabolic rate support) is the mechanistic rationale for the CagriSema combination — both pathways converge on hypothalamic satiety circuits but through distinct receptor systems, preventing the receptor downregulation tachyphylaxis that single-agent therapy develops over time. The Novo Nordisk Phase III REDEFINE trial program for CagriSema demonstrated weight loss of approximately 22.7% of body weight at 68 weeks at the full 2.4mg/2.4mg weekly dose — exceeding semaglutide (Wegovy) monotherapy weight loss of approximately 15% in the STEP trials and confirming the additive mechanistic synergy between GLP-1R and amylin receptor pathways. The pharmacokinetic rationale for the 1:1 co-lyophilization is grounded in the comparable elimination half-lives of the two components: Semaglutide's half-life of approximately 168 hours (7 days) and Cagrilintide's half-life of approximately 160–168 hours are closely matched, making weekly co-administration pharmacokinetically rational — both compounds accumulate to steady-state over approximately 4–5 weeks of weekly dosing and maintain matched plasma concentration profiles through the dosing interval. The co-lyophilized vial format preserves both peptides in a single reconstitutable lyophilized cake, with stability validated for the combined formulation. The dose escalation protocol from 0.25mg of each compound (0.5mg total weekly) to 2.4mg of each compound (4.8mg total weekly) follows the Novo Nordisk clinical trial titration schedule, with each dose step providing 4 weeks for gastrointestinal tolerance adaptation before escalation — a critical safety feature given the additive gastroparesis-inducing potential of both components when combined. The biohacker split-dosing alternative (every 3.5 days rather than weekly) is pharmacokinetically supported: while semaglutide's 7-day half-life is well-suited to weekly dosing, the twice-weekly split flattens the peak serum concentration seen on Days 1–3 post-injection (the period of maximal gastric paralysis and nausea in weekly dosing subjects) by reducing the peak-to-trough ratio, at the cost of twice-weekly injection convenience. The interaction profile and contraindication list for CagriSema inherits the complete contraindication sets of both Semaglutide and Cagrilintide simultaneously. The thyroid C-cell tumor risk associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists (Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma/MEN2 contraindication) is carried entirely by the Semaglutide component — amylin receptors do not have a demonstrated thyroid C-cell tumor risk. The gastroparesis contraindication is additive: both GLP-1R agonism and amylin receptor agonism independently delay gastric emptying through independent vagal and area postrema mechanisms; in subjects with pre-existing gastroparesis, the combined gastric motility inhibition of CagriSema can produce severe gastric stasis, aspiration risk, and medically significant impaired gastric function. The contraindication list for other incretin/metabolic agents (semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide, mazdutide, survodutide, liraglutide, cagrilintide individually, adipotide) reflects the fundamental principle that CagriSema already contains the maximum reasonable GLP-1R and amylin receptor loading — stacking additional incretin or dual/triple agonists on top of CagriSema would produce pharmacological redundancy on the GLP-1R (for semaglutide, liraglutide, and the GLP-1 component of tirzepatide/retatrutide/mazdutide) and additive risks without additive benefit.
