contraindications: Personal or family history of Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC) — the GLP-1 receptor agonist (Semaglutide) component carries a class-level FDA boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumor risk based on rodent carcinogenicity data; MTC risk in humans is not established but the warning applies to all GLP-1RAs; personal or family history of MTC is an absolute contraindication.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN2) — MEN2 patients have a near-universal predisposition to MTC; the GLP-1RA component's thyroid C-cell stimulation is absolutely contraindicated in this genetic syndrome.

Pre-existing gastroparesis (any severity) — both Semaglutide (via GLP-1R-mediated vagal suppression of gastric motility) and Cagrilintide (via amylin receptor-mediated area postrema and vagal gastric emptying delay) independently inhibit gastric emptying; in subjects with pre-existing gastroparesis, the combined gastric motility inhibition of CagriSema can produce severe gastric stasis, vomiting, aspiration, and medically significant deterioration of gastric function; absolute contraindication.

Active pancreatitis or history of pancreatitis — GLP-1 receptor agonists carry a class-level association with acute pancreatitis; history of pancreatitis is a relative-to-absolute contraindication depending on clinical context.

Concurrent use of other GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) — CagriSema already contains a full-dose GLP-1RA; adding a second GLP-1RA produces receptor saturation without additional benefit and magnifies all GLP-1-mediated adverse effects.

Concurrent use of tirzepatide, retatrutide, mazdutide, or survodutide — these compounds contain GLP-1R agonist components; combining with CagriSema produces redundant GLP-1R loading, significantly elevated gastroparesis risk, and additive nausea/vomiting without therapeutic benefit beyond CagriSema alone.

Concurrent cagrilintide (standalone) — CagriSema already contains the full amylin receptor agonist component; adding standalone Cagrilintide produces amylin receptor saturation and magnifies all amylin-mediated adverse effects.

Severe renal impairment (eGFR <15 ml/min) — the pharmacokinetics of both components in severe renal failure require dose adjustment or avoidance; GLP-1RA-associated nausea and dehydration in subjects with severely compromised renal function carries acute kidney injury risk.
Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) — semaglutide pharmacokinetics are not significantly altered by liver disease but severe hepatic impairment context warrants medical supervision.
Known hypersensitivity to semaglutide, cagrilintide, or any formulation excipients.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding — weight loss pharmacotherapy is contraindicated during pregnancy; the fetal effects of GLP-1RA and amylin agonist exposure are not established and significant weight loss during pregnancy carries fetal risk.

Concurrent insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas, meglitinides) without dose adjustment — GLP-1RA-mediated enhancement of glucose-dependent insulin secretion combined with insulin secretagogues increases hypoglycemia risk requiring dose adjustment of the secretagogue.

Pre-surgical procedures requiring general anesthesia — the profound gastric emptying delay of CagriSema increases aspiration risk under general anesthesia; a minimum 7-day (ideally 14-day) cessation period before elective general anesthesia is required.

Adipotide — concurrent use of a proapoptotic adipose-targeting compound adds significant metabolic stress to the already profound caloric restriction and adipose loss of CagriSema; combined use without medical supervision carries risks of excessive fat mass depletion, electrolyte imbalance, and renal stress.
sideEffects: Severe delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis-like syndrome) — the most clinically significant adverse effect unique to CagriSema versus semaglutide monotherapy; the additive GLP-1R and amylin receptor gastric motility inhibition produces markedly more pronounced and prolonged gastric stasis than semaglutide alone; manifests as persistent post-meal fullness, early satiety, nausea for 24–48 hours post-injection, and in severe cases, inability to tolerate solid food for days following the weekly dose.

Nausea and vomiting — most severe in the first 4–8 weeks of each dose escalation step; the incidence and severity exceed semaglutide monotherapy due to the additive amylin receptor contribution to nausea signaling in the area postrema; typically improves within 2–4 weeks at each dose level.
Fatigue and asthenia — commonly reported during dose escalation; related to caloric restriction, altered nutrient absorption timing, and possible direct central effects of amylin receptor agonism.

Hypoglycemia (in the context of severe caloric restriction) — CagriSema itself does not directly cause hypoglycemia in non-diabetic subjects as GLP-1 receptor agonism is glucose-dependent; however, the profound appetite suppression and caloric restriction achieved on CagriSema can drive blood glucose to low-normal or mildly hypoglycemic values in subjects who do not compensate with adequate carbohydrate intake; more significant in subjects with concurrent insulin secretagogue use.
Constipation — common; secondary to the profound slowing of gastrointestinal motility from both components; can be severe and require active management (osmotic laxatives, adequate hydration, fiber).
Diarrhea — paradoxically, some subjects experience diarrhea alternating with constipation as gastric motility patterns change during dose escalation.

Injection site reactions — subcutaneous injection site erythema, bruising, or nodule formation; more common than semaglutide monotherapy possibly related to the higher concentration of the co-formulated product.

Muscle mass loss (lean body mass depletion) — the most clinically important body composition concern; the profound caloric deficit produced by CagriSema, if not actively managed with adequate protein intake and resistance exercise, produces significant skeletal muscle loss alongside fat loss; anabolic support compounds (GH secretagogues, IGF-1 axis compounds) are frequently co-administered to mitigate this effect.

Hair thinning (telogen effluvium) — commonly reported during rapid weight loss periods; secondary to the metabolic stress of significant caloric restriction rather than a direct pharmacological effect of either compound; typically reversible.

Elevated resting heart rate — a class-level effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists; Semaglutide increases mean resting heart rate by 2–4 BPM; typically not clinically significant but warrants monitoring in subjects with pre-existing tachyarrhythmias.

Gallstones and biliary disease — GLP-1 receptor agonists increase gallstone formation risk related to rapid weight loss and altered gallbladder motility; risk is amplified with the accelerated weight loss of CagriSema versus semaglutide monotherapy.
Acute pancreatitis (rare) — the class-level GLP-1RA pancreatitis association; subjects should be aware of persistent severe abdominal pain as a warning sign requiring immediate medical evaluation.

records.name: Cardiogen
records.description: Cardiogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg) Khavinson bioregulator derived from cardiac muscle polypeptide extracts — identified as the bioactive core sequence responsible for the cardioprotective and cardiomyocyte regenerative activity of the native heart tissue extract. The heart is a post-mitotic organ in which adult cardiomyocytes have extremely limited regenerative capacity — the human heart replaces approximately 1% of cardiomyocytes per year, declining further with age, meaning that ischemic cardiomyocyte loss and age-related cardiomyocyte functional decline cannot be meaningfully compensated by endogenous regeneration alone. This regenerative deficit underlies the progressive nature of heart failure following myocardial injury and the cumulative functional decline of cardiac output with aging. Cardiogen acts at the cardiomyocyte level as a tissue bioregulator — interacting with cardiomyocyte-specific transcription factors and cell surface receptors to normalize the gene expression programs governing myocardial function, including the contractile protein synthesis pathways (myosin heavy chain isoform expression, troponin stoichiometry), mitochondrial biogenesis in cardiomyocytes (which are among the most mitochondria-dense cells in the body, deriving 90% of ATP from oxidative phosphorylation), and anti-apoptotic survival pathways that protect existing cardiomyocytes from stress-induced cell death. The bedtime dosing window reflects both the circadian-gated nature of myocardial repair processes (cardiomyocyte autophagy, mitochondrial turnover, and DNA repair are most active during sleep-associated reduction in metabolic demand) and the established cardiac biorhythm research showing that regenerative interventions timed to the cardiac circadian program achieve better tissue uptake and response. The clinical research context for Cardiogen in the Khavinson literature spans multiple cardiovascular disease states. Studies demonstrated that Cardiogen administration in subjects with ischemic heart disease and post-myocardial infarction cardiomyopathy produced: improvements in echocardiographic parameters of systolic and diastolic function, reduction in NT-proBNP (a validated biomarker of myocardial wall stress and heart failure severity), normalization of cardiomyocyte electrical conduction properties as measured by ECG parameters, and reduction in arrhythmia frequency in subjects with aging-associated rhythm disturbances. In animal models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, Cardiogen pretreatment reduced infarct size and improved post-ischemic functional recovery — consistent with its cardiomyocyte-protective mechanism. The 3–4 cycles per year protocol (versus the 1–2 cycles per year of most Khavinson compounds) reflects both the importance of the heart as a therapeutic target in aging and the absence of documented cumulative adverse effects from more frequent cycling — the 20-day cycle with the 6–8 week inter-cycle interval provides regular bioregulator support without continuous stimulation. The synergistic relationship between Cardiogen and Vesugen represents the most physiologically complete cardiovascular bioregulator protocol in this database. The heart's function depends on two distinct tissue systems: the cardiomyocytes (addressed by Cardiogen) that generate contractile force, and the coronary vascular endothelium (addressed by Vesugen) that delivers the oxygen and nutrients required to fuel that contractile activity. Age-related decline in cardiac function involves both progressive cardiomyocyte dysfunction (reduced contractile protein quality, mitochondrial inefficiency, increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis) and coronary endothelial dysfunction (reduced coronary flow reserve, impaired vasodilation, microvascular disease). Cardiogen + Vesugen addresses both pathological components simultaneously — the most mechanistically complete cardiovascular aging intervention available from the Khavinson bioregulator toolkit.

records.name: Cartalax
records.description: Cartalax is a synthetic tripeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp) Khavinson bioregulator derived from cartilage and connective tissue polypeptide extracts — identified as the bioactive core sequence responsible for the chondrocyte regulatory, cartilage matrix synthesis-supporting, and articular joint tissue-normalizing activity of the native cartilaginous tissue extract. Articular cartilage is a highly specialized avascular connective tissue covering the load-bearing surfaces of synovial joints — composed primarily of type II collagen fibers and proteoglycans (aggrecan being the dominant large aggregating proteoglycan) embedded in a high water-content extracellular matrix maintained by a sparse population of chondrocytes. Cartilage has severely limited regenerative capacity: chondrocytes in adult articular cartilage are terminally differentiated, largely post-mitotic, and lack the progenitor cell population density required for meaningful repair of significant cartilage damage. The age-related and stress-related degradation of articular cartilage involves: progressive proteoglycan loss (reducing the osmotic resistance and compressive modulus of the matrix), type II collagen fibril disruption and surface fibrillation, chondrocyte senescence and apoptosis, reduced synthesis of matrix components by the remaining chondrocytes, and elevated catabolic enzyme activity (MMP-13, ADAMTS-4/5) that degrades cartilage matrix faster than it is replaced. These changes produce the characteristic cartilage thinning, surface irregularity, and eventual bone-on-bone contact of osteoarthritis. Cartalax acts as a bioregulator at the chondrocyte level — interacting with chondrocyte surface receptors and transcription factors to normalize the gene expression programs governing type II collagen and aggrecan synthesis, anti-catabolic enzyme regulation, chondrocyte survival, and the anabolic/catabolic balance of cartilage matrix turnover. The research evidence for Cartalax and its predecessor cartilaginous bioregulator compounds in the Khavinson literature demonstrates effects on cartilage and connective tissue function across both clinical and animal study contexts. Documented outcomes include: improvement in joint mobility and range of motion in subjects with osteoarthritis, reduction in joint pain scores, improvement in biochemical markers of cartilage matrix synthesis (serum COMP — cartilage oligomeric matrix protein, urinary hydroxyproline markers of collagen turnover), histological improvement in cartilage surface quality in animal arthritis models, and reduction in synovial inflammatory markers. The synergy designations with BPC-157 and TB-500 are mechanistically layered: Cartalax provides the chondrocyte-specific gene program normalization that restores the intrinsic matrix synthesis capacity of cartilage cells; BPC-157 contributes angiogenic support of the periarticular vasculature (cartilage depends on synovial fluid nutrient diffusion from the vascular synovium), tendon and ligament repair, and anti-inflammatory activity in periarticular tissues; TB-500 provides actin cytoskeletal dynamics normalization and cell migration enhancement that supports the limited chondrocyte remodeling capacity available. The three compounds together address cartilage degradation from the chondrocyte gene program level (Cartalax), the periarticular vascular and inflammatory support level (BPC-157), and the cellular repair mechanics level (TB-500). The bedtime fasted administration requirement for Cartalax is the most distinctive and pharmacokinetically important dosing specification in this database. Cartilage is avascular — it receives nutrients and bioregulator peptides exclusively through diffusion from the synovial fluid, which is itself an ultrafiltrate of blood from the synovial membrane vasculature. The overnight fasted state produces: reduced circulating triglycerides and lipoproteins that would compete with peptide transport across synovial membrane capillaries, lower systemic insulin levels that reduce receptor-mediated endocytosis competition in synovial endothelial cells, and the highest relative proportion of available peptide transport capacity in the synovial capillary bed. Additionally, the mechanical compression and decompression cycles of cartilage during sleep (positional changes, muscle relaxation producing joint space widening) enhance synovial fluid nutrient diffusion into the avascular cartilage matrix — providing the bioregulator access window that the bedtime fasted dosing is designed to exploit.

records.name: Cerebrolysin
records.description: Cerebrolysin is a standardized mixture of low-molecular-weight neuropeptides and free amino acids derived from purified porcine brain protein through a proprietary enzymatic hydrolysis process. Unlike single-molecule peptides, Cerebrolysin is a complex biological extract — approximately 25% consists of active peptide fragments and 75% free amino acids. The active peptide fraction contains fragments with structural and functional homology to BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor), NGF (Nerve Growth Factor), GDNF (Glial Cell Line-Derived Neurotrophic Factor), and CNTF (Ciliary Neurotrophic Factor) — the four most important neurotrophic proteins governing neuronal survival, axonal growth, synaptic maintenance, and glial support. These endogenous neurotrophic proteins cannot be administered systemically because they do not cross the blood-brain barrier; Cerebrolysin's peptide fragments, being small (molecular weight under 10,000 Da), do cross the BBB, where they activate the same TrkA, TrkB, TrkC, and GFRα receptor pathways that the full-length proteins engage. This makes Cerebrolysin the only compound in this database that delivers multi-pathway exogenous neurotrophic factor activity directly to the CNS following systemic injection. The clinical evidence base for Cerebrolysin is one of the strongest of any compound in Category V: it holds regulatory approval in multiple countries for Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, stroke recovery, and traumatic brain injury, with randomized controlled trial data demonstrating improvements in cognitive global function, activities of daily living, and neurological deficit scores across these conditions. The mechanism by which Cerebrolysin produces neurological benefit operates across several parallel pathways simultaneously. NGF-like fragments activate TrkA receptors on cholinergic neurons, preserving the basal forebrain cholinergic system that is the primary neuronal population lost in Alzheimer's disease and that mediates encoding and retrieval of declarative memory. BDNF-like fragments activate TrkB on hippocampal neurons, driving dendritic spine formation, long-term potentiation, and the synaptic plasticity required for memory consolidation. GDNF-like fragments support dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and striatum — relevant to Parkinson's disease and to the motivational and reward circuitry that supports goal-directed behavior and mood. CNTF-like fragments support motor neurons and the oligodendrocytes responsible for myelin maintenance, which explains Cerebrolysin's utility in TBI and stroke contexts where white matter integrity is compromised. Additionally, Cerebrolysin has documented anti-apoptotic activity in neurons under ischemic, oxidative, and excitotoxic stress conditions — reducing glutamate-induced calcium overload, reducing caspase-3 activation, and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential in the face of the energy failure that drives post-ischemic neuronal death. The intramuscular and subcutaneous administration routes for Cerebrolysin replace the original intravenous route used in clinical trials. IV administration achieved the highest peak plasma concentrations but the subcutaneous and IM routes are more practical for research protocols and still achieve meaningful systemic concentrations of the active peptide fragments. The IM injection volume at higher doses (20–32mg/day split doses) is the source of the injection site soreness noted in the side effects — larger volume injections into muscle produce mechanical and mild inflammatory discomfort that is expected and self-resolving. The 2–3 month washout period between 6-week cycles reflects the sustained neuroplastic changes Cerebrolysin induces: unlike compounds whose effects are pharmacokinetic (present while the drug is active, absent when it clears), Cerebrolysin's neurotrophic signaling produces structural synaptic changes — new dendritic spines, new synaptic proteins, altered receptor expression — that persist and consolidate during the washout period. Running consecutive cycles without adequate washout does not produce additive benefit; the structural changes from the first cycle need time to stabilize before the second cycle can build further.

records.name: Cerluten
records.description: Cerluten is a Khavinson cytomedin — peptide complex A-5 — extracted from the brain and spinal cord tissue of young animals, developed as the oral central nervous system bioregulator of the Khavinson framework. It works by delivering a mixture of CNS tissue-derived low-molecular-weight peptides that interact with neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes at the transcriptional level — normalizing the gene expression programs governing neuronal survival, neurotrophic factor production (BDNF, NGF, GDNF), mitochondrial energy supply to neurons, anti-apoptotic neuroprotection, and the myelin maintenance programs of oligodendrocytes. In practical terms, Cerluten signals aging brain cells to restore the gene activity patterns of younger, more resilient neural tissue — slowing the accumulation of neuronal damage and supporting the brain's inherent repair capacity. Cerluten's clinical research evidence spans multiple neurological application domains. The published Khavinson clinical study explicitly documented the absence of any adverse effects, complications, or drug dependence — an exceptional finding that sets it apart from most CNS-active compounds. Positive outcomes documented include improvements in neuropsychological test performance (attention, memory, processing speed) in subjects with age-related cognitive decline, normalization of EEG patterns toward younger profiles, improvement in cerebral blood flow velocity by Doppler ultrasound, and functional improvement scores in subjects with mild to moderate post-stroke cognitive impairment. It has also been studied as adjunctive support in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, where documented benefits are symptomatic — meaningful quality-of-life improvements — rather than disease modification. What distinguishes Cerluten from Pinealon and Cortagen — the injectable synthetic CNS peptides also in this database — is the same oral/injectable breadth-vs-precision distinction seen across all Khavinson pairs. Pinealon delivers the defined neuroprotective tripeptide (Glu-Asp-Arg) by injection; Cortagen delivers the defined cortical tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro) by injection; Cerluten delivers the full CNS tissue extract peptide repertoire covering neuronal, glial, and oligodendrocyte signals simultaneously in a single oral capsule. For subjects who prefer oral-only protocols, Cerluten is the single compound covering the entire CNS bioregulator space that Pinealon and Cortagen together address with injectables. For subjects on injectable protocols, Cerluten oral cycles add the breadth of the full CNS cytomedin matrix to the precision of those defined sequences.

records.name: Chonluten
records.description: Chonluten is a synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) Khavinson bioregulator derived from lung and colon tissue polypeptide extracts — uniquely, the only Khavinson compound in this database with two distinct primary tissue targets. This dual-target architecture reflects the shared embryological origin of pulmonary and gastrointestinal epithelium from the foregut endoderm — the same primitive tissue layer that differentiates into both bronchial and intestinal epithelium — and the functional parallel between these two epithelial systems as mucosal barrier surfaces exposed to external environments that require coordinated immune surveillance, mucociliary or peristaltic clearance, and rapid regenerative response to injury. The alveolar epithelium of the lung parenchyma (the Chonluten lung target) is composed of Type I alveolar cells that form the ultra-thin gas-exchange surface and Type II pneumocytes that produce surfactant and serve as the alveolar progenitor cell population. Age-related and disease-related alveolar epithelial dysfunction involves: progressive loss of surfactant production quality (increasing alveolar surface tension and collapse risk), reduced Type II pneumocyte regenerative capacity, accumulation of fibroblast-driven subepithelial fibrosis, and impaired alveolar macrophage clearance of inhaled particles and pathogens. Chonluten acts as a bioregulator at both alveolar epithelial cells and colonic epithelial cells simultaneously — normalizing the gene expression programs governing epithelial barrier integrity, regenerative proliferation, mucosal immune function, and inflammatory cytokine profiles in both tissues. The colonic target of Chonluten is physiologically significant and often underappreciated in descriptions of this compound. The colon — the final 1.5 meters of the large intestine — is home to the densest microbial community in the human body (approximately 10^11 organisms per gram of luminal content), and the colonic epithelium is the primary barrier between this microbial ecosystem and the systemic circulation. Colonic epithelial cell homeostasis — maintained through rapid cell turnover (complete epithelial renewal every 3–5 days from stem cells in the crypts of Lieberkühn), tight junction integrity, and mucosal immune surveillance through IgA secretion and innate immune pattern recognition — is fundamental to preventing the low-grade endotoxemia and bacterial translocation that drive systemic inflammation in aging and metabolic disease. Chonluten's colonic bioregulator activity normalizes the gene expression programs governing colonocyte survival, tight junction protein expression (claudin, occludin, ZO-1), mucin production, and the innate immune sentinels of the colonic mucosa — addressing the gut barrier dysfunction component of systemic inflammatory aging (inflammaging) that is now recognized as a major driver of age-associated disease across multiple organ systems. The synergy with Bronchogen is the most precisely complementary tissue pairing in the entire Khavinson bioregulator set: Bronchogen targets the bronchial epithelium of the conducting airways (the tubes); Chonluten targets the alveolar epithelium of the gas exchange surface (the terminal air sacs). Together they provide complete respiratory system bioregulator coverage from the nasal cavity through the alveoli — Bronchogen handling the mucociliary clearance and barrier function of the conducting airways, Chonluten handling the surfactant production and gas exchange efficiency of the terminal respiratory units. The additional colonic benefit of Chonluten extends its utility beyond respiratory applications into any protocol targeting systemic inflammaging, gut barrier restoration, or microbiome support — making it one of the most versatile Khavinson bioregulators in this database.

records.name: CJC-1295 (No DAC / Modified GRF 1-29)
records.description: CJC-1295 (No DAC), also known as Modified GRF 1-29, is a synthetic analog of the first 29 amino acids of endogenous Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone (GHRH). The human body normally releases GHRH in discrete pulses from the hypothalamus, which travel to the anterior pituitary and trigger timed bursts of growth hormone secretion. The problem with native GHRH is that it is destroyed by dipeptidyl peptidase-IV (DPP-IV) enzymes within minutes of release, making it useless as a therapeutic agent without modification. CJC-1295 (No DAC) solves this with four strategic amino acid substitutions at positions 2, 8, 15, and 27 that block DPP-IV cleavage — extending the half-life from under 2 minutes to approximately 30 minutes while preserving the precise GHRH receptor binding profile. The result is a compound that accurately mimics the body's natural GH pulse physiology: a short, sharp burst of pituitary GH secretion rather than a sustained elevation. The "No DAC" distinction is the most important pharmacological differentiator in the CJC family. CJC-1295 with DAC adds a Drug Affinity Complex that binds the peptide to serum albumin and extends its half-life to 8 days, creating continuous GH and IGF-1 elevation. CJC-1295 No DAC does the opposite — its 30-minute window produces a single clean GH pulse that mirrors the body's natural nighttime secretion pattern. This pulsatile approach maintains receptor sensitivity, prevents pituitary downregulation over 12–16 week cycles, and avoids the chronic GH-bleed side effects (sustained water retention, insulin resistance) that come with long-acting GHRH analogs. When stacked with a GHRP like ipamorelin at the same time, the two compounds hit the pituitary simultaneously via separate receptor pathways (GHRH-R and GHS-R1a), producing a synergistic GH pulse that is 2–10x larger than either compound alone. Fasting discipline is non-negotiable for this compound. Insulin and somatostatin — both of which spike in response to carbohydrates and fat — directly suppress GH release at the pituitary level. Dosing while fed, particularly with carbs or fats present, will blunt or completely abolish the GH pulse. The strict pre-bed, 2-hour fasted window takes advantage of the body's natural nocturnal GH surge: the pituitary is already primed to release GH during deep sleep, and CJC-1295 amplifies that pulse at the optimal moment. Black coffee and water are acceptable during the fasting window because they do not provoke meaningful insulin response.

records.name: CJC-1295 (No DAC) + Ipamorelin
records.description: The CJC-1295 (No DAC) + Ipamorelin blend is a 10mg co-lyophilized fixed-ratio combination (5mg CJC-1295 No DAC / 5mg Ipamorelin) widely regarded as the gold standard GH pulse amplification protocol in the research peptide community — the combination that most closely mimics and amplifies the physiological dual-axis GH secretion system that produces the endogenous nocturnal GH pulse. CJC-1295 (No DAC) is a modified GHRH(1-29) analog (the minimally active GHRH sequence retaining full GHRHR binding) with substitutions at positions 2 (Ala→D-Ala), 8 (Asn→Gln), 15 (Gly→Aib), and 27 (Met→Nle) that collectively increase resistance to dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DPP-IV) cleavage and oxidative methionine degradation — extending the half-life from native GHRH's approximately 7 minutes to approximately 30 minutes for CJC-1295 (No DAC); long enough to trigger a clean single GH pulse window at the receptor but short enough to produce the pulsatile GH secretion pattern rather than the continuous GH stimulation of CJC-1295 with DAC. The "No DAC" designation distinguishes it from CJC-1295 with Drug Affinity Complex (DAC), which adds a lysine-maleimide linker that covalently bonds to albumin and produces a half-life of approximately 6–8 days — converting the episodic GHRH pulse to a continuous GH stimulation with fundamentally different physiological and safety implications. The 1:1 ratio of CJC-1295 (No DAC) to Ipamorelin is the pharmacologically validated ratio from the academic and clinical research that established this combination — equimolar dual-axis stimulation with GHRHR and GHS-R1a at equal molar doses produces the optimal GH pulse amplitude that is reliably above single-agent monotherapy but below the physiological ceiling that would trigger negative feedback GH suppression or somatostatin blunting. The mechanism of synergy between CJC-1295 (No DAC) and Ipamorelin at the pituitary somatotroph represents a textbook example of receptor pathway convergence producing supra-additive responses. CJC-1295 (No DAC) acts on GHRHR to activate adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → CREB → GH gene transcription and somatotroph sensitization; simultaneously GHRH signaling primes GH vesicle docking machinery through calcium-independent mechanisms. Ipamorelin acts on GHS-R1a to activate Gq → PLC → IP3 → intracellular calcium release, which directly triggers GH vesicle exocytosis. The GHRH pathway prepares the somatotroph (increases GH gene expression, primes vesicles, sensitizes the cell) while the GHS-R1a pathway pulls the trigger (calcium-triggered exocytosis). Neither signal alone produces the maximal physiological GH pulse — GHRH without ghrelin receptor input produces GH secretion but not the full pulse amplitude; ghrelin receptor agonism without GHRH priming produces limited GH release from an unprimed somatotroph. Together they replicate the endogenous pulse-generating mechanism with greater fidelity than either compound alone. This is why the CJC-1295 No DAC + Ipamorelin combination specifically (rather than CJC-1295 DAC, which produces tonic rather than pulsatile GH) is described as the gold standard anti-aging GH protocol — it produces the pulsatile physiological GH pattern, including the nocturnal pulse that drives overnight tissue repair, IGF-1 production, and growth hormone-dependent body composition effects. The protocol variants from the standard 200mcg/day (100mcg each compound) anti-aging approach through the "Bodybuilder Saturation" protocol (200mcg 3x daily, totaling 600mcg/day) to "The Hulk" (escalating to 500mcg/day) reflect the progressive transition from anti-aging pulse optimization to performance enhancement and body recomposition applications. At the standard 200mcg/day anti-aging dose, the GH pulse produced is modest — approximately 1.5–3x above baseline — which optimizes overnight repair and IGF-1 production to youthful reference range levels without producing supraphysiological IGF-1 elevation. The 3x daily saturation protocol at 600mcg/day produces IGF-1 levels that in many subjects exceed the young adult reference range, entering the performance enhancement territory that drives muscle protein synthesis, fat mobilization, and recovery acceleration beyond anti-aging baseline support. The fasted state requirement for each injection in the multi-dose protocols — morning fasted, post-workout fasted (requiring no food for 2 hours post-exercise), and pre-bed fasted — represents a significant adherence challenge but is pharmacologically non-negotiable for achieving the full GH pulse amplitude; insulin-stimulated somatostatin from any fed-state injection would blunt the GHRHR + GHS-R1a synergistic pulse.

records.name: CJC-1295 DAC
records.description: CJC-1295 DAC is the long-acting version of the CJC GHRH analog family. The DAC — Drug Affinity Complex — is a chemical modification that causes the peptide to covalently bind to serum albumin immediately upon injection. Albumin is the most abundant protein in blood plasma, and binding to it transforms CJC-1295 DAC from a peptide that would otherwise clear in 30 minutes into one that recirculates for approximately 8 days. The practical consequence is that a single or twice-weekly injection maintains continuously elevated GH and IGF-1 levels around the clock, rather than producing the timed pulsatile surges that CJC-1295 No DAC creates. This is the fundamental pharmacological split between the two CJC variants: No DAC restores natural GH pulse physiology, DAC replaces it with a steady hormonal "bleed." Strict fasting is not required with DAC because the GH elevation is not timed to a peak — it is sustained at all times regardless of feeding status. The primary research advantages of CJC-1295 DAC are convenience and IGF-1 maximization. With only 1–2 injections per week required versus daily injections for No DAC, compliance is significantly easier. The steady-state IGF-1 elevation is higher in aggregate than what pulsatile protocols produce, which translates to more consistent tissue recovery, more sustained lean mass support, and measurable improvements in skin, collagen, and connective tissue quality over 12–16 week cycles. Clinical data from Teichman et al. (2006) confirmed that CJC-1295 DAC produced dose-dependent increases in GH and IGF-1 that persisted for 6+ days following a single injection, with IGF-1 increases of 20–50% from baseline sustained over the full cycle period. This makes it the preferred CJC variant for anti-aging, body composition maintenance, and protocols where consistent anabolic signaling is prioritized over GH pulse optimization. The trade-off for this convenience is a less physiological GH pattern and a higher side effect load relative to No DAC. Continuous GH elevation — rather than timed pulses — produces more persistent water retention, greater risk of insulin resistance with prolonged use, and somewhat stronger joint stiffness compared to the pulsatile approach. Because DAC creates a sustained albumin-bound depot of peptide in the bloodstream, the effects build gradually over 2–4 weeks and do not fully clear for 2+ weeks after the last injection, which means side effects from overexposure also persist. It is contraindicated alongside CJC-1295 No DAC, sermorelin, tesamorelin, and HGH 191aa — all of which act on the same GHRH receptor or the same downstream GH/IGF-1 pathway.

records.name: Cortagen
records.description: Cortagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro) Khavinson bioregulator derived from cerebral cortex tissue polypeptide extracts — identified as the bioactive core sequence responsible for the neuroprotective, neuroregenerative, and cognitive-supporting activity of the native cortical tissue extract. The cerebral cortex — the outermost layer of the brain responsible for higher cognitive functions including memory consolidation, executive function, language processing, sensory integration, and voluntary motor control — undergoes characteristic age-related structural and functional changes: progressive synaptic pruning, reduced dendritic arborization, declining neurotrophic factor production (particularly BDNF and NGF), increased neuroinflammation from microglial activation, oxidative stress accumulation, and loss of cortical neuronal plasticity. Cortagen acts as a cortex-specific bioregulator by binding to cortical neuron and glial cell surface receptors to normalize the gene expression programs governing neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and neurotrophic factor production — partially reversing the age-related decline in cortical tissue homeostasis. The morning dosing window is specifically calibrated to the cortical activation cycle: administration upon waking aligns Cortagen's bioregulator activity with the period of highest cortical metabolic demand and synaptic activity, maximizing the overlap between the bioregulator's tissue-targeted gene program normalization and the cortical network activity that most benefits from it. The cognitive enhancement and neuroprotective applications of Cortagen are documented across multiple research contexts in the Khavinson literature. Studies demonstrated improvements in: memory consolidation tasks and verbal recall performance in aging subjects, electroencephalographic (EEG) parameters of cortical activity showing normalization of alpha and theta wave patterns toward younger adult profiles, reduction in markers of cortical oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, improvements in reaction time and processing speed, and partial restoration of the cortical synaptic density reductions seen in aging brain tissue. In neurological disease contexts, Cortagen administration produced improvements in cognitive function metrics in subjects with early-stage vascular dementia and post-stroke cognitive impairment — suggesting that the cortical bioregulator mechanism extends beyond healthy aging to pathological neuronal recovery contexts. The specific synergy with Pinealon is mechanistically precise: Cortagen restores cortical neuron gene programs from the cortical tissue level while Pinealon provides the broader CNS oxidative defense and neuroprotective signaling from the central neural regulatory level — Cortagen is the cortex-specific bioregulator and Pinealon is the pan-CNS bioregulator, with their combined use providing both organ-specific and system-wide neural support simultaneously. The synergy with Cerebrolysin — a broader neuropeptide complex with BDNF-like, NGF-like, and CNTF-like activities — creates a complementary layering: Cortagen provides bioregulator normalization of the cortical gene expression programs, while Cerebrolysin provides direct neurotrophic factor supplementation that supports the neuronal survival and plasticity machinery that Cortagen's gene program restoration requires to function. Neither compound alone addresses both the gene regulatory and the neurotrophic factor supplementation dimensions of cortical aging — their combination targets both simultaneously. The morning dosing and the cognitive performance window that follows make Cortagen practically useful for subjects with age-related cognitive complaints, post-neurological-injury recovery, and performance-oriented cognitive optimization — provided the contraindications for active neurological disease requiring managed treatment are observed.

records.name: Crystagen
records.description: Crystagen is a synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) Khavinson bioregulator derived from immune system tissue polypeptide extracts with primary activity on the peripheral adaptive and innate immune compartments — specifically targeting natural killer (NK) cells, macrophages, T-lymphocytes, and B-lymphocytes as the primary effector cell populations of systemic immune defense. While Vilon (also in this database) focuses specifically on the thymic arm of immune function — the production and maturation of naive T-cells from the thymic epithelium — Crystagen operates downstream at the peripheral immune effector level, targeting the already-matured immune cell populations in the blood, lymph nodes, and peripheral tissues that carry out surveillance, pathogen clearance, and immune regulation. NK cells — the innate immune lymphocytes that recognize and eliminate virus-infected cells, tumor cells, and stressed cells without prior antigen sensitization — are among the most directly relevant targets for aging-associated immune decline: NK cell cytotoxic function declines markedly with age (NK cell immunosenescence), reducing cancer immune surveillance and antiviral clearance in the elderly. Crystagen normalizes NK cell gene expression programs governing cytotoxic granule synthesis, activating receptor expression, and the signaling pathways governing target cell recognition and elimination — restoring the cytotoxic efficiency of immunosenescent NK cells toward the functional profile of younger immune systems. The T-lymphocyte and B-lymphocyte effects of Crystagen operate through the same bioregulator mechanism — normalizing the gene expression programs that govern T-cell activation threshold, cytokine production profiles (IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-α balance), and B-cell antibody class switching and somatic hypermutation quality. The aging immune phenotype involves not only the reduced output of naive T-cells from the involuted thymus (addressed by Vilon) but also the functional exhaustion and senescence of the peripheral memory T-cell pool — the accumulated T-cells that have undergone repeated antigen stimulation over decades and have lost proliferative capacity, acquired the senescent phenotype (CD28−, CD57+), and begun producing pro-inflammatory cytokines that contribute to the chronic low-grade inflammation of immunosenescence. Crystagen's peripheral T-cell bioregulator activity normalizes these senescent T-cell gene programs — moving the senescent T-cell pool back toward a functional, non-inflammatory, competent phenotype. The macrophage component of Crystagen's activity addresses the polarization shift in aging macrophages from the balanced M1/M2 phenotype of younger immune systems toward the chronic M1-dominant pro-inflammatory state that contributes to tissue damage in aging — normalizing macrophage inflammatory gene programs toward the homeostatic balance that supports repair rather than destruction. The bedtime fasted administration requirement for Crystagen is the most critical dosing constraint among the immune Khavinson bioregulators. NK cell, T-cell, and macrophage proliferative and gene expression activity follow a circadian rhythm with peak activity during sleep — consistent with the well-established circadian regulation of immune function where lymphocyte trafficking, NK cell maturation, and T-cell proliferative responses are all maximized during the nocturnal sleep period. Fasted administration at bedtime ensures that the bioregulator reaches peripheral immune tissue with minimal competition from post-prandial metabolic activity, insulin-driven cellular anabolic programs, and the gastrointestinal immune activation that occurs during active digestion. The synergistic designation with Vilon creates the most complete immunosenescence reversal protocol in the database: Vilon restores the thymic T-cell generation supply, and Crystagen normalizes the peripheral immune execution by the T-cells, B-cells, NK cells, and macrophages that Vilon's restored thymic output supports.

contraindications: Active autoimmune disease — the broad and intense peripheral immune activation mechanism of Crystagen is directly contraindicated in any autoimmune condition where immune activation amplifies the self-reactive immune response; this includes rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease, type 1 diabetes, psoriasis, and other autoimmune conditions in active phase; this is the strictest autoimmune contraindication among the Khavinson immune bioregulators.

Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy — Crystagen's NK cell activation, T-cell normalization, and broad immune competence restoration directly opposes the immunosuppressive regimen required to prevent rejection; absolute contraindication.

Concurrent biologic immunosuppressive therapy (TNF-alpha inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors) — Crystagen's immune activation mechanism conflicts with the intended immunosuppressive mechanism of these biologics.

Active hematological malignancies involving lymphoid lineages (lymphoma, CLL, T-cell malignancies) — NK cell activation, T-cell normalization, and B-cell stimulation in the context of malignant lymphoid clonal expansion requires oncological evaluation.
Known hypersensitivity to Crystagen (Lys-Glu-Asp tripeptide) or formulation excipients.
Active severe infection requiring antimicrobial management — Crystagen's immune activation during acute severe infection could dysregulate the already activated innate immune response.

Pregnancy — broad immune system modulation during pregnancy, where maternal immune tolerance of the semi-allogeneic fetus is critically maintained, has not been evaluated and carries theoretical risks to the maternal-fetal immune interface.

Pediatric subjects with normally functioning immune systems — intense immune bioregulator stimulation in subjects with fully competent immune function has no established therapeutic target and could produce immune hyperactivation.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab) for oncological indications — concurrent NK/T-cell activation with checkpoint inhibitor-mediated T-cell unleashing could produce additive immune-related adverse events (irAE) of unpredictable severity.
sideEffects: Mild flu-like symptoms in first cycle days — the most commonly reported adverse effect; as NK cells, T-cells, and macrophages are activated and cytokine production normalizes, a transient systemic immune activation response manifests as mild fatigue, myalgia, and low-grade temperature elevation; typically resolves within 2–4 days as the immune normalization equilibrates.
Mild lymph node awareness or tenderness — regional lymph node activation as lymphocyte proliferation and immune cell trafficking increases; benign; typically self-limiting within the first week.
Mild fatigue — related to the metabolic demand of immune system activation; most pronounced in the first 3–5 days of a new cycle.

Fasting requirement compliance challenge — unlike most Khavinson compounds, Crystagen requires a fasted state at bedtime; subjects who eat late or have acid reflux conditions that worsen with fasting may find this administration requirement difficult.

Transient worsening of subclinical autoimmune manifestations — subjects with undiagnosed autoimmune predisposition may experience a mild flare of previously subclinical autoimmune symptoms as immune surveillance and reactivity are restored; warrants discontinuation and evaluation if it occurs.

Mild skin changes — as NK cell and T-cell surveillance improves, some subjects with chronic viral skin manifestations (subclinical herpes, HPV-related) may notice transient flares as the immune system engages these previously tolerated infections more actively.

Mild fever on initiation (rare) — a small minority reports low-grade fever (< 38.0°C) in the first 1–2 days; a sign of immune activation rather than infection; resolves spontaneously without intervention.

No serious immune adverse events documented in the Khavinson literature at standard protocol doses — Crystagen's safety profile in the aging and immunosenescence research cohorts is clean at standard doses; the most practically significant safety dimension is the autoimmune and transplant contraindication.

records.name: Deep Immune
records.description: Deep Immune is a systemic immune restoration blend combining Thymosin Alpha-1, LL-37, and Thymulin into a single coordinated immune-support platform. The blend is structured around a 6mg Thymosin Alpha-1, 3mg LL-37, and 2mg Thymulin ratio, creating an 11mg total vial with a 3:1.5:1 composition. Thymosin Alpha-1 provides the adaptive immune orchestration layer through dendritic cell maturation, MHC class I upregulation, NK cell cytotoxicity support, CD4:CD8 ratio normalization, and Th1 balance restoration. LL-37 adds innate antimicrobial defense through broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, biofilm disruption, and neutrophil and monocyte recruitment. Thymulin provides the thymic restoration layer by supporting final T-lymphocyte precursor differentiation into competent immunocompetent T-cells. From a performance and optimization standpoint, Deep Immune is positioned for immunosenescence, chronic viral immune depletion, post-antibiotic immune dysregulation, impaired immune surveillance, poor vaccine response, and age-related thymic decline. This is not an intranasal blend. The source document identifies Deep Immune as requiring systemic immune-cell distribution and specifically marks intranasal administration as unsupported. The blend is therefore best treated as a subcutaneous immune-system protocol, with dosing built around controlled immune restoration rather than acute stimulation.

records.name: Dihexa
records.description: Dihexa (PNB-0408) is a synthetic peptide derived from angiotensin IV — modified at both ends to dramatically improve its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier and survive oral digestion. Where most cognitive peptides target neurotransmitter systems or protect existing neurons, Dihexa works at a more fundamental level: it acts as a potent amplifier of HGF (hepatocyte growth factor) at the c-Met receptor in the brain, triggering the formation of entirely new synaptic connections — a process called synaptogenesis. This mechanism is responsible for its reputation as one of the most potent neuroplasticity compounds ever studied. Preclinical models have shown Dihexa fully reversing induced memory deficits and improving cognitive performance in aged subjects — effects that required doses orders of magnitude lower than other known synaptogenic agents. Critically, Dihexa does not appear to enhance cognition in animals that are already healthy and unimpaired; its activity is specifically upregulated in the context of cognitive decline, aging, or injury, which gives it a more targeted profile than broad-spectrum stimulants. The two available routes — oral and subcutaneous — produce the same mechanism but through different bioavailability profiles. Oral dosing requires higher milligram amounts (8–15mg) because of first-pass hepatic processing before the drug reaches systemic circulation; subcutaneous injection bypasses this entirely, achieving effective CNS concentrations at doses of 0.5–2.0mg. Both routes are valid; the choice typically comes down to convenience preference and sensitivity — subcutaneous allows finer dose control for subjects who find oral doses overstimulating. Dihexa has an unusually long half-life of approximately 8–12 days, meaning it accumulates steadily over the first several weeks of a cycle and takes weeks to fully clear after the last dose. This is not a daily fast-acting nootropic — it is a structural neuroplasticity intervention that builds over a cycle and produces durable changes in synaptic architecture that outlast the drug itself. The synergy designations reflect a layered cognitive restoration stack: Semax and Selank address the acute neurotransmitter environment and stress response while Dihexa drives the structural new synapse formation that gives those signals more hardware to work with; Cerebrolysin provides the peptide growth factor environment that supports neuronal survival during the active synaptogenesis process; BPC-157 contributes both its neurotrophic NGF/VEGF-adjacent activity and its dopaminergic buffering effect, reducing the overstimulation and mood volatility that Dihexa occasionally produces. NAD+ supports the cellular energy demands of the metabolically intensive synaptogenesis process. Together this represents a complete structural and functional neuroplasticity protocol — Dihexa builds new connections, the supporting compounds ensure those connections form in a stable, well-supported neurochemical environment.

washout: Cycle Length: 4-8 weeks for oral protocols. 4-6 weeks for subcutaneous protocols.

Washout: Minimum 4-6 weeks off between cycles. Given the ~12-day half-life, full pharmacological clearance (5+ half-lives) requires approximately 8-10 weeks — plan accordingly if precise drug-free windows are required.

Post-Cycle Effects: Cognitive effects from completed synaptogenesis (newly formed dendritic spines and synapses) may persist well beyond drug clearance — this represents the durable structural neuroplasticity change rather than pharmacological drug presence. Subjective cognitive enhancement may be reported weeks to months after cycle cessation in favorable responders.
Important: Do not run concurrent cycles of Dihexa with P21 or other potent synaptogenesis-targeting compounds. The combined synaptogenic load has not been characterized.
contraindications: Active malignancy (any cancer, any stage) — Dihexa's mechanism of action requires c-Met receptor activation; c-Met is a well-characterized oncogene whose aberrant activation drives tumor cell proliferation, survival (resistance to apoptosis), cell motility and invasion, and tumor angiogenesis across a wide spectrum of human cancers including gastric, lung (NSCLC), hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, breast, glioblastoma, and colorectal cancer; pharmaceutical oncology has invested heavily in c-Met inhibitors as cancer therapeutics precisely because c-Met activation promotes tumor progression; exogenous Dihexa-mediated c-Met activation in subjects with active malignancy represents the most critically enforced and highest-priority contraindication for this compound; absolute.

History of any cancer — the long half-life (8-12 days) and absence of any long-term human safety data mean that residual or micrometastatic disease, dormant cancer cells, and genetically predisposed cells that have not yet undergone malignant transformation could theoretically be promoted toward proliferation or invasion by c-Met activation; history of cancer requires oncological clearance and is considered at minimum a strong relative contraindication; for cancers with documented c-Met overexpression (gastric, lung, hepatocellular, renal cell, glioblastoma) this approaches absolute.

Precancerous conditions (dysplasia of any organ, Barrett's esophagus, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, colon polyps with high-grade dysplasia, leukoplakia) — cells in precancerous transition states have frequently acquired partial c-Met pathway activation as part of their malignant progression; exogenous c-Met amplification could accelerate the transition from precancerous to invasive malignancy.

Strong family history of cancer with known genetic predisposition (BRCA1/2 mutation, Lynch syndrome, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, VHL syndrome) — germline cancer predisposition in the setting of exogenous c-Met activation represents a compounded oncological risk that has not been characterized; relative-to-absolute contraindication depending on specific syndrome and organ involvement.

Immunocompromised state (HIV/AIDS, primary immunodeficiency, post-transplant immunosuppression, active immunosuppressive therapy for autoimmune disease) — immune surveillance of nascent malignant c-Met-activated cells is the primary protective mechanism against Dihexa-driven oncogenic risk; in immunocompromised subjects where this surveillance is impaired, the theoretical oncogenic risk is materially elevated.

Concurrent acetylcholinesterase inhibitor therapy (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine, huperzine A) — the fosgonimeton ACT-AD Phase 2 trial (fosgonimeton shares the HGF/c-Met mechanism with Dihexa) identified that AChE inhibitor co-administration appeared to reduce efficacy of HGF/c-Met-axis compounds; the mechanism may involve competing synaptic plasticity pathway effects; this is an efficacy contraindication rather than a safety contraindication, but concurrent use is discouraged.

Concurrent P21 peptide — both Dihexa and P21 are potently synaptogenic through distinct but convergent neuroplasticity mechanisms; the combined synaptogenic load is uncharacterized and has the potential to produce excessive neuroplasticity-related adverse effects (seizure risk, cognitive disorganization, severe sleep disruption); concurrent use is to be avoided.

Concurrent CYP450-metabolized medications with narrow therapeutic index — Dihexa has been reported in some sources to inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes (the primary hepatic drug-metabolizing enzyme system); formal in vitro or in vivo CYP inhibition studies have not been published, but the theoretical interaction is: Dihexa CYP inhibition → reduced clearance of co-medications → accumulation → toxicity; drugs at particular risk include warfarin, benzodiazepines, antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, digoxin), certain antidepressants (TCAs, MAOIs), immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), and statins; specific CYP enzyme interactions are uncharacterized and require clinical monitoring.

Active epilepsy or seizure disorder — the potent synaptogenic and neuroplasticity-enhancing activity of Dihexa represents a theoretical increase in cortical excitability; the relationship between Dihexa-induced synaptogenesis and seizure threshold has not been characterized in human populations; the fosgonimeton Phase 2 Parkinson's trial exclusion criteria included epilepsy, providing indirect clinical guidance.

Clinically significant cardiac arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy — excluded from fosgonimeton ATH-1017 clinical trials; the c-Met pathway has cardiac roles in cardiomyocyte repair and survival; the effect of exogenous c-Met activation in subjects with existing cardiac disease is uncharacterized.

Significant hepatic impairment — excluded from fosgonimeton clinical trials; HGF/c-Met is a primary hepatic growth and repair signaling axis; in subjects with significant hepatic disease, exogenous HGF/c-Met amplification through Dihexa could interact with the hepatic repair and fibrotic processes already active.
Significant hypertension (uncontrolled, >160/100) — excluded from fosgonimeton clinical trials; the HGF/c-Met pathway has vascular effects; interaction with hypertension is uncharacterized.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding — the c-Met pathway is essential in embryonic development and organogenesis; exogenous c-Met potentiation during fetal development could have teratogenic consequences; absolute contraindication.
Known hypersensitivity to Dihexa or formulation excipients.
WADA-registered competitive athletes — Dihexa is listed on the WADA Prohibited Substances List; use constitutes a doping violation.

Psychiatric instability, active psychosis, bipolar disorder in manic phase, or severe anxiety disorder — Dihexa's potent neuroplasticity induction and the cognitive overstimulation it can produce in sensitive subjects could exacerbate psychiatric instability; the fosgonimeton Parkinson's trial reported increased hallucinations in 4/10 high-dose subjects (40% discontinuation rate), suggesting that the CNS-active HGF/c-Met mechanism is not benign in neurologically vulnerable populations.
sideEffects: Headache — the most commonly reported adverse effect across both anecdotal community reports and formal research contexts; predominantly frontal or bifrontal; mechanism likely reflects the rapid induction of synaptogenesis and the associated neurochemical flux in cortical and hippocampal circuits during the adaptation phase; most prominent in the first 1-2 weeks of a new cycle and at dose escalation steps; managed by starting at the lowest dose (5mg oral) and slow escalation.

Cognitive overstimulation and racing thoughts — Dihexa's extraordinary potency at promoting neuroplasticity can produce a subjective experience of excessive mental activity, racing thoughts, difficulty filtering irrelevant stimuli, and a "wired" cognitive state that is uncomfortable rather than performance-enhancing; most pronounced at doses above 10mg oral or above 1.5mg subcutaneous; dose reduction or cycle interruption is the appropriate management.

Anxiety and nervousness — a subset of subjects report increased anxiety, social anxiety, or a jittery nervous quality particularly in the first weeks of a cycle; likely related to increased synaptic density and associated heightened sensory and cognitive processing; tends to attenuate as the cycle progresses if the dose is maintained rather than escalated; dose reduction is the primary management strategy.

Sleep disruption and insomnia — the CNS stimulatory component of Dihexa's neuroplasticity induction produces sleep disruption when taken in the afternoon or evening; strict morning administration is critical; subjects who take Dihexa within 6 hours of their intended sleep time consistently report delayed sleep onset, reduced sleep quality, and vivid dream intensification; the morning dosing window is non-negotiable for sleep-quality preservation.

Vivid dreams — independently of dose timing, some subjects report intensified and highly vivid dreaming during Dihexa cycles; the mechanism reflects HGF/c-Met-driven synaptic plasticity changes in hippocampal and limbic memory consolidation circuits that alter the character of REM sleep memory processing; typically reported as neutral to notable rather than distressing, unless accompanied by nightmare content.

Mood fluctuations — direction is variable between subjects; some report mild mood elevation and increased motivation (consistent with enhanced dopaminergic and glutamatergic synaptic activity from new synapse formation); others report transient dysphoria or irritability; the neuroplasticity-driven mood changes typically stabilize within 2-3 weeks as the new synaptic landscape establishes a new functional equilibrium.

Mild nausea — uncommon at standard oral doses; may reflect GI c-Met activation (the gut epithelium expresses c-Met as part of its repair machinery) rather than CNS effects; typically mild and transient.
Tachycardia — rare, anecdotal; causal relationship to Dihexa unconfirmed; discontinue and evaluate if sustained.
Dizziness — occasional, transient; more common during dose escalation; mechanism unclear.
Injection site reaction (subcutaneous route) — mild erythema or swelling at injection site; standard response for subcutaneous peptide administration; rotated injection sites recommended.

CNS overstimulation in neurologically vulnerable subjects — the fosgonimeton Phase 2 Parkinson's disease trial reported a 40% discontinuation rate in the high-dose arm due to adverse events including tremor exacerbation, increased hallucinations, and agitation; while fosgonimeton is a distinct IV-formulated compound, the shared HGF/c-Met mechanism indicates that the CNS-active effects of this pathway are not without risk in neurologically impaired or vulnerable subjects; Dihexa should be used with extreme caution in any subject with neurological disease beyond the cognitively impaired target population.

Long-term safety unknown — no long-term human safety studies exist; no prospective cancer surveillance, no organ toxicity monitoring, no neuroimaging outcomes; the absence of documented serious adverse events in the community use population reflects the relatively small number of users and the absence of systematic follow-up rather than confirmed safety.

records.name: DSIP (Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide)
records.description: DSIP (Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide) is an endogenous nonapeptide (Trp-Ala-Gly-Gly-Asp-Ala-Ser-Gly-Glu) first isolated in 1974 from the cerebral venous blood of rabbits in which slow-wave sleep had been induced by electrical thalamic stimulation. The name reflects its original identification as a factor capable of inducing delta (slow-wave) sleep when injected into the cerebral ventricles of naive recipient animals — a remarkable finding that suggested the existence of endogenous sleep-promoting signaling molecules distinct from sedative neurotransmitters like GABA. DSIP is found in the hypothalamus, limbic system, pituitary, adrenal cortex, gut, and peripheral blood, where it participates in the regulation of the sleep-wake cycle, stress response, pain sensitivity, and neuroendocrine function. Its molecular mechanism is not mediated by a single well-characterized receptor in the manner of most peptides in this database — instead, DSIP appears to act through multiple simultaneous pathways: modulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, influence on serotonergic and noradrenergic neurotransmission, interaction with delta-opioid receptors in sleep-regulating circuits, and direct modulation of the delta-wave EEG oscillations generated by thalamocortical circuits during deep sleep. The effect on EEG is the most directly documented: DSIP administration increases the proportion of delta wave (0.5–4 Hz) activity in sleep EEG recordings, specifically extending the duration and depth of Stage 3 (slow-wave, N3) sleep — the phase of deepest restorative sleep during which growth hormone secretion is maximal, metabolic waste clearance via the glymphatic system is greatest, and cellular repair and memory consolidation are most active. The physiological importance of slow-wave sleep quality — the parameter DSIP most directly improves — extends across virtually every system in this database. GH axis compounds (CJC-1295, Ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Sermorelin) all release the majority of their growth hormone pulse during the first slow-wave sleep bout of the night; DSIP deepens and extends this pulse by enhancing the N3 sleep architecture that gates GH secretion. The glymphatic system — the brain's waste clearance mechanism that flushes amyloid-beta, tau, and other metabolic byproducts from the interstitium into CSF — is approximately 10-fold more active during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness; DSIP's enhancement of N3 sleep duration directly supports this clearance function, providing mechanistic rationale for pairing DSIP with the neural/neuroprotective compounds in Category V (Semax, Adamax, Cerebrolysin, P021). Additionally, DSIP has demonstrated direct anti-stress activity — reducing stress-induced basal and reactive corticosterone elevation in animal models, suggesting a direct HPA axis-modulating effect that compounds its sleep benefits by reducing the cortisol-mediated sleep architecture disruption that characterizes stress-related insomnia. The dosing window (pre-bed, 30–60 minutes before sleep) is functionally critical — DSIP acts on sleep-initiating thalamic and hypothalamic circuits that are specifically responsive to endogenous sleep-promoting signals during the pre-sleep behavioral window. Administration at any other time does not produce the same delta-wave promoting effect and may produce inappropriate daytime drowsiness. The circadian reset application (1–2 nights of 200mcg after severe time-zone displacement) reflects DSIP's ability to drive delta sleep onset in a body whose circadian phase has been displaced — forcing the sleep oscillator into a restorative cycle at the new local time rather than waiting for gradual circadian re-entrainment. The contraindication with narcolepsy reflects the fact that narcoleptic subjects already have dysregulated transitions between sleep states including sudden delta sleep intrusions; adding exogenous DSIP could destabilize an already-fragile wake maintenance system. The severe depression contraindication reflects the EEG abnormality of depression — characterized by shortened REM latency and disturbed NREM architecture — where artificially deepening delta sleep without addressing the underlying monoamine and stress-axis pathophysiology may alter sleep architecture in unpredictable ways.

contraindications: Narcolepsy — DSIP drives delta sleep-state induction in thalamocortical circuits; in subjects with narcolepsy, which is characterized by dysregulated and abrupt sleep-state transitions (REM intrusions, cataplexy, sleep paralysis), exogenous delta sleep promotion may further destabilize the already-fragile boundary between sleep and wake states.

Severe major depressive disorder with psychomotor retardation — the altered NREM/REM sleep architecture characteristic of severe depression (shortened REM latency, reduced slow-wave sleep proportion) may respond unpredictably to exogenous DSIP; artificially deepening delta sleep without addressing the underlying HPA axis dysregulation and monoamine depletion could worsen the condition.
Known hypersensitivity to DSIP or peptide excipients.

Daytime or non-pre-bed administration — DSIP must be administered within the pre-sleep behavioral window (30–60 minutes before intended sleep onset); administration at any other time of day produces inappropriate drowsiness, circadian disruption, and loss of the specific thalamocortical sleep-induction mechanism.

Operating heavy machinery, driving, or any safety-critical activity within 4–6 hours of DSIP administration — the delta sleep-inducing effect creates significant drowsiness; subjects must be in a position to sleep following administration.

Concurrent use with CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, z-drugs, opioids, barbiturates, alcohol) — additive CNS depression; the combined sedative effect could produce dangerous respiratory depression and excessive sedation.
Pregnancy — no safety data; neuromodulatory peptide effects on fetal thalamic and hypothalamic development are not characterized.
Breastfeeding — no safety data.
Pediatric use — sleep architecture differs substantially in children and adolescents; safety not established.
sideEffects: Next-day grogginess and lethargy — the most commonly reported adverse effect; dose-dependent; excessive delta sleep induction extends into early morning hours producing post-sleep inertia; most pronounced when doses exceed individual threshold (typically >400mcg); managed by starting at 100mcg and escalating slowly.

Excessive sedation within the dosing window — if DSIP takes effect before the subject has completed necessary pre-bed activities; the 30–60 minute administration window is a precise recommendation, not a loose guideline.

Unusual dreams or altered dream content — delta sleep promotion alters the REM/NREM cycle architecture; the subsequent REM rebound that follows deep NREM may produce more vivid or intense dreaming in some subjects.
Morning hypotension and dizziness on standing — sluggish autonomic recovery from deep delta sleep in some subjects; drink water before standing; do not stand abruptly.
Mild headache on waking — uncommon; possibly related to the altered neurovascular tone during deep sleep or glymphatic activity changes.

Rebound insomnia on cessation — mild; not a withdrawal syndrome in the pharmacological sense but a functional consequence of DSIP-habituated sleep architecture adjusting back to baseline; typically resolves within 1–3 nights.

HPA axis modulation — DSIP has documented effects on corticosterone and LH pulsatility; at high doses, chronic use may produce subclinical changes in cortisol awakening response or LH pulse amplitude; monitor in subjects with pre-existing endocrine conditions.

Tolerance development with continuous long-term use — the mechanistic basis for the 8–12 week cycle limit and 4–8 week washout; continuous exposure reduces the sleep-promoting response as receptor systems adapt.

records.name: Eloralintide
records.description: Eloralintide (development code LY3841136) is a synthetic long-acting amylin analog developed by Eli Lilly as a selective amylin receptor agonist — its defining pharmacological distinction from earlier amylin-class compounds being its 12-fold preferential potency at AMY1R (amylin receptor 1) over the calcitonin receptor (CTR). Amylin receptors are heterodimeric complexes formed from the calcitonin receptor paired with one of three receptor activity-modifying proteins: RAMP1+CTR = AMY1R, RAMP2+CTR = AMY2R, RAMP3+CTR = AMY3R. Earlier amylin analogs — pramlintide (native sequence, multiple daily dosing), cagrilintide (Novo Nordisk, once-weekly), and petrelintide (Zealand/Roche) — activate both amylin receptor complexes and the calcitonin receptor with comparable potency; calcitonin receptor activation governs calcium homeostasis, bone metabolism, and is hypothesized to contribute to the tolerability limitations seen with non-selective amylin analogs. Eloralintide's AMY1R selectivity is designed to preserve the full metabolic satiety benefits of amylin receptor activation while minimizing calcitonin receptor-mediated signals. The structural engineering also produced a half-life of approximately 14 days — significantly longer than cagrilintide's 7-day half-life — which produces exceptionally flat pharmacokinetic concentration-time profiles across the weekly dosing interval: peak-to-trough ratios of only 1.28–1.38 at steady state, compared to the higher peaks of weekly GLP-1 receptor agonists. This flat pharmacokinetic profile is the second pharmacological feature believed to contribute to eloralintide's improved gastrointestinal tolerability relative to other amylin and incretin agents — the spike in drug concentration that correlates with nausea at the peak of weekly GLP-1RA dosing is substantially attenuated with eloralintide's slow absorption and ultra-long half-life. Eloralintide acts centrally — at AMY1R in the area postrema, nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), and hypothalamic arcuate nucleus — to reduce food intake, increase satiety, reduce fasting appetite, and suppress glucagon secretion through circuits that are anatomically and pharmacologically distinct from GLP-1 receptor signaling pathways. The Phase 2 Lancet trial (Billings LK et al., November 2025, n=263, 48 weeks, 46 US centers) established eloralintide's dose-response efficacy and safety profile as a once-weekly subcutaneous monotherapy for obesity: mean placebo-adjusted weight loss ranged from −9.0% at 1mg to −20.1% at 9mg, with the 6→9mg escalation arm achieving −19.7% — comparable to the 9mg fixed dose while providing better early tolerability. The 9mg and 6→9mg groups achieved the highest rates of ≥20% and ≥25% weight loss among participants. These Phase 2 figures position eloralintide competitively against the incretin class: 20.1% weight loss at 48 weeks approaches tirzepatide's 22.5% at 72 weeks (Phase 3 SURMOUNT-1) and retatrutide's 24.2% at 48 weeks (Phase 2) — a remarkable outcome for a single-receptor mechanism that historically achieved 5–7% weight loss with pramlintide. The gastric emptying effect of eloralintide is an important mechanistic differentiator: unlike GLP-1 receptor agonists (which produce sustained, clinically significant gastric emptying delay throughout treatment) and the native amylin analog pramlintide (which produces persistent gastric emptying inhibition), eloralintide's Phase 1 acetaminophen absorption data showed a modest initial gastric emptying effect at Week 1 that returned to baseline by Week 12 — suggesting adaptation or AMY1R receptor-specific regulation of gastric motility that is distinct from calcitonin receptor-mediated gastroparesis. This transient rather than sustained gastric emptying effect, if confirmed in Phase 3, would represent a major safety and tolerability advantage over semaglutide and cagrilintide for pre-surgical and aspiration-risk populations. The strategic role of eloralintide in the obesity pharmacotherapy landscape is as both a monotherapy for incretin-intolerant subjects and as a complementary combination partner for incretin therapies. Eli Lilly is actively evaluating eloralintide in combination with retatrutide-class agents (NCT06916065) on the hypothesis that AMY1R agonism and GLP-1/GIP/glucagon receptor agonism act through distinct hypothalamic and brainstem circuits, with the combination producing additive or synergistic weight loss at more tolerable individual doses than maximal incretin monotherapy. In this database's compatibility mapping, eloralintide is therefore classified as synergistic with cagrilintide (amylin receptor dual-axis co-stimulation, as in CagriSema) and with the GLP-1R agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) through the same non-overlapping circuit rationale; it is contraindicated in combination with other eloralintide sources and with CagriSema (which already contains cagrilintide as the amylin component). As of July 2026, eloralintide is investigational — Phase 3 ENLIGHTEN-1 monotherapy trial is enrolling — and has not received FDA or EMA approval for any indication.
