washout: Cycle Length: Indefinite maintenance use at the established tolerated dose is the likely clinical model, consistent with the obesity pharmacotherapy paradigm.
Washout: Given the ~14-day half-life, full pharmacological clearance requires approximately 8-10 weeks (5-7 half-lives) after the final dose if ceasing treatment.
Rebound: Gradual step-down over 4-6 weeks is recommended before full cessation to reduce the rate of weight regain, consistent with the step-down approach used for GLP-1 receptor agonists.
contraindications: Personal or family history of Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC) — the theoretical thyroid C-cell tumor risk associated with calcitonin receptor-family agonism applies to this class; although eloralintide's AMY1R selectivity substantially reduces calcitonin receptor activation relative to cagrilintide, residual AMY3R and CTR activity remains and the MTC class-level caution should be observed pending long-term Phase 3 thyroid safety data.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN2) — MEN2 patients have near-universal MTC predisposition; the calcitonin receptor-family class signal warrants avoidance pending definitive eloralintide-specific thyroid safety data from Phase 3.

Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes — excluded from all eloralintide clinical trials to date; the amylin receptor-mediated glucagon suppression in the context of existing diabetes management (particularly insulin therapy) carries hypoglycemia risk; the glycemic effects of eloralintide in dysglycemic populations have not been characterized and are being evaluated in separate studies.

Concurrent insulin therapy — the amylin class carries a precedent for severe hypoglycemia when co-administered with insulin, established by the FDA boxed warning on pramlintide (Symlin); eloralintide's amylin receptor agonism in the context of insulin-dependent subjects carries this class-level hypoglycemia risk.

Concurrent insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas, meglitinides) — increased hypoglycemia risk from the combination of enhanced glucose-dependent insulin secretion amplification and amylin receptor-mediated appetite/caloric suppression.

Concurrent use of other amylin receptor agonists (cagrilintide, pramlintide, petrelintide) or CagriSema — redundant amylin receptor loading produces additive adverse effects without additional therapeutic benefit; CagriSema already contains cagrilintide as the amylin component.

Pre-existing gastroparesis — while eloralintide's Phase 1 data suggests the gastric emptying delay may be transient rather than sustained, the initial gastric motility effect at cycle initiation in subjects with pre-existing gastroparesis warrants caution; this contraindication may be revised as Phase 3 gastric emptying data matures.
Chronic heart disease, hepatic impairment, or renal impairment — excluded from Phase 1 and Phase 2 trials; pharmacokinetics and safety in these populations have not been characterized.

Abnormal resting heart rate at baseline — eloralintide produced dose-dependent decreases in mean pulse rate of up to −14.4 bpm at the 12mg dose in Phase 1; subjects with pre-existing bradycardia or conduction disorders require cardiac evaluation before initiation.
Known hypersensitivity to eloralintide (LY3841136) or formulation excipients.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding — weight loss pharmacotherapy is contraindicated during pregnancy; eloralintide's effects on fetal development and lactation have not been evaluated.

Pre-surgical procedures requiring general anesthesia — while the gastric emptying effect appears transient with eloralintide, the amylin class aspiration risk consideration warrants a minimum 4-week cessation (3 half-lives, approximately 90% drug clearance) before elective general anesthesia pending definitive Phase 3 gastric emptying characterization.
Pediatric subjects — not evaluated in subjects under 18 years of age.
sideEffects: Nausea — the most common adverse event in Phase 2; highly dose-dependent, ranging from 11% at 1mg to 64% at 6mg (fixed dose without titration) versus 14% in placebo; the Phase 2 escalation arms (3→9mg and 6→9mg) produced lower nausea rates than the fixed 6mg and 9mg arms, confirming that gradual titration significantly mitigates nausea burden; lower overall nausea incidence than comparable semaglutide and tirzepatide data.

Fatigue and asthenia — dose-dependent; 0% at 1mg to 46% at 9mg in Phase 2 versus 12% placebo; related to both central AMY1R CNS effects and the metabolic consequences of rapid weight loss; typically most pronounced in the first 4–8 weeks of each dose escalation step and attenuates with continued dosing.

Decreased appetite — the intended pharmacological effect; reported as an adverse event in 19% of Phase 1 subjects (11% in Phase 1b at doses up to 12mg); reflects the appetite suppression mechanism that drives the weight loss benefit; classified as adverse only in subjects who found the degree of appetite reduction distressing or who underate to a degree producing nutritional deficit.
Headache — reported in 12% of Phase 1b subjects overall; more common at higher dose levels (6mg and 12mg); mechanism unclear; typically mild and transient; attenuates with dose stabilization.

Pulse rate reduction — a notable and dose-dependent pharmacodynamic effect: mean decreases from baseline of −7.1 bpm at 3mg, −8.3 bpm at 6mg, and −14.4 bpm at 12mg in Phase 1b; the mechanism reflects AMY1R-mediated cardiac chronotropic modulation; no symptomatic bradycardia was reported in Phase 1 or Phase 2 trials at doses up to 9mg, but this vital sign change warrants monitoring at higher doses and in subjects with pre-existing low heart rate.

Injection site reactions — dose-dependent; injection site pain, erythema, and edema more common at 3mg and above; typically mild; the slow subcutaneous absorption profile (slow tmax, flat concentration curve) means the injection depot persists longer than short-half-life peptides, which may contribute to the injection site reaction rate.
Diarrhea — reported in approximately 10% of Phase 1b subjects; more common at higher doses (12mg: 11.1%); typically mild.
Vomiting — reported in approximately 4% of Phase 1b subjects and up to 8.3% at 12mg; less common than nausea; dose-dependent; managed by dose reduction and gradual titration.

Constipation — reported at 6mg in Phase 1b; consistent with the amylin class effect on gastrointestinal motility; less pronounced than with GLP-1 receptor agonists based on the Phase 2 tolerability comparison.
Abdominal pain — reported in approximately 8.3% of the 12mg Phase 1b cohort; abdominal discomfort is consistent with GI motility changes at higher doses.

Mood changes and depressed mood — a safety signal that emerged in Phase 1b: depressed mood was reported in 4.3% of the 6mg cohort and 5.6% of the 12mg cohort; one case of persistent depressive disorder (moderate severity, lasted 4 days, resolved upon discontinuation) was reported in the 12mg arm; all three participants with mood events in the 12mg cohort were discontinued from treatment; this mood signal does not exist for GLP-1 receptor agonists and may reflect a central AMY1R CNS effect distinct from the incretin class; requires Phase 3 characterization.

Lean body mass depletion — as with all agents producing significant caloric restriction and weight loss, skeletal muscle loss accompanies fat loss in the absence of adequate protein intake and resistance exercise; active lean mass preservation strategies are recommended.

Long-term safety not fully characterized — eloralintide is investigational with Phase 2 data to 48 weeks in 263 subjects; cardiovascular outcomes, bone metabolism effects (despite AMY1R selectivity reducing calcitonin receptor activation, the long-term skeletal effects are uncharacterized), long-term thyroid safety, and effects in diabetic, cardiac, hepatic, or renally impaired populations are not established and are being evaluated in Phase 3.

records.name: Endoluten
records.description: Endoluten is a Khavinson cytomedin — peptide complex A-8 — extracted from the pineal gland tissue of young animals, and widely regarded as the most foundational oral bioregulator in the Khavinson longevity framework. The pineal gland is the body's master neuroendocrine clock: a small structure deep in the brain that synthesizes melatonin in response to darkness, sets the amplitude of all hormonal circadian rhythms, and coordinates the immune-endocrine axis through pineal regulatory peptides including epithalamin and arginine vasotocin. Endoluten delivers a multi-peptide pineal tissue extract that normalizes the gene expression programs in pinealocytes governing melatonin biosynthesis enzyme production, circadian clock gene activity (BMAL1, PER, CRY, CLOCK), and neuroendocrine pacemaker peptide output — in plain terms, it signals aging pineal cells to resume the melatonin production and circadian pacemaker function they progressively abandon after age 30. The research evidence for Endoluten and its predecessor pineal cytomedin preparations includes some of the strongest longevity data in the entire Khavinson catalog. Long-term administration studies documented 1.6-1.8-fold reductions in mortality rates in elderly populations over multi-year follow-up. Additional documented outcomes include restoration of melatonin production toward young-adult levels, normalization of the cortisol circadian rhythm, improvement in sleep architecture with deeper slow-wave sleep, reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) through melatonin's anti-inflammatory pathway, direct thymopoietic immune stimulation, and telomere length preservation through pineal-level epigenetic mechanisms. Evening dosing is biologically mandated — pineal gene programs are circadian-gated, and Endoluten performs best when administered in alignment with the natural darkness-triggered melatonin synthesis window. What makes Endoluten uniquely important in this database is its position as the oral cytomedin counterpart to Epithalon — but with a meaningfully broader scope. Epithalon is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) designed around the telomerase-activating core sequence isolated from pineal extract; Endoluten retains the full native pineal peptide repertoire including the neuroendocrine regulatory components, thymic-stimulating pineal hormones, and circadian architecture signals that Epithalon's minimized sequence does not replicate. For subjects on injectable protocols, Endoluten oral cycling adds neuroendocrine breadth to Epithalon's telomeric precision. For subjects preferring oral-only protocols, Endoluten is the most complete single-compound pineal aging intervention available — simultaneously addressing circadian restoration, melatonin normalization, neuroendocrine amplitude recovery, and the broad longevity evidence base that has made the Khavinson pineal bioregulator the cornerstone of the entire anti-aging framework.

contraindications: Hormone-sensitive cancers with melatonin receptor expression — pineal gland peptides and melatonin have complex relationships with certain hormone-sensitive tumors; subjects with active breast cancer, melanoma, or other melatonin receptor-expressing tumors should obtain oncological evaluation before initiating.

Autoimmune conditions requiring strict immune suppression — melatonin has direct thymopoietic and immunostimulatory effects; Endoluten's melatonin-normalizing mechanism could stimulate immune activity in subjects requiring immunosuppression for autoimmune disease management.

Concurrent high-dose exogenous melatonin supplementation — Endoluten normalizes endogenous melatonin synthesis; combining with high-dose exogenous melatonin creates an uncharacterized additive effect on circadian amplitude and receptor sensitivity.
Known hypersensitivity to Endoluten (pineal gland tissue cytomedin peptide complex A-8) or formulation excipients including gelatin.

Pregnancy — pineal-regulated circadian and neuroendocrine programs during pregnancy involve specific gestational adaptations; exogenous pineal bioregulator activity has not been evaluated in this context.

Active endocrine tumors (pituitary adenoma, carcinoid, pheochromocytoma) — Endoluten's neuroendocrine axis modulation in the context of active endocrine hypersecretion requires endocrinological evaluation.

Severe active depression or bipolar disorder in manic phase — circadian rhythm disruption is both a feature and driver of mood disorders; Endoluten's circadian normalization activity in subjects with active psychiatric circadian dysregulation requires psychiatric supervision.
sideEffects: Mild transient sleep changes in first cycle days — as melatonin synthesis normalizes and circadian amplitude is restored, subjects occasionally experience vivid dreams, transiently deeper sleep, or mild initial sleep quality changes in the first 3-5 days; typically resolves as circadian rhythms stabilize.

Mild morning grogginess on initiation (rare) — if Endoluten is taken too close to bedtime and produces more pronounced nocturnal melatonin normalization than expected, mild morning grogginess is occasionally reported in the first few days; resolve by taking earlier in the evening.

Mild mood or energy fluctuation in first days — neuroendocrine circadian normalization occasionally produces subtle mood or energy level changes as the HPA axis cortisol rhythm normalizes; typically experienced as positive.
Mild gastrointestinal discomfort from oral capsule — as a before-meals oral cytomedin; occasional mild gastric discomfort in first days; resolves with continued administration.

No serious adverse events documented in the Khavinson research literature at standard protocol doses — Endoluten's safety profile across decades of Russian clinical use in elderly, immunosenescent, and neuroendocrine aging populations is clean; no serious hormonal, cardiovascular, or neurological adverse events have been attributed to Endoluten.

Unknown interaction profile with synthetic melatonin receptor agonists (ramelteon, tasimelteon) — Endoluten's endogenous melatonin synthesis normalization combined with exogenous melatonin receptor agonist pharmacotherapy creates an uncharacterized combined circadian signal; monitoring for excessive sedation or circadian over-amplitude effects is appropriate.

Potential modest cortisol rhythm changes — as the circadian HPA axis amplitude normalizes, subjects on exogenous corticosteroid therapy may experience minor shifts in cortisol suppression patterns; monitor in subjects on daily corticosteroids.

records.name: Epithalon (Epitalon)
records.description: Epithalon (also spelled Epitalon) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) developed by Vladimir Khavinson at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, derived from epithalamin — a natural polypeptide extract of the pineal gland. The tetrapeptide sequence was identified as the bioactive core of epithalamin responsible for its anti-aging and neuroendocrine regulatory effects, and synthesized as a defined single-molecule compound to overcome the batch variability limitations of the natural extract. Epithalon's primary and most extensively documented mechanism is activation of telomerase (TERT — Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase) — the enzyme responsible for extending telomeric DNA repeats (TTAGGG hexanucleotide repeats) at chromosome ends. Telomeres shorten with each cell division due to the end-replication problem inherent in DNA polymerase biology; when telomere length reaches a critical threshold, cells enter replicative senescence (the same state that FOXO4-DRI targets for clearance). Telomerase activation by Epithalon has been demonstrated in multiple in vitro and in vivo studies to elongate telomeres in somatic cells that normally lack telomerase activity — effectively resetting a fundamental molecular clock of cellular aging. Beyond TERT activation, Epithalon acts on the pineal gland to restore melatonin synthesis and secretion that declines with age — the age-related decline in pineal melatonin output contributes to circadian rhythm dysregulation, impaired sleep architecture, reduced antioxidant protection (melatonin is a direct free radical scavenger), and HPA axis dysregulation. Epithalon normalizes these pineal functions by binding to and modulating pinealocyte gene expression through a bioregulator peptide mechanism shared by all Khavinson compounds. The human clinical evidence for Epithalon is unique among longevity peptides in that it extends to actual mortality outcome data — not merely biomarker or quality-of-life endpoints. The Khavinson group published longitudinal studies following elderly subjects (age 60–80 at enrollment) over 10–15 year periods in which twice-yearly Epithalon (or Epithalon + Thymalin) administration was associated with 28–45% reductions in all-cause mortality, significant reductions in cardiovascular events, reduced cancer incidence, and maintained immune function compared to age-matched controls. While these studies have the methodological limitations characteristic of much Russian longevity research (single center, not double-blind placebo-controlled by Western standards), the consistency of the mortality outcomes across multiple cohorts and the 15-year follow-up duration make them among the most compelling longevity intervention data available for any peptide in this database. Additional research demonstrated Epithalon's ability to: suppress oncogene expression in human mammary gland cells in vitro, normalize disturbed cell cycle kinetics in aging tissue, reduce chromosomal aberration frequency, and restore melatonin rhythm amplitude in elderly subjects to values closer to young adult levels. Epithalon's melatonin-restoring activity mechanistically explains its pre-bed dosing window — administration timed to coincide with the natural pineal activation window of darkness maximizes the synergy between the drug's pineal stimulatory effect and the circadian-gated melatonin synthesis machinery. The synergistic designations for Epithalon — Vilon (the immune system bioregulator), Thymalin (the thymic bioregulator), DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide), FOXO4-DRI (senolytic), and Selank (anxiolytic/neuroprotective) — reflect the multi-axis anti-aging strategy at the core of the Khavinson longevity protocol. Epithalon addresses the telomeric/circadian/melatonin axis. Thymalin restores thymic immune competence. Vilon normalizes immune-neuroendocrine cross-regulation. DSIP deepens the slow-wave sleep that Epithalon's melatonin restoration supports architecturally. FOXO4-DRI clears the senescent cells that Epithalon's telomere-lengthening prevents future cells from becoming. Together these compounds create a comprehensive biological age intervention spanning the molecular clock (telomeres), the circadian clock (melatonin/pineal), the immune aging clock (thymus/T-cells), the sleep restorative architecture (DSIP/delta waves), and the senescent cell burden (FOXO4-DRI) — arguably the most mechanistically complete anti-aging protocol in this database.

No documented toxicity at standard doses in the 40+ year Russian clinical use history — the safety profile of Epithalon across decades of Russian and Ukrainian clinical application is exceptionally clean; no serious adverse events have been documented in the published Khavinson literature at standard protocol doses.

Theoretical cancer promotion risk (not documented in clinical data) — the TERT activation mechanism raises the theoretical concern above; however, in the 40+ year human use history including elderly subjects (who have the highest background cancer incidence), no increase in cancer rates has been documented — and the published data shows reduced cancer incidence; this remains a mechanistic theoretical concern not supported by the available observational data.

records.name: EROS
records.description: EROS is a sexual wellness and reproductive-axis blend combining Kisspeptin-10, Oxytocin, and PT-141 into a single coordinated libido, arousal, bonding, and HPG-axis support system. The blend is structured around a 5mg Kisspeptin-10, 2mg Oxytocin, and 5mg PT-141 ratio, creating a 12mg total vial with a 5:2:5 composition. Kisspeptin-10 provides the hormonal infrastructure layer through KISS1R activation upstream of GnRH, LH, and FSH signaling. Oxytocin adds the emotional bonding, attachment, intimacy, and trust-signaling component through OXTR-mediated social and limbic circuitry. PT-141 provides the central arousal and desire layer through melanocortin MC3R/MC4R signaling. From a performance and optimization standpoint, EROS is positioned for low libido, HSDD, menopausal or andropausal libido decline, post-SSRI sexual dysfunction, sexual dysfunction with emotional disconnection, fertility-support contexts, and situational intimacy enhancement. Unlike a single acute arousal peptide, EROS can be used either as a foundation-style HPG restoration protocol or as a true event-based intimacy protocol. Subcutaneous administration is preferred for structured HPG-axis restoration and longer-cycle libido work, while intranasal administration is appropriate for faster-onset acute intimacy use because the source document supports full intranasal use for the blend.

records.name: Erythropoietin (EPO)
records.description: Erythropoietin (EPO) is an endogenous glycoprotein hormone produced primarily by peritubular cells in the renal cortex in response to tissue hypoxia — sensed via the HIF-1α (Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1-alpha) pathway. When oxygen delivery to the kidneys drops, HIF-1α is stabilized rather than degraded, driving transcription of the EPO gene and releasing EPO into the bloodstream. EPO binds to the erythropoietin receptor (EPOR) on erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow, activating the JAK2/STAT5 signaling pathway that drives erythroid progenitor proliferation, differentiation, and survival — suppressing apoptosis in burst-forming units erythroid (BFU-E) and colony-forming units erythroid (CFU-E) to produce mature red blood cells (erythrocytes). The result is increased red blood cell mass, elevated hemoglobin concentration, and substantially enhanced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. Recombinant human EPO (rhEPO) — the synthetic form used in research and medicine — is glycoprotein-identical to endogenous EPO and activates the same EPOR pathway with the same downstream biology. The performance impact of elevated hematocrit is direct: VO2max and aerobic endurance are rate-limited by oxygen delivery to mitochondria in working muscle, and increasing hemoglobin concentration from a normal ~15 g/dL to 17–18 g/dL increases aerobic capacity by a magnitude that no other single intervention can replicate. EPO's medical applications are well-established and FDA-approved: treatment of anemia in chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy-induced anemia, and anemia associated with zidovudine therapy in HIV. In these clinical contexts, EPO is dosed to target hemoglobin of 10–12 g/dL — a level that corrects anemia without producing erythrocytosis. The research and performance application is pharmacologically distinct: doses targeting hematocrit elevation above the normal range (above 50% in males, above 45% in females) are used to push oxygen-carrying capacity beyond physiological norms. This is the context that makes EPO simultaneously the most potent endurance performance compound in this database and the one with the most serious acute safety risk profile. EPO has been directly implicated in the deaths of approximately 20 professional cyclists in the late 1980s and 1990s — athletes who used extremely high doses without hematocrit monitoring, developing hematocrits above 60%, polycythemia-level blood viscosity, and fatal thrombotic events during low-heart-rate sleep when cardiac output dropped and thick blood formed clots in coronary and cerebral vessels. These deaths defined EPO's risk profile and established the non-negotiable requirement for rigorous hematocrit and blood viscosity monitoring throughout any EPO protocol. The hematocrit monitoring requirement is not precautionary language — it is the primary life-safety intervention for EPO use. The standard safety threshold is a hematocrit ceiling of 50% for males and 47% for females; protocols must include hematocrit testing every 1–2 weeks during loading phases, and EPO must be held immediately if hematocrit approaches these thresholds. Hydration status dramatically affects hematocrit: dehydration hemoconcentrates the blood and can push a borderline hematocrit into the dangerous range without any additional EPO dose — mandatory hydration (minimum 3L water daily) is a non-negotiable co-requirement. The maintenance micro-dosing protocol (500–1000 IU once weekly) represents a harm-reduction approach for subjects who have completed a loading cycle: it maintains the elevated erythrocyte mass without continued bone marrow stimulation, reduces the magnitude of inter-dose hematocrit swings, and allows for lower total EPO exposure while preserving the performance benefit.

washout: Cycle Length: Varies.
Washout: Requires continuous, rigorous monitoring of hematocrit and blood viscosity. Do not run blindly.
contraindications: Elevated baseline hematocrit (>50% males, >45% females) — EPO will drive hematocrit further above normal range into dangerous polycythemia territory; absolute contraindication until baseline is confirmed normal.

Uncontrolled hypertension — EPO increases blood pressure through increased blood viscosity, direct vasoconstriction via EPOR on vascular smooth muscle, and endothelin-1 upregulation; pre-existing hypertension is dramatically worsened and increases stroke risk.

History of thromboembolism, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism — EPO-induced polycythemia creates a profoundly hypercoagulable state; any history of clotting disorders makes EPO potentially lethal.
History of stroke or TIA — increased blood viscosity in subjects with prior cerebrovascular events creates extremely high risk of repeat ischemic stroke.
Coronary artery disease or recent myocardial infarction — viscous blood in narrowed coronary vessels significantly elevates risk of acute myocardial infarction.
Known hypersensitivity to erythropoietin, albumin, or any formulation excipients — including pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) antibody development.

Active malignancy — EPO receptors are expressed on many tumor cell types; EPOR signaling can drive tumor cell proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis; EPO administration in cancer is associated with reduced survival in several randomized trials.
Hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease, thalassemia) — increasing red cell mass in subjects with abnormal hemoglobin dramatically worsens blood viscosity and vaso-occlusive crisis risk.
Polycythemia vera or other myeloproliferative disorders — EPO in subjects with autonomous erythroid overproduction will produce life-threatening erythrocytosis.
Chronic liver disease with coagulopathy — impaired clotting factor synthesis combined with EPO-induced hypercoagulability creates unpredictable coagulation risk.

Athletes competing under WADA or USADA anti-doping regulations — EPO is one of the most tested-for prohibited substances in competitive sport; detection window extends several weeks with current urine and blood passport methodologies.
Pregnancy — EPO during pregnancy has not been established as safe; EPOR is expressed in trophoblasts and its role in placental development is not fully characterized.

Dehydration — hemoconcentration from dehydration combined with EPO-elevated red cell mass can push hematocrit to fatal levels; adequate hydration (3L+ daily) is a mandatory co-requirement for any EPO protocol.
sideEffects: Polycythemia and hyperviscosity — the direct pharmacological consequence of EPO's mechanism at supratherapeutic doses; hematocrit above 50–55% dramatically increases whole blood viscosity, reducing microcirculatory flow and creating systemic thrombotic risk; the primary reason EPO has killed athletes.

Thromboembolism (stroke, MI, DVT, PE) — the most serious and potentially fatal adverse effect; blood clots forming in cerebral, coronary, or deep venous vessels from hyperviscous blood; risk is highest during sleep when heart rate and cardiac output are lowest, slowing already-thick blood through vessels.

Hypertension — EPO raises blood pressure in virtually all subjects; multiple mechanisms including viscosity, direct EPOR-mediated vascular smooth muscle vasoconstriction, and endothelin upregulation; blood pressure monitoring throughout protocol is mandatory.
Headache — commonly reported; related to increased blood viscosity and mild hypertension.
Flu-like symptoms (fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia) — particularly during loading phase; related to the acute hematopoietic response and cytokine release from bone marrow stimulation.
Injection site reactions — pain, redness, bruising at subcutaneous injection site; standard.

Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) — a rare but serious immunological adverse effect where anti-EPO neutralizing antibodies develop, cross-reacting with endogenous EPO and eliminating all erythropoiesis; results in severe transfusion-dependent anemia; reported primarily with subcutaneous administration of certain EPO formulations.
Seizures — reported in clinical use, particularly in subjects with uremia or rapid hematocrit increases; mechanism involves cerebral blood flow changes from viscosity and blood pressure effects.

Iron deficiency — EPO-driven erythropoiesis rapidly depletes iron stores; functional iron deficiency limits the erythropoietic response and produces microcytic anemia despite normal ferritin; iron supplementation is required during loading protocols.
Thrombocytosis — platelet count may increase alongside red cell mass; additional contribution to hypercoagulable state.

Rebound anemia on cessation — endogenous EPO production is suppressed during exogenous administration; abrupt cessation can produce a transient period of reduced erythropoiesis and relative anemia before the axis recovers.

Cardiac hypertrophy — chronic EPO use with sustained elevated hematocrit increases cardiac afterload from blood viscosity; long-term risk of left ventricular hypertrophy with chronic supraphysiological use.

records.name: FOXO4-DRI
records.description: FOXO4-DRI is a D-amino acid retro-inverso peptide designed to competitively disrupt the protein-protein interaction between FOXO4 (Forkhead Box O4) and p53 (tumor protein 53) — a critical survival complex that senescent cells exploit to resist apoptosis. Senescent cells are cells that have permanently exited the cell cycle following replication-induced DNA damage, oncogenic stress, or oxidative injury, and which persist in tissues producing a chronic inflammatory secretome known as the SASP (Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype) — a cocktail of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α), matrix metalloproteinases, and growth factors that degrades surrounding tissue architecture and drives the chronic inflammation underlying aging, fibrosis, metabolic disease, and neurodegenerative conditions. In normal cells, p53 in the nucleus drives apoptosis in response to DNA damage — but senescent cells re-route p53 into the cytoplasm where FOXO4 binds it and sequesters it, preventing nuclear re-entry and the initiation of apoptotic gene transcription. The senescent cell thereby retains an anti-apoptotic phenotype indefinitely: it cannot replicate (cell cycle arrest) but it also cannot die (p53 sequestration). FOXO4-DRI was designed by Peter de Keizer and colleagues at the Erasmus University Medical Center (published Cell, 2017) as a high-affinity competitive inhibitor of the FOXO4-p53 interaction — by occupying the FOXO4 binding interface, it displaces p53 back into the nucleus where it can execute its pro-apoptotic transcriptional program, selectively killing senescent cells while sparing healthy proliferating cells (which do not depend on the FOXO4-p53 survival interaction). The landmark 2017 Cell paper by de Keizer and colleagues remains the foundational evidence for FOXO4-DRI. In naturally aged mice and in fast-aging XFE progeroid mice, FOXO4-DRI administration reduced senescent cell burden in liver, kidney, and adipose tissue, improved physical fitness (grip strength, running endurance), restored liver architecture, reduced liver fibrosis, improved renal function, and produced fur regrowth in alopecia-affected animals — all hallmarks of biological age reversal rather than merely slowing aging. The D-amino acid retro-inverso design is critical to the compound's in vivo efficacy: natural L-amino acid peptides corresponding to the same sequence are rapidly degraded by serum and cellular proteases within minutes to hours, making them pharmacologically impractical for achieving intracellular protein-protein interaction disruption. The retro-inverso modification — reversing the peptide backbone while substituting D-amino acids throughout — creates a protease-resistant mirror-image structure that maintains the 3D surface complementarity needed for FOXO4 binding while achieving plasma half-lives sufficient for intracellular delivery. FOXO4-DRI is therefore not a natural peptide analog but a de novo engineered therapeutic peptidomimetic — among the most sophisticated molecular designs of any compound in this database. The senolytic category and the 1–2 times per year cycle protocol reflect the fundamental biology of cellular senescence clearance. Senescent cells accumulate over decades of aging and stress; they cannot be meaningfully replenished from a damage-accumulation standpoint in a matter of weeks. A single FOXO4-DRI cycle clears a fraction of the existing senescent cell burden, and the months-long off period serves two functions: it allows the body time to replace cleared senescent cells with functional progenitor-derived replacements that restore tissue architecture, and it allows the SASP-cleared inflammatory milieu to normalize before the next cycle. Running FOXO4-DRI continuously would not provide ongoing benefit beyond the initial clearance — senescent cells require time to re-accumulate before a subsequent cycle achieves meaningful additional clearance. The synergy with Epithalon reflects the complementary anti-aging mechanisms: FOXO4-DRI addresses the cellular senescence burden (removing the aging cells), while Epithalon addresses the telomeric/epigenetic aging clock through TERT activation (protecting the remaining cells from reaching the damage threshold that drives future senescence) — targeting the two most mechanistically important axes of cellular aging simultaneously.

contraindications: Active malignancy or history of cancer — FOXO4-DRI disrupts the FOXO4-p53 survival interaction that senescent cells depend on; however, many cancer cells also exploit FOXO4-mediated p53 sequestration as a pro-survival mechanism; in the oncological context, uncontrolled p53 nuclear re-entry in tumor cells without clinical supervision could produce unpredictable outcomes; use in active cancer subjects requires oncological evaluation.

Pregnancy — the pro-apoptotic cellular clearance mechanism of FOXO4-DRI has not been evaluated in the context of pregnancy; placental trophoblast cells and fetal cells share some characteristics with senescent cells and the developmental safety profile is entirely uncharacterized.

Active systemic immunosuppression (organ transplant recipients, high-dose corticosteroid therapy, chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression) — the clearance of senescent cells generates a transient acute inflammatory response as cleared cell debris is processed by the immune system; in immunosuppressed subjects this response may be dysregulated.
Severe autoimmune disease in active flare — the acute inflammatory pulse from senescent cell clearance could worsen an already hyperactivated autoimmune inflammatory state.

Severe hepatic or renal impairment — the cellular clearance and metabolic demands of FOXO4-DRI-induced apoptosis place additional burden on hepatic and renal clearance pathways; safety in severe organ impairment is uncharacterized.
Known hypersensitivity to FOXO4-DRI, D-amino acid retro-inverso peptides, or formulation excipients.

Subjects under age 25 — the cellular senescence burden in young subjects is negligible; senolytic activity in tissue with a low senescent cell fraction has no meaningful therapeutic target and could theoretically disrupt progenitor cell populations that express stress-related FOXO4 activity transiently.

Concurrent use of other senolytics (dasatinib, quercetin, navitoclax) — additive senolytic activity may produce excessive simultaneous senescent cell clearance, overwhelming the immune system's capacity to process cleared debris and producing severe SASP-related inflammatory responses.
sideEffects: Lethargy and fatigue during cellular clearance — the most consistently reported adverse effect; as large numbers of senescent cells undergo apoptosis, the immune system mobilizes to clear the cellular debris; the metabolic demand and the transient SASP cytokine release during clearance produce a flu-like fatigue state; duration correlates with the senescent cell burden being cleared.

Joint aches and musculoskeletal discomfort — senescent cells are disproportionately abundant in joint-adjacent tissues (cartilage, synovium, periarticular fat); their clearance produces a transient local inflammatory response characterized by joint stiffness and aching; typically self-limiting as inflammation resolves post-clearance.

Transient acute inflammatory pulse — as senescent cells die and SASP factors are abruptly released from clearing cells, serum inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6) transiently elevate before falling to below-baseline levels as the senescent cell burden decreases; the net long-term effect is anti-inflammatory but the acute clearance phase may be transiently pro-inflammatory.
Mild headache — uncommon; possibly related to the systemic inflammatory response during cellular clearance.
Injection site reactions — mild redness and soreness at the subcutaneous administration site; standard for peptide injection.

Transient liver enzyme elevation — liver contains a high density of senescent hepatic stellate cells and hepatocytes; FOXO4-DRI-driven clearance in liver tissue may transiently elevate ALT/AST as hepatocyte turnover occurs; typically resolves within 2–4 weeks.

Skin changes — some subjects report changes in skin texture, tone, or mild hair regrowth consistent with the de Keizer mouse data showing fur regrowth; these are the desired senolytic tissue restoration effects rather than adverse events.

Unknown long-term safety profile — the human clinical evidence base for FOXO4-DRI is entirely preclinical; the full long-term safety spectrum in humans is not established; all use is strictly research-context with this caveat acknowledged.

records.name: GHK-Cu (Copper Tripeptide-1)
records.description: GHK-Cu (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine copper complex) is a naturally occurring tripeptide found in human plasma, saliva, and urine that declines significantly with age — dropping from roughly 200 ng/mL in plasma at age 20 to under 80 ng/mL by age 60. The copper ion is not merely incidental: it is a required cofactor for the enzymatic machinery that makes GHK-Cu's biological activity possible. Specifically, copper activates lysyl oxidase (the enzyme responsible for crosslinking collagen and elastin into structurally strong fibers), superoxide dismutase (the primary intracellular antioxidant enzyme), cytochrome c oxidase (mitochondrial electron transport chain), and tyrosinase. The tripeptide component acts as a carrier that delivers copper in a bioavailable, tightly chelated form directly into tissues where these enzymes are active. At the signaling level, GHK-Cu simultaneously upregulates TGF-beta-mediated collagen synthesis, activates VEGF and VEGFR2 to drive angiogenesis, suppresses NF-kB to reduce inflammation, and modulates matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-3) and their tissue inhibitors (TIMP-1, TIMP-2) in a context-dependent manner — stimulating matrix breakdown in fibrotic or scar tissue while protecting new collagen in healing tissue. The gene regulation data for GHK-Cu is among the most striking in the peptide research space. Genomic analyses indicate that GHK-Cu modulates the expression of over 4,000 human genes, including upregulation of collagen genes (COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1), antioxidant response genes, DNA repair genes, and stem cell markers — while downregulating inflammatory mediator genes, metastasis-associated genes, and tissue destruction pathways. Research by Pickart and colleagues has noted that the overall gene expression profile after GHK-Cu exposure shifts toward a pattern associated with younger, more regeneratively active tissue. Practically, this translates to dramatically accelerated wound closure, improved skin thickness and elasticity, hair follicle activation (via Wnt/beta-catenin signaling in dermal papilla cells), nerve outgrowth stimulation, and reduction of UV-induced MMP activity that drives collagen fragmentation and photoaging. The most important practical reality of injectable GHK-Cu is the injection site pain — this is not a minor inconvenience but a defining characteristic of the compound at subcutaneous doses. The pain is caused by the copper ion itself interacting with subcutaneous tissue and is dose-dependent and site-dependent. The clinical workaround is well-established: drawing BPC-157 into the same syringe virtually eliminates the sting (the "BPC Blend Buffer" protocol). Frequent site rotation is mandatory to prevent chronic bruising and tissue irritation. The 5-days-on/2-days-off rest schedule exists specifically to allow injection sites to recover between administrations. At extreme doses or with concentrated preparation, there is a theoretical risk of "copper uglies" — paradoxical MMP overactivation causing collagen fragmentation rather than synthesis, particularly with topical forms — though this has not been documented in injectable research at standard doses. Subjects with Wilson's disease or copper metabolism disorders should avoid GHK-Cu entirely.

contraindications: Wilson's disease or other genetic copper metabolism disorders — the copper component of GHK-Cu bypasses normal hepatic copper regulation; copper accumulation in subjects with impaired copper transport (ATP7B mutations) is a serious risk.
Known copper hypersensitivity or copper allergy — systemic injection of a copper complex in a hypersensitive subject may provoke significant immune reactions.

Active malignancy — GHK-Cu promotes angiogenesis via VEGF/VEGFR2 upregulation; while preclinical data suggests anti-metastatic gene regulation, the pro-angiogenic mechanism remains a contraindication in subjects with active tumors.
Pregnancy — no human safety data; copper homeostasis is tightly regulated during fetal development; avoid.
Breastfeeding — no established safety data.
Known hypersensitivity to GHK-Cu or peptide excipients.
Concurrent use of copper-chelating agents (e.g., penicillamine, trientine, zinc supplementation) — will directly neutralize the active copper complex.
Hemochromatosis or iron overload disorders — impaired metal metabolism may affect copper handling.
Individuals with elevated baseline serum copper levels — risk of copper toxicity at systemic injectable doses.
sideEffects: Severe Post-Injection Pain (PIP) — the defining adverse effect of subcutaneous GHK-Cu; caused by the copper ion reacting with subcutaneous tissue; characterized by burning, stinging, redness, and welts at the injection site; intensity varies by concentration, volume, and injection location; nearly eliminated by co-injecting with BPC-157.
Bruising and hematoma formation at injection sites — particularly with daily protocols; mandatory site rotation mitigates this but does not eliminate it.
Local redness and induration — tissue response to copper deposition; resolves between injection sessions; the 5-on/2-off schedule provides recovery time.

Copper toxicity at excessive doses — symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting, metallic taste, nausea, chills, fever, general weakness, and anemia; not typically observed at standard protocol doses but a risk with chronic high-dose use.

"Copper uglies" — a rare paradoxical effect where excessive MMP-1 stimulation at high concentrations causes collagen fragmentation rather than synthesis, resulting in apparent skin quality degradation; primarily documented anecdotally in topical overuse; not formally documented at injectable doses.
Mild systemic fatigue — occasionally reported in first 1–2 weeks of use; likely related to initial tissue remodeling signal load.
Headache — uncommon; possibly related to VEGF-mediated vasodilation.
Temporary melanin increase at injection sites — tyrosinase activation from copper delivery can produce local hyperpigmentation; resolves over weeks after cessation.
Nausea — rare; may be copper-related at higher doses.
Potential MMP overactivation at supraphysiological concentrations — theoretical; context-dependent MMP regulation can shift from constructive to destructive at excessive doses.

records.name: GHK-Cu Glutathione Recovery Blend (GGH)
records.description: The GHK-Cu Glutathione Recovery Blend (product code GGH) is a regeneration and antioxidant injection that combines the copper peptide GHK-Cu with glutathione and supporting amino acids and coenzymes. It is a hybrid blend that pairs a peptide with vitamin and amino acid components, and it is given as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains GHK-Cu 2000mcg, Glutathione 200mg, Histidine 100mg, Glycine 50mg, and NADH 50mg. GHK-Cu is a copper-binding peptide known for supporting skin remodeling, collagen production, wound healing, and tissue regeneration, glutathione is the master antioxidant supporting detoxification and cellular protection, histidine and glycine are amino acids that support tissue repair and are components of glutathione synthesis, and NADH provides a reduced coenzyme that supports cellular energy production. In practice, GGH is used by people focused on tissue regeneration, skin quality, recovery, and antioxidant support, blending the well-known cosmetic and healing reputation of GHK-Cu with the detoxification and cellular-protection profile of glutathione. It appeals to users who want both the structural and appearance benefits of the copper peptide and the antioxidant and recovery support of the accompanying ingredients in a single injection. It can be administered in the morning or evening and is typically run as a standing recovery and regeneration protocol. Because it contains GHK-Cu, it is often positioned alongside skin, anti-aging, and repair goals rather than fat loss, and it complements the healing and aesthetics categories of the broader codex. Mechanistically, GGH combines a regenerative copper peptide (GHK-Cu supporting collagen, remodeling, and healing) with antioxidant and glutathione-synthesis support (glutathione, histidine, glycine) and a cellular energy substrate (NADH), so the injection supports both tissue repair and the antioxidant environment that healing depends on. Users should expect gradual improvements in skin quality, recovery, and general regeneration with consistent use. Because GHK-Cu delivers copper, users running it long term or stacking other copper sources should be mindful of cumulative copper intake and periodically monitor status. Injection sites should be rotated, and anyone with Wilson disease, copper metabolism disorders, or on chelation therapy should avoid this blend or use it only under medical supervision.

records.name: GHRP-2
records.description: GHRP-2 (also known as pralmorelin or KP-102) is a second-generation synthetic hexapeptide Growth Hormone Releasing Peptide and the most scientifically validated GHRP in this database. It is the only GHRP to have achieved any regulatory approval in the world — approved in Japan as pralmorelin for clinical diagnosis of growth hormone deficiency (the GHRP-2 stimulation test), providing a level of formal human pharmacokinetic and safety data uncommon among research peptides. GHRP-2 activates GHS-R1a (the ghrelin receptor) on anterior pituitary somatotrophs, triggering rapid, dose-dependent GH release typically within 15–30 minutes of injection. Its unique D-beta-naphthylalanine (D-BNal) residue at position 2 produces slightly different receptor binding kinetics than GHRP-6, resulting in a pharmacological profile that sits precisely between GHRP-6's non-selective broad stimulation and ipamorelin's highly selective clean profile. In practical terms, GHRP-2 produces strong GH pulses — in head-to-head clinical studies, GH release ranking runs GHRP-6 > GHRP-2 > ipamorelin at equivalent doses. The cost of this potency is moderate elevation of cortisol and prolactin alongside the GH pulse, approximately 40% less cortisol elevation than GHRP-6 at equipotent GH-releasing doses. This makes GHRP-2 the preferred GHRP when raw GH output matters most but the cortisol burden of GHRP-6 is unacceptable — it is better than GHRP-6 on selectivity, and better than ipamorelin on sheer GH pulse amplitude. Like all GHRPs, GHRP-2 also produces appetite stimulation via ghrelin pathway activation, though significantly less intense than GHRP-6. The appetite effect is moderate and manageable for most subjects. The synergistic stacking logic with GHRH analogs (CJC-1295, tesamorelin, sermorelin) applies identically to GHRP-2 as it does to ipamorelin: the GHRP activates GHS-R1a while the GHRH analog activates GHRH-R, and the convergence on pituitary somatotrophs produces a 2–10x amplified GH pulse versus either compound alone. GHRP-2 is contraindicated with GHRP-6 and ipamorelin because stacking two GHRPs targeting the same GHS-R1a receptor creates competitive binding without meaningful additive benefit while doubling the cortisol/prolactin load. Fasted administration is required because insulin elevation from food consumption suppresses GH release at the pituitary.

records.name: GHRP-6
records.description: GHRP-6 is the original first-generation synthetic Growth Hormone Releasing Peptide — the foundational compound of the entire GHRP class. Developed in the 1980s, it is a hexapeptide that activates GHS-R1a (ghrelin receptor) on pituitary somatotrophs to trigger pulsatile GH release, but unlike its successors, it activates GHS-R1a with minimal selectivity. The receptor is expressed throughout the body — in the pituitary, hypothalamus, adrenal glands, stomach, and CNS appetite centers — and GHRP-6 hits all of these targets simultaneously. The result is a compound with the strongest appetite stimulation of any GHRP (mediated centrally via NPY/AgRP pathways in the hypothalamus), significant cortisol and prolactin elevation, and robust GH release. In terms of raw GH pulse amplitude at equivalent doses, GHRP-6 produces the largest pulses of any GHRP in this database — but with the least favorable hormonal collateral. The appetite stimulation from GHRP-6 is its defining characteristic and its primary clinical application outside GH axis optimization. Within 15–20 minutes of injection, most subjects experience a sharp, urgent hunger signal that is qualitatively different from normal hunger — it is ghrelin-mediated central appetite drive with a strong compulsive quality. This effect has made GHRP-6 the primary tool in research protocols targeting cachexia, post-illness weight restoration, and deliberate bulk caloric intake. The 30-minute pre-meal timing recommendation is specifically to synchronize the appetite spike with the meal window rather than triggering extreme hunger at an inconvenient time. For researchers using GHRP-6 in combination with GLP-1 compounds — which are appetite-suppressing — the appetite conflict is significant and needs to be carefully considered in protocol design. GHRP-6 has been largely superseded in most modern protocols by ipamorelin (cleaner profile) and GHRP-2 (stronger pulse with less cortisol). Its relevance persists in two specific contexts: bulk/muscle gain protocols where the hunger stimulation is actively desirable, and when maximum raw GH pulse output justifies the cortisol and prolactin trade-off. It desensitizes less rapidly than hexarelin, allowing 6–12 week cycles, but the 2–4 week washout is important to prevent significant receptor downregulation. The combination with CJC-1295 No DAC or other GHRH analogs follows the same synergistic logic as all GHRPs.

records.name: GLOW (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu)
records.description: GLOW is a 70mg co-lyophilized tri-compound tissue repair and aesthetic blend containing BPC-157 (10mg), TB-500 (10mg), and GHK-Cu (50mg) in fixed ratios designed to deliver a daily dose of 2.0mg GHK-Cu + 400mcg BPC-157 + 400mcg TB-500. The three components operate through mechanistically distinct and complementary repair pathways that span angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, actin cytoskeletal dynamics, and copper-mediated gene regulation — making GLOW the most pharmacologically layered of all the repair blends in this database. BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound 157, a 15-amino acid pentadecapeptide derived from the cytoprotective protein BPC found in gastric juice) acts primarily through VEGFR2 (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2) stimulation to drive angiogenesis — the formation of new blood vessels into hypoxic or damaged tissue — and through the NO-synthase system to normalize nitric oxide production in damaged endothelium, restoring vascular perfusion to injured tissue beds; BPC-157 also acts as a potent anti-inflammatory through suppression of NF-κB and STAT3 signaling and produces significant gastrointestinal mucosal protective effects through prostaglandin-independent cytoprotective mechanisms. TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4 fragment Ac-SDKP through full sequence in research contexts) acts on G-actin sequestration — binding free monomeric actin to promote actin filament dynamics that enable cell migration, wound edge keratinocyte migration, and tissue repair cell mobility; TB-500's principal mechanism is the restoration of directional cellular movement into wound beds that is required for the second phase of wound healing after the initial inflammatory response. GHK-Cu (Glycine-Histidine-Lysine copper tripeptide) acts through cell surface collagen receptor interaction and copper-mediated transcription factor activation to upregulate a comprehensive wound healing and anti-aging gene program: increased production of collagen I, III, VI, dermatan sulfate, and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans; upregulation of matrix metalloprotease expression for matrix remodeling; and antioxidant gene activation through SOD1, SOD2, and metallothionein upregulation. The rationale for the 50mg GHK-Cu / 10mg BPC / 10mg TB ratio is pharmacokinetic and functional: GHK-Cu is dosed at 5x the concentration of each healing peptide because its primary mechanism (collagen gene upregulation and copper-mediated transcriptional activation) requires sustained higher molar concentrations at target fibroblasts to achieve the anabolic matrix gene expression thresholds identified in the Pickart research literature, while BPC-157 and TB-500 exert their angiogenic and cytoskeletal effects at lower microgram-range concentrations. This is not a reflection of GHK-Cu's potency relative to BPC-157 or TB-500 — it reflects the different pharmacodynamic concentration-response curves of three mechanistically distinct compounds that happen to cooperate in tissue repair. The GLOW blend specifically addresses the GHK-Cu injection site pain problem: pure GHK-Cu at the 2mg/day doses required for systemic anti-aging effects produces significant injection site pain (PIP) when administered as standalone injections due to its copper chelate chemistry and concentration; the co-lyophilization with BPC-157 and TB-500 allows the delivery of a full GHK-Cu dose within a blended injection volume that is better tolerated than standalone GHK-Cu at equivalent doses, while simultaneously delivering the full BPC-157 and TB-500 repair benefits in the same injection event. The 5-days-on, 2-days-off protocol (skip weekends) is a critical safety feature unique among the injectable peptide blends in this database — it is driven specifically by the copper content of GHK-Cu. Copper at therapeutic doses accumulates systemically with daily administration; the two-day weekly break allows hepatic copper processing and biliary copper excretion to prevent progressive copper accumulation that would occur with 7-day continuous dosing. This is not a pharmacokinetic tolerance concern for BPC-157 or TB-500 (which would benefit from daily continuous dosing) — it is an elemental copper toxicity prevention protocol. The 8–12 week maximum cycle length and 4-week minimum washout reinforce the same copper safety principle: cumulative copper load from a 12-week daily (5-day/week) GLOW cycle must be cleared before re-initiating. The synergy with Ipamorelin adds the GH axis anabolic stimulus to the tissue repair foundation — growth hormone's activation of local IGF-1 production in healing tissue directly amplifies the fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis that GHK-Cu has gene-regulatory-primed, creating a coordinated anabolic repair environment.

records.name: Glutathione
records.description: Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly) — the most abundant endogenous antioxidant molecule in the human body, present in essentially all mammalian cells at concentrations of 1–10 mM intracellularly. Unlike most antioxidants that function through direct free radical scavenging, glutathione operates as the centerpiece of a catalytic antioxidant system: it donates a hydrogen atom via its cysteine thiol group to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS), hydroxyl radicals, and lipid peroxides — becoming oxidized glutathione (GSSG) in the process — and is then regenerated back to reduced GSH by glutathione reductase using NADPH as the electron donor. This catalytic regeneration mechanism means a single glutathione molecule can neutralize multiple ROS events over its cellular lifetime, making GSH far more metabolically efficient than stoichiometric antioxidants like vitamin C or E. The GSH-dependent enzyme system includes glutathione peroxidase (GPx — detoxifies hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides), glutathione-S-transferase (GST — conjugates electrophilic xenobiotics and metabolic byproducts for excretion via Phase II detoxification), glutaredoxin (Grx — repairs oxidatively damaged proteins), and the thioredoxin-glutaredoxin system that maintains the cellular redox state. The liver contains the highest glutathione concentration of any organ — reflecting its role as the primary detoxification organ where Phase II GST conjugation reactions are central to metabolic processing of drugs, environmental toxins, endogenous metabolic byproducts (bilirubin, estrogen metabolites, catechol amines), and heavy metals. The skin lightening/brightening effect of glutathione that makes it widely used cosmetically is mediated through a specific biochemical interaction with the melanin synthesis pathway. Melanin production by melanocytes involves tyrosinase-catalyzed oxidation of tyrosine → DOPA → dopaquinone → eumelanin (dark brown-black) or pheomelanin (yellow-red). Glutathione inhibits this pathway through two mechanisms: direct inhibition of tyrosinase enzyme activity through binding to its copper active site (copper chelation reduces tyrosinase activity) and shifting the melanin synthesis pathway from eumelanin toward pheomelanin production — pheomelanin is lighter in color than eumelanin, producing the visible skin lightening observed with sustained glutathione use. This mechanism is dose-dependent and reversible: glutathione skin lightening requires sustained elevated GSH levels (achieved through repeated injection cycles) and gradually reverses when supplementation is discontinued and endogenous GSH levels return to baseline. The subcutaneous and intramuscular routes achieve significantly higher plasma and tissue GSH levels than oral supplementation, which is subject to first-pass hepatic extraction and reduction to its constituent amino acids by intestinal brush border enzymes — making injectable glutathione the predominant administration route for cosmetic skin lightening and systemic antioxidant applications. The synergy with NAD+ and GHK-Cu is mechanistically layered: NAD+ is required for NADPH production through the pentose phosphate pathway (NADPH drives glutathione reductase to regenerate GSH from GSSG — maintaining the reduced active form), meaning NAD+ supplementation directly supports the glutathione regeneration cycle; GHK-Cu is a copper-binding peptide that modulates copper availability in tissue — since tyrosinase (the target of glutathione's melanin-inhibiting activity) requires copper as its catalytic cofactor, GHK-Cu's copper mobilization and redistribution activity interacts with glutathione's copper chelation mechanism on tyrosinase. Together with its Category X aesthetic companions Matrixyl and SNAP-8, glutathione provides the antioxidant and depigmentation foundation while Matrixyl drives collagen synthesis and SNAP-8 reduces dynamic wrinkle formation — a mechanistically complete skin rejuvenation stack addressing oxidative damage, pigmentation, structural collagen loss, and muscular wrinkle formation simultaneously.

records.name: Gonadorelin
records.description: Gonadorelin is synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) — a decapeptide (pGlu-His-Trp-Ser-Tyr-Gly-Leu-Arg-Pro-Gly-NH₂) with an identical amino acid sequence to endogenous human GnRH, making it the only compound in Category VII that acts at the apex of the HPG axis: the hypothalamic level. Endogenous GnRH is synthesized in GnRH neurons of the arcuate nucleus and preoptic area and released in discrete pulses — typically every 60–120 minutes in men — into the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal blood supply to reach GnRH receptors (GnRHR) on anterior pituitary gonadotroph cells. Each GnRH pulse triggers a corresponding LH pulse (and to a lesser extent FSH), which then drives Leydig cell testosterone synthesis in a pulsatile pattern that underlies the normal diurnal testosterone rhythm. This pulsatile architecture is pharmacologically critical: GnRHR on gonadotroph cells desensitize and downregulate rapidly under continuous GnRH stimulation — which is the mechanism exploited by GnRH agonist drugs (leuprolide, triptorelin, buserelin) used to chemically castrate prostate cancer patients and suppress sex hormones in conditions like precocious puberty and endometriosis. Gonadorelin, because it has an identical half-life to endogenous GnRH (2–4 minutes), must be administered in a pulsatile fashion to maintain HPG axis stimulation rather than suppression — making it the most physiologically faithful but practically demanding HPG axis compound in this database. The mechanistic superiority and practical limitation of gonadorelin versus hCG and kisspeptin are mirror images of each other. Mechanistic superiority: gonadorelin activates GnRH receptors at the pituitary, producing simultaneous LH AND FSH release in the physiologically correct pulsatile pattern — mimicking the natural hormonal cascade more precisely than hCG (which bypasses the pituitary entirely) or kisspeptin (which acts one synapse upstream at the hypothalamic GnRH neuron). Practical limitation: the 2–4 minute plasma half-life means a single subcutaneous injection produces a GnRH pulse lasting only minutes — followed by rapid degradation. Three injections per day (the standard protocol) represents a very rough approximation of the normal pulsatile pattern, but with much lower frequency than the 8–15 natural GnRH pulses per day in healthy men. For truly physiological GnRH delivery, a subcutaneous pump delivering a gonadorelin pulse every 90–120 minutes is the clinical standard, as used in treating idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH) — a context where pulsatile GnRH pump therapy reliably restores full HPG axis function including spermatogenesis. The 3x-daily subcutaneous injection protocol is a practical approximation that produces meaningful LH/FSH pulses but cannot fully replicate normal pulsatile dynamics. The HPG axis suppression risk from incorrect gonadorelin use is the most critical safety consideration and the primary driver of all protocol design for this compound. If gonadorelin is administered continuously or at excessively high doses without adequate inter-dose intervals, the GnRHR desensitization mechanism that pharmaceutical GnRH agonists exploit therapeutically will be triggered — converting a compound intended to support HPG axis activity into a compound that suppresses it. This paradoxical suppression occurs because sustained GnRHR occupation uncouples the receptor from its Gq signaling cascade and drives receptor internalization and downregulation, leaving gonadotroph cells unresponsive to subsequent GnRH pulses. Recovery from gonadorelin-induced GnRHR desensitization requires cessation and a washout period; in severe cases it may require weeks of recovery before LH/FSH secretion normalizes.

Pregnancy — GnRH receptor activation during pregnancy has unpredictable effects on luteal support and placental function.
Ovarian hyperstimulation risk in women — FSH stimulation from gonadorelin-driven pituitary activation in PCOS or high-responder states can produce OHSS.
Severe GnRH receptor mutations (Kallmann syndrome variant with receptor-null phenotype) — gonadorelin will be ineffective in subjects with complete GnRHR loss-of-function mutations.
sideEffects: HPG axis suppression from incorrect dosing — the most serious and mechanistically important adverse effect; non-pulsatile, continuous, or excessively frequent administration converts gonadorelin from an HPG stimulator to an HPG suppressor through GnRHR desensitization; clinical manifestation is worsening hypogonadism, loss of libido, fatigue, and testicular atrophy — the opposite of the intended effect.
Headache — commonly reported after GnRH pulse injections; related to the rapid LH/FSH surge and downstream testosterone pulse produced by each dose.
Nausea — mild; transient; reported in a subset of subjects particularly at higher doses.
Injection site reactions — mild redness, tenderness, and bruising at the subcutaneous administration site; more frequent with the 3x-daily injection schedule.
Flushing — transient; from the acute hormonal pulse produced by each gonadorelin injection.
Mood and libido fluctuations — from the pulsatile testosterone oscillations between doses; subjects may experience mood variability correlated with the inter-dose hormonal troughs.

Antibody formation against gonadorelin (rare) — repeated GnRH peptide injection can rarely trigger low-level immune sensitization; clinically significant antibodies neutralizing gonadorelin's activity are rare but documented with prolonged exposure.
Ovarian hyperstimulation (women) — FSH pulsatility from gonadorelin-driven pituitary activation in high-responder women creates OHSS risk comparable to exogenous FSH administration.
Testicular sensitivity and ache — from the increased Leydig and Sertoli cell stimulation from LH/FSH pulses.

records.name: Gotratix
records.description: Gotratix is a Khavinson cytomedin — peptide complex A-18 — extracted from skeletal muscle tissue of young animals, developed at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as the dedicated muscle bioregulator of the Khavinson framework. It works at the transcriptional level inside myocytes (muscle fibers) and satellite cells (the stem cells that regenerate muscle), normalizing the gene expression programs governing myosin and actin synthesis, mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative stress resistance, and the activation of MyoD and myogenin — the master regulators of muscle cell identity and repair. In plain terms, Gotratix signals aging muscle cells to restore the protein synthesis capacity, energy efficiency, and regenerative responsiveness they had in youth — independent of any hormonal signal. Gotratix has been studied in athletes, elderly subjects with sarcopenia, and post-surgical muscle recovery populations. Documented outcomes include improvement in muscle metabolism markers after intense physical load, reduction in lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress in muscular tissue, restoration of muscle function following immobilization, and improvement in strength and mobility parameters in elderly subjects with sarcopenia. The antioxidant dimension of its mechanism — documented reduction in reactive oxygen species burden in muscle tissue — is particularly relevant to subjects undergoing intensive training, where cumulative oxidative damage to myofibers is a primary driver of impaired recovery and training adaptation. What makes Gotratix uniquely positioned in this database is that it is the only compound targeting skeletal muscle at the gene expression level rather than through hormonal signaling. GH secretagogues (CJC-1295, ipamorelin), IGF-1-LR3, MGF, and ACE-031 all amplify the anabolic hormonal signals telling muscle to grow; Gotratix works on the quality of the muscle cells receiving those signals — restoring the intrinsic cellular machinery that makes the hormonal stimulus effective. A myocyte with normalized gene programs (Gotratix) responds more robustly to the GH pulse from a secretagogue stack, which is the mechanistic basis for its synergy designations with CJC-1295/ipamorelin, MGF, and IGF-1-LR3 and its particular relevance during GLP-1 agonist-driven caloric deficit, where lean mass preservation depends on muscle cell quality rather than hormonal amplification alone.

rows.notes: Standard intensive course. 60-capsule pack. Repeat every 3-6 months. Maintenance: 2 capsules daily for 10 days, repeated every 3 months.

rows.notes: Monthly maintenance throughout competitive season.

protocols.label: Alternative Titration 2: Sarcopenia Reversal Protocol (Goal — maximum muscle bioregulator gene program normalization for elderly subjects with confirmed sarcopenia; run concurrent with resistance exercise program)

rows.notes: Baseline DEXA (appendicular lean mass), grip strength, and 6-minute walk test before initiating. Resistance exercise 3x/week minimum during course — Gotratix normalizes the gene program quality that exercise stimulus acts upon; without the mechanical stimulus, the bioregulator benefit is attenuated.

protocols.label: Alternative Titration 3: GH Secretagogue + Gotratix Synergy Stack (Goal — combine GH-axis hormonal signaling (CJC-1295/ipamorelin SC) with muscle gene program normalization (Gotratix oral); addresses both the hormonal signal and the receiving tissue quality simultaneously)

Gotratix normalizes muscle protein synthesis gene programs during the caloric deficit-induced risk of lean mass catabolism. Concurrent resistance exercise 3x/week is the essential co-intervention. Combine with adequate protein intake (1.6-2.2g/kg lean body mass).

washout: Standard Protocol — 30-day intensive course. Repeat every 3-6 months.
Athletic Performance Protocol — 30-day pre-season intensive, 10-day monthly maintenance during season.
Sarcopenia Protocol — 30-day intensive course. Monthly 10-day maintenance thereafter. DEXA reassessment at 6 months.
GH Secretagogue Synergy Protocol — 30-day concurrent course with GH secretagogues. Repeat every 4-6 months.

GLP-1 Lean Mass Preservation Protocol — 30-day course. Repeat every 3 months while on GLP-1 agonist.
contraindications: Rhabdomyolysis in active phase — myocyte bioregulator activity during active skeletal muscle destruction is not characterized; medical management of acute rhabdomyolysis takes priority.

Inflammatory myopathies in active flare (polymyositis, dermatomyositis) — skeletal muscle cell gene program normalization during active autoimmune myositis has not been evaluated; immunosuppressive management takes priority.
Skeletal muscle malignancy (rhabdomyosarcoma) — myocyte gene program normalization in the context of malignant muscle cells is contraindicated.
Known hypersensitivity to Gotratix (skeletal muscle tissue cytomedin peptide complex A-18) or formulation excipients including gelatin.

Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy in severe stage — the dystrophin-deficiency-related structural skeletal muscle failure in advanced DMD/BMD creates a context where bioregulator gene program normalization of surviving myocytes has not been characterized.
sideEffects: Mild transient muscle soreness in first cycle days — as myocyte metabolic activity and protein synthesis increase in response to bioregulator stimulation, some subjects report mild muscle soreness in the first 2-3 days; similar to DOMS but not exercise-induced; resolves within the first week.
Mild fatigue on initiation — the metabolic demands of muscle gene program activation impose a transient energy cost; mild fatigue in days 1-3 is occasionally reported; resolves rapidly.
Mild gastrointestinal discomfort — as an oral cytomedin taken with meals; occasional mild gastric discomfort in first days; resolves with continued administration.
Injection site — not applicable (oral route).

Mild increased appetite in early cycle days — as muscle metabolic rate normalizes and protein synthesis gene programs activate, a mild increase in appetite is reported by some subjects; reflects increased anabolic energy demand; not a safety concern.

No serious musculoskeletal adverse events documented in the Khavinson research literature at standard protocol doses — Gotratix's safety profile in athletes, sarcopenic elderly subjects, and post-surgical populations is clean; no myotoxicity, rhabdomyolysis, or serious muscle pathology has been attributed to Gotratix.

Unknown interaction profile with statin therapy — statins produce myopathy as a dose-dependent adverse effect through mitochondrial CoQ10 depletion and myocyte metabolic disruption; Gotratix's mitochondrial biogenesis normalization activity in myocytes could theoretically partially counteract statin myopathy; not documented as a clinical interaction but mechanistically plausible.

records.name: HCG (Human Chorionic Gonadotropin)
records.description: Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) is a 37.5 kDa glycoprotein hormone consisting of an alpha subunit (identical to LH, FSH, and TSH) and a unique beta subunit that confers LH receptor (LHCGR) binding specificity. It is produced physiologically by the syncytiotrophoblast cells of the placenta immediately following fertilization, serving as the molecular signal that prevents corpus luteum regression (luteal rescue) and maintains progesterone production during early pregnancy — which is why it is the analyte detected by pregnancy tests. In males, hCG acts as a functional LH mimetic with exceptionally high potency: it binds the LH/hCG receptor on testicular Leydig cells with greater affinity than endogenous LH and produces a more prolonged receptor activation signal due to its half-life of 24–36 hours (versus 20–30 minutes for endogenous LH). This Leydig cell LHCGR activation drives the intracellular cAMP cascade that upregulates steroidogenic enzymes (StAR, CYP11A1, 3β-HSD, 17β-HSD), producing robust intratesticular testosterone (ITT) synthesis that is the primary driver of spermatogenesis. ITT concentrations are 50–100-fold higher than serum testosterone and are maintained by functional LH/hCG signaling independent of pituitary LH secretion — this is the mechanistic foundation of hCG's utility during exogenous testosterone therapy where pituitary LH is suppressed. The clinical evidence base for hCG in male hormone management is extensive and well-characterized across multiple decades of endocrinological practice. In men on testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), hCG co-administration at 500 IU 3x/week has been demonstrated in multiple studies to: (1) maintain ITT concentrations comparable to untreated eugonadal men, (2) preserve Leydig cell morphology and testicular volume that would otherwise atrophy under LH suppression, (3) maintain Sertoli cell function and spermatogenesis — allowing fertility preservation during TRT that would be impossible without it, and (4) maintain the intra-testicular DHEA production and other local androgenic metabolites that contribute to mood, libido, and wellbeing beyond serum testosterone alone. In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (secondary hypogonadism from pituitary or hypothalamic pathology), hCG can restore testicular testosterone production and spermatogenesis as the primary treatment — replacing the absent LH signal at the gonadal level. In post-anabolic steroid suppression, high-dose hCG protocols (1,500–2,000 IU 3x/week) are used to reactivate severely suppressed Leydig cells before transitioning to selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) for full HPG axis restoration. The estrogen management consideration is the most practically important hCG side effect to understand. Leydig cells express aromatase (CYP19A1), and hCG-driven intratesticular testosterone synthesis produces intratesticular estradiol as a byproduct of aromatization. At physiological LH stimulation levels this is normally regulated; at supraphysiological hCG doses (particularly 1,500 IU and above), the Leydig cell steroidogenic surge produces enough intratesticular estradiol to meaningfully elevate serum estradiol — producing gynecomastia, water retention, emotional lability, and loss of libido from estrogen excess. This dose-dependent aromatization explains why lower-dose maintenance protocols (250–500 IU 3x/week) are generally preferred over higher doses for chronic TRT support. The prostate cancer contraindication is absolute and physiological: hCG-driven testosterone production directly fuels androgen receptor-expressing prostate cancer cell growth — any active or suspected prostate malignancy is an absolute contraindication.

rows.notes: To maintain intratesticular testosterone during exogenous testosterone therapy and support fertility preservation.
Lighter maintenance dose.
To reactivate testosterone production after prolonged anabolic steroid use or severe hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
Peak saturation phase.
Tapering phase.
