records.name: HMG (Human Menopausal Gonadotropin)
records.description: Human Menopausal Gonadotropin (hMG, menotroPin) is a purified biological extract derived from the urine of postmenopausal women — a source chosen specifically because postmenopausal pituitary gonadotropin output is dramatically elevated (due to absent negative sex hormone feedback), making postmenopausal urine a rich biological source of both LH and FSH in approximately a 1:1 ratio. Unlike recombinant FSH or hCG, which are single-hormone preparations, hMG delivers both gonadotropin signals simultaneously — LH activity (predominantly from the hCG-like molecules present in postmenopausal urine) acting on Leydig cells to drive testosterone synthesis, and FSH activity acting on Sertoli cells to drive spermatogenesis. This dual gonadotropin delivery is the defining pharmacological advantage of hMG over hCG monotherapy in fertility applications: spermatogenesis requires both Sertoli cell FSH stimulation (for the blood-testis barrier support and local growth factor production that sustains developing spermatids) and Leydig cell ITT from LH/hCG stimulation — hCG alone can restore intratesticular testosterone but provides no FSH signal for Sertoli cells, which is why men with severely suppressed pituitary gonadotropins and absent spermatogenesis often fail to restore sperm production on hCG alone and require hMG co-administration to supply the FSH component. The mechanistic specialization of hMG within the HPG axis peptide toolkit is its FSH activity — the gonadotropin that hCG does not replace. FSH acts on Sertoli cell FSH receptors (FSHR) to drive the transcriptional programs required for spermatogenesis: ABP (androgen-binding protein) production that concentrates testosterone in the seminiferous tubule, inhibin B production for negative feedback regulation, activin signaling for spermatogonial stem cell proliferation, and the physical tight junction and nutrient support infrastructure of the blood-testis barrier. In men whose spermatogenesis has been completely suppressed by prolonged exogenous androgen exposure (anabolic steroid use, long-term TRT without hCG), the Sertoli cells may be functionally quiescent with markedly reduced FSHR expression — hMG administration reactivates the FSHR/FSH axis and the spermatogenic cascade from the Sertoli cell level upward. The standard clinical protocol combines hMG 75 IU 3x/week with hCG 500–1,000 IU 3x/week, addressing both FSH (hMG) and LH (hCG) deficiency simultaneously — the basis of the hCG synergy designation. The high baseline FSH contraindication requires specific explanation. In men with primary hypogonadism (testicular failure), the pituitary elevates FSH in response to absent spermatogenesis feedback from the damaged testes — a high serum FSH indicates irreversible Sertoli cell or seminiferous tubule damage where the tissue is no longer present to respond to FSH stimulation. Administering hMG in this context provides no spermatogenic benefit (there are no functional Sertoli cells to stimulate) while exposing the subject to the side effects and cost of the intervention. The ovarian hyperstimulation risk in women is the most serious adverse event in the female fertility context: FSH stimulation of multiple follicular cohorts simultaneously can produce dramatic ovarian enlargement, ascites, pleural effusion, thrombosis, and potentially fatal complications — this must be managed under clinical monitoring in any female fertility protocol.

rows.notes: Often combined with HCG for maximum fertility restoration.

washout: Cycle Length: Varies.
Washout: Use until fertility is restored or pregnancy is achieved.
contraindications: High baseline FSH (indicative of primary testicular failure/Sertoli cell damage) — elevated serum FSH in men signals irreversible testicular damage with absent or severely compromised Sertoli cell function; hMG provides no spermatogenic benefit when the target tissue is non-functional and only adds side effect burden.

Known or suspected hormone-dependent tumors (prostate cancer, ovarian cancer, endometrial cancer, breast cancer) — gonadotropin stimulation of sex hormone production is contraindicated in hormone-sensitive malignancies.

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) history or high risk — in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) or other high-responder states, FSH stimulation from hMG can trigger severe and potentially life-threatening OHSS.

Uncontrolled adrenal dysfunction, thyroid dysfunction, or hyperprolactinemia — these endocrine conditions must be treated before gonadotropin therapy to ensure the HPG axis is capable of responding appropriately.
Presence of ovarian cysts unrelated to PCOS (in women) — exogenous FSH may stimulate cyst growth or rupture.
Intracranial lesions (pituitary tumor, hypothalamic disease) incompatible with gonadotropin therapy.
Known hypersensitivity to hMG, urinary-derived gonadotropin preparations, or any formulation excipients.
Pregnancy (outside medically supervised ovulation induction) — absolute contraindication to any gonadotropin administration in established pregnancy.
sideEffects: Injection site pain and local reaction — the most consistently reported adverse effect; hMG is a urinary protein extract and produces more injection site discomfort than synthetic peptides; local redness, induration, and tenderness; more pronounced than hCG.

Estrogen elevation — FSH drives Sertoli cell aromatase activity and follicular estradiol production; in men, FSH-driven Sertoli cell function produces estradiol that contributes to overall estrogen elevation alongside the hCG-driven Leydig cell estradiol.

Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) in women — the most serious potential adverse event in female applications; ranges from mild (bloating, pelvic discomfort, nausea) to severe (massive ovarian enlargement, ascites, pleural effusion, thromboembolism); requires clinical monitoring.
Abdominal bloating and discomfort — common in both sexes; secondary to hormonal changes and, in women, ovarian follicular development.
Headache — commonly reported; mechanism related to the rapid hormonal fluctuations produced by gonadotropin stimulation.
Mood changes and emotional lability — from the testosterone, estradiol, and inhibin fluctuations driven by concurrent LH and FSH stimulation.

Multiple pregnancies (in women undergoing ovulation induction) — FSH stimulation of multiple follicles simultaneously creates risk of multiple egg release and multiple pregnancy; a well-known complication of gonadotropin fertility treatments.
Gynecomastia in men — from the combined estradiol elevation driven by both FSH-stimulated Sertoli aromatase and LH-stimulated Leydig aromatase.
Potential antibody formation against urinary proteins — as a urinary extract, hMG contains non-gonadotropin urinary proteins that can rarely trigger immune sensitization with repeated use.

records.name: Humanin
records.description: Humanin is a 21-amino acid mitochondrial-derived peptide (MDP) encoded within the 16S ribosomal RNA gene of the mitochondrial genome — making it, alongside MOTS-c, one of the founding members of the recognized mitochondrial-derived peptide family. Its discovery in 2001 by Hashimoto et al. emerged from a screen for factors that protect neurons from Alzheimer's disease-related apoptosis — specifically the toxicity of amyloid-beta (Aβ), mutant presenilin-2, and the Alzheimer's-associated V642I APP mutation. Humanin rescued neurons from all three forms of Alzheimer's-related cell death in vitro, establishing it as a neuronal cytoprotective peptide of unusual potency. At the receptor level, Humanin binds a heterotrimeric receptor complex involving FPRL1 (formyl peptide receptor-like 1), CLR (calcitonin-like receptor), and CRLR, and also signals through STAT3, Bcl-2 family proteins, and IGF-1 receptor pathways. The anti-apoptotic activity is mechanistically broad: Humanin suppresses cytochrome c release from mitochondria, activates Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL expression, inhibits Bax mitochondrial translocation, and activates STAT3-mediated survival gene transcription. The cytoprotective activity of Humanin extends well beyond neurons: cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle cells, endothelial cells, pancreatic beta cells, and retinal photoreceptors all respond to Humanin with reduced apoptotic death under stress conditions. In animal models, Humanin administration reduces infarct size in cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, preserves beta cell mass in streptozotocin-induced diabetic models, protects retinal ganglion cells from oxidative stress-induced death, and reduces atherosclerotic plaque formation. A critical epidemiological observation is that circulating Humanin levels decline with age in humans — with particularly low levels documented in the blood of Alzheimer's disease patients and their family members carrying genetic risk factors, suggesting Humanin's decline is not merely a biomarker of aging but may be a mechanistic contributor to age-related neurodegeneration and cardiovascular disease. Humanin is the most under-characterized compound in Category IV from a human clinical data standpoint. While the preclinical mechanistic evidence is robust and reproducible across multiple laboratories, there are no published randomized controlled trials in humans, no established clinical dosing, and the research-grade dose ranges in this database represent extrapolations from animal dosing studies and early clinical observation rather than validated human pharmacokinetics. The conservative protocol note ("dose conservatively") reflects this knowledge gap. The synergy with MOTS-c and cerebrolysin is mechanistically sound: MOTS-c activates systemic metabolic resilience while Humanin specializes in neuronal and cellular apoptosis protection — complementary survival mechanisms from the same mitochondrial genome. The cerebrolysin synergy reflects convergent neuroprotective mechanisms via different pathways (growth factor-mediated vs. mitochondrial anti-apoptotic).

rows.notes: Under-researched compared to MOTS-c; dose conservatively.

washout: Cycle Length: 6 weeks.
Washout: 6 weeks off.
contraindications: Active malignancy — Humanin's potent anti-apoptotic mechanisms (Bcl-2 upregulation, Bax inhibition, cytochrome c suppression) that protect healthy cells from death are mechanistically identical to the pathways cancer cells exploit to become chemotherapy-resistant; exogenous Humanin may protect tumor cells from apoptosis-inducing therapy.

Concurrent cytotoxic chemotherapy — Humanin's anti-apoptotic activity directly opposes the mechanism of action of most chemotherapy agents, which rely on triggering apoptosis in rapidly dividing cells.
Known hypersensitivity to Humanin or peptide excipients.
Pregnancy — mitochondrial-encoded peptide signaling in fetal development is not characterized; safety not established.
Breastfeeding — no data.
Pediatric use — no safety data.
Severe cardiac arrhythmia — IGF-1 receptor and STAT3 pathway activation by Humanin may affect cardiac electrophysiology at high doses; limited human data.
sideEffects: Injection site reactions — redness, soreness, mild swelling at subcutaneous injection site; standard peptide injection response; expected and manageable.

Under-documented adverse effects — Humanin has the least human safety data of any compound in Category IV; all side effect characterization derives from animal studies and early-stage human observation; unknown adverse effects may exist that have not yet been documented.

Theoretical protection of cancer cells from apoptosis — the mechanistically most significant theoretical adverse effect; Bcl-2 upregulation and Bax inhibition are the same pathways that confer chemotherapy resistance in cancer; not observed as a clinical adverse event but represents the primary safety concern.
Mild fatigue — reported anecdotally in early weeks of use; possibly related to mitochondrial membrane signaling adjustments.
Mild headache — uncommon; not well characterized.

Potential IGF-1 receptor pathway modulation — Humanin signals through the IGF-1 receptor at certain concentrations; theoretical implications for insulin-sensitive conditions warrant monitoring in diabetic subjects.
No documented endocrine disruption, receptor desensitization, or hormonal suppression in available preclinical literature.

records.name: IGF-1 LR3
records.description: IGF-1 LR3 (Long R3 Insulin-like Growth Factor-1) is an engineered analog of Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 — the primary downstream mediator of growth hormone's anabolic effects. In normal physiology, GH stimulates the liver to produce IGF-1, which then travels through the bloodstream to promote tissue growth, protein synthesis, and cell survival across multiple organ systems. Standard IGF-1 has a very short functional half-life because it is rapidly bound and inactivated by IGF Binding Proteins (IGFBPs) in the blood. IGF-1 LR3 circumvents this by incorporating two modifications: an arginine substitution at position 3 that dramatically reduces IGFBP binding affinity, and an extended N-terminal sequence (13 amino acid extension) that adds additional binding resistance. The result is an IGF-1 analog with approximately 60–120 times longer functional half-life (20–30 hours) than native IGF-1, which remains active and receptor-available throughout the bloodstream for an extended window. The primary metabolic effects of IGF-1 LR3 are muscle protein synthesis stimulation, prevention of muscle protein breakdown (anti-catabolism), and promotion of hyperplasia — the creation of new muscle fibers by driving satellite cells through differentiation and fusion. This hyperplasia mechanism is what distinguishes IGF-1 from standard anabolic approaches: while testosterone and GH primarily drive hypertrophy (existing fiber enlargement), IGF-1 LR3 at the appropriate doses drives actual new fiber generation, which represents a permanent structural change to the muscle rather than temporary enlargement dependent on continued hormonal support. Post-workout administration capitalizes on the training-induced nutrient uptake window — IGF-1 receptors are sensitized, and the presence of carbohydrates and protein allows the anabolic signal to be maximally productive. The most important safety distinction between IGF-1 LR3 and the GHRPs in this database is the severity of the hypoglycemia risk. Unlike GH secretagogues that indirectly affect glucose metabolism via GH-mediated insulin resistance, IGF-1 directly activates IGF-1 receptors that are structurally and functionally similar to insulin receptors — meaning it drives glucose into cells similarly to insulin. At doses of 50–100mcg, this effect is clinically significant, producing acute blood sugar drops within 30–60 minutes of injection. This is why IGF-1 LR3 must never be taken fasted and must always be administered with concurrent carbohydrate intake. The intestinal growth risk from sustained high-dose or abused use (visceral organ growth, gut hypertrophy) is a real concern documented in case reports and must be contextualized against the dose-limiting guidelines here.

rows.notes: 1x/day, 7 days per week. Dose immediately post-workout (within 30 mins) with carbs and protein.
1x/day, 7 days per week. Avoid taking at bedtime or while fasted.
1x/day, 7 days per week. Ensure adequate calories/protein are consumed.
1x/day, 7 days per week. Maximum recommended dosage phase.
Administered intramuscularly into the trained muscle group (e.g., left and right bicep) immediately post-workout.

washout: Cycle Length: 8-week cycle.
Washout: Must be followed by a 4-8 week washout period.
Administration Rules: Do not take at bedtime. Do not take fasted. Always use with adequate calories/protein to support nutrient uptake.
contraindications: Active cancer — IGF-1 is a potent mitogen; direct IGF-1 receptor activation accelerates proliferation of malignant cells.
History of malignancy — especially hormone-sensitive cancers; IGF-1 receptor signaling drives tumor growth in breast, prostate, and colorectal cancers.
Hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia unawareness — acute hypoglycemia is the primary risk; IGF-1 receptor activity mimics insulin; never administer fasted.
Diabetic ketoacidosis.
Type 1 or insulin-dependent diabetes — IGF-1's insulin-like activity requires careful glycemic management.
Concurrent use with insulin — severe additive hypoglycemia risk; extreme caution required.
Concurrent administration without food — administration without concurrent carbohydrates and protein is contraindicated; hypoglycemia risk is immediate.
Pre-existing visceral organ enlargement — IGF-1 at high doses drives growth in all IGF-1 receptor-expressing tissues, including intestinal epithelium and visceral organs.
Active acromegaly — additive IGF-1 receptor stimulation in a state of existing IGF-1 excess.
Pregnancy — IGF-1 analog activity not established in pregnancy; potential fetal risk.
Breastfeeding — safety not established.
Known hypersensitivity to IGF-1 LR3 or excipients.
Pediatric use — safety and efficacy not established; open growth plates in children risk inappropriate and disproportionate skeletal growth.
sideEffects: Severe hypoglycemia — the most critical adverse effect; direct insulin-like glucose uptake via IGF-1 receptor activation; onset typically 30–60 minutes post-injection; more pronounced with fasted administration; always administer with carbohydrates present.

Intestinal growth and gut hypertrophy — with abused long-term or excessive dosing, IGF-1 receptor stimulation in gastrointestinal epithelium can cause measurable organ enlargement; this is the primary long-term misuse risk.
Visceral organ growth — liver, spleen, kidneys; IGF-1 receptor is expressed in all visceral organs; supraphysiologic IGF-1 exposure over extended periods may drive size increases.
Localized swelling at injection site — tissue response to subcutaneous or intramuscular injection.
Edema — IGF-1-mediated sodium and fluid retention.
Jaw tightening or facial growth (at high doses/extended abuse) — IGF-1 receptors in craniofacial tissues; acromegalic-type effects at very high doses.
Joint pain — GH/IGF-1 axis-mediated periarticular fluid.
Headache.
Fatigue — transient post-injection.
Nausea — dose-dependent.
Increased appetite — orexigenic effect of IGF-1 receptor activity.
Tingling or numbness in extremities — insulin-like effects and fluid shifts.
Carpal tunnel syndrome risk — with extended high-dose use.
Downregulation of endogenous GH production — negative feedback from elevated IGF-1 on hypothalamic-pituitary axis; natural GH production suppressed during and after long cycles.

records.name: Immunological Enhancement (GAZ)
records.description: Immunological Enhancement (product code GAZ) is an antioxidant and immune-support injection built around glutathione, vitamin C, and zinc. It is a vitamin and antioxidant blend rather than a peptide, working through antioxidant defense and immune-cofactor pathways, and given as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains Glutathione 200mg, Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C) 200mg, and Zinc Sulfate 2.5mg. Glutathione is the body master antioxidant and plays a central role in detoxification, immune cell function, and cellular protection, vitamin C is a potent antioxidant that supports immune function and regenerates glutathione, and zinc is an essential mineral that supports immune cell development, wound healing, and hundreds of enzymatic processes. In practice, GAZ is used by people who want to support their immune system, antioxidant status, and general resilience, particularly during periods of high stress, heavy training, travel, or seasonal illness risk. The glutathione content also makes it popular for its skin-brightening and detoxification reputation, since glutathione is widely used for those cosmetic and cellular-cleansing purposes. It is typically administered as a standing weekly injection, or more frequently during periods when immune support is a priority. Because vitamin C helps recycle glutathione back to its active form, the two are commonly paired, and the zinc rounds out the immune-cofactor profile. This is a wellness and resilience blend rather than a body-composition or performance tool. Mechanistically, GAZ combines a direct dose of the master antioxidant (glutathione) with a supporting antioxidant that regenerates it (vitamin C) and an essential immune mineral (zinc), so the injection supports the body antioxidant defense and immune readiness on multiple fronts at once. Injectable delivery is valued for glutathione in particular because oral glutathione is poorly absorbed. Users should expect general immune and antioxidant support that builds with consistent use, and some report improved skin clarity over time from the glutathione. Injection sites should be rotated, and because high-dose vitamin C can contribute to kidney stones in predisposed individuals and zinc can affect copper balance at high chronic intakes, anyone with kidney concerns or on long-term high-dose regimens should consult a physician.

rows.notes: Direct-dose antioxidant and immune-support injection with no titration required. A typical protocol is 0.5 to 1 mL administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly 1 to 3 times per week, and can be increased in frequency during periods of high immune demand. Rotate injection sites. Suitable for continuous use.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to glutathione, ascorbic acid, zinc, or any formulation excipient.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding unless directed and supervised by a physician.
History of kidney stones or active kidney disease, due to the vitamin C content, without medical supervision.
G6PD deficiency, in which high-dose vitamin C should be used cautiously.
sideEffects: Injection site irritation, redness, warmth, or tenderness.
Mild gastrointestinal upset or nausea.
A metallic taste after injection.
Lightening of skin tone over time from glutathione.
Headache.

records.name: Ipamorelin
records.description: Ipamorelin is a third-generation Growth Hormone Releasing Peptide (GHRP) and the cleanest GH secretagogue available. While all GHRPs work by activating the GHS-R1a (ghrelin receptor) to stimulate pituitary GH release, they differ dramatically in their selectivity. First-generation GHRP-6 and second-generation GHRP-2 both activate GHS-R1a in ways that also elevate cortisol, prolactin, and ACTH alongside GH — producing a messy hormonal picture that limits their long-term utility. Ipamorelin was engineered specifically to resolve this. Its unique pentapeptide structure (Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2) produces potent GHS-R1a activation in pituitary somatotrophs while failing to trigger the cortisol or prolactin responses seen with other GHRPs. This was confirmed in head-to-head pharmacology studies comparing ipamorelin directly against GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 — ipamorelin does not significantly elevate cortisol or ACTH at any studied dose. The clinical relevance of this selectivity is substantial. Cortisol is catabolic — chronically elevated cortisol degrades muscle tissue, impairs immune function, disrupts sleep, and promotes central fat accumulation. Running a GHRP that elevates cortisol with every injection partially defeats the purpose of GH axis optimization. Ipamorelin avoids this entirely, making it the logical first choice for GHRP protocols where the goal is lean mass preservation, recovery enhancement, or anti-aging. Its saturation dose is approximately 300mcg per injection — dosing above this threshold does not produce meaningfully larger GH pulses because somatotroph GHS-R1a binding is already saturated. This makes it highly dose-predictable: the optimal single injection window is 100–300mcg, with multiple daily injections used to create multiple discrete GH pulses rather than single large ones. The synergy with CJC-1295 (No DAC) is the foundational stack in GH axis research. Ipamorelin activates GHS-R1a (ghrelin pathway), while CJC-1295 No DAC activates GHRH-R (GHRH pathway) — two completely separate receptor systems that converge on the same pituitary somatotroph to stimulate GH release. When dosed simultaneously, the two compounds produce a GH pulse 2–10x larger than either alone. Ipamorelin also produces a mild increase in appetite — unlike GHRP-6 where hunger is extreme and immediate, ipamorelin's appetite increase is subtle and manageable, and many researchers do not notice it at standard doses.

rows.notes: Administered pre-bed, usually stacked with CJC-1295.
Ipamorelin has a saturation dose of roughly 300mcg/injection. Dosing higher yields diminishing returns.

washout: Cycle Length: 12-16 weeks.
Washout: 4 weeks off.
contraindications: Active cancer or history of malignancy — GH/IGF-1 elevation may promote tumor cell proliferation.
History of hormone-sensitive malignancies (breast, prostate, colorectal) — IGF-1 is a growth factor for these tumor types.
Active acromegaly or pituitary disorders involving GH excess.
Diabetic ketoacidosis.
Diabetes mellitus or significant insulin resistance — GH elevation reduces insulin sensitivity; monitor fasting glucose.
Concurrent use with GHRP-2 or GHRP-6 — receptor competition at GHS-R1a; do not combine two GHRPs.
Concurrent use with HGH 191aa — additive GH elevation creates redundant axis overstimulation.
Concomitant glucocorticoid therapy — suppresses pituitary GH response.
Pregnancy — safety not established.
Breastfeeding — safety not established.
Known hypersensitivity to ipamorelin or any formulation excipients.
Pediatric use in children with closed growth plates.
Severe cardiac disease or heart failure — GH elevation can increase cardiac workload.
sideEffects: Headache — most commonly reported adverse effect; caused by acute GH pulse-induced vasodilation; typically occurs in the first 1–2 weeks and diminishes with continued use; reported in approximately 20–35% of users in early weeks.
Mild fatigue or lethargy — transient; within 30–60 minutes post-injection; associated with the GH pulse.
Dizziness or lightheadedness — approximately 10–15% anecdotally; transient vasodilation; resolves within 30 minutes.
Injection site irritation — redness, swelling, minor discomfort; reported in approximately 20–30% with subcutaneous injection.
Mild water retention — GH-mediated sodium and fluid retention; approximately 15% anecdotally; less than CJC-1295 alone; more common in first 2–4 weeks.
Mild nausea — rare; less than 5% at standard doses; more common at 300mcg+.
Slight increase in appetite — modest orexigenic effect from GHS-R1a activation; minimal compared to GHRP-6.
Joint stiffness — GH-mediated periarticular fluid; typically at higher-dose multi-injection protocols.
Tingling or numbness in hands or feet — paresthesia; less common than with CJC-1295 DAC.
Vivid dreams — GH elevation during nocturnal sleep cycle.
Transient mild hypoglycemia — possible when combining with CJC-1295 in a fasted state; GH pulse transiently shifts glucose partitioning.

Long-term insulin resistance (theoretical, dose and duration dependent) — sustained IGF-1 elevation may reduce insulin sensitivity over extended cycles; no direct evidence from ipamorelin-specific studies.

records.name: Ipamorelin + Tesamorelin
records.description: The Ipamorelin + Tesamorelin blend is an 18mg co-lyophilized advanced GH axis stimulation and visceral fat reduction stack (12mg Tesamorelin / 6mg Ipamorelin) — a 2:1 Tesamorelin-dominant ratio reflecting Tesamorelin's outsized role as the primary therapeutic driver in this combination. Tesamorelin is a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) consisting of the full 44-amino acid GHRH(1-44) sequence with a trans-3-hexenoic acid modification at the N-terminus that dramatically increases plasma stability versus native GHRH (half-life approximately 30 minutes versus native GHRH's 7 minutes); it acts directly on GHRH receptors (GHRHR) in the anterior pituitary somatotroph cells to stimulate pulsatile growth hormone (GH) secretion and downstream hepatic IGF-1 production. Tesamorelin is the only GHRH analog with an FDA-approved indication (Egrifta — approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy visceral fat reduction) — making it the most clinically validated compound in the GH secretagogue category for visceral adipose tissue (VAT) reduction specifically. Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide growth hormone secretagogue acting on the GHS-R1a (ghrelin receptor) in the pituitary and hypothalamus — stimulating GH secretion through a pathway independent of and complementary to the GHRH pathway; Ipamorelin is the most selective GHS-R1a agonist in clinical research, producing GH pulses with minimal concurrent stimulation of cortisol, prolactin, or ACTH that characterizes the less selective GHRPs (GHRP-2, GHRP-6), making it the cleanest ghrelin-axis GH secretagogue available. The mechanistic rationale for the Tesamorelin + Ipamorelin combination exploits the two-receptor dual-axis GH stimulation system: GHRH (mimicked by Tesamorelin) and ghrelin (mimicked by Ipamorelin) act on distinct receptor systems in the somatotroph cell — GHRHR signaling through cAMP/PKA to increase GH gene transcription and somatotroph sensitivity, GHS-R1a signaling through Gq/IP3/calcium to trigger GH vesicle exocytosis. When both receptors are stimulated simultaneously, they produce synergistic GH pulse amplification far exceeding either agent alone — this dual-receptor synergy is the physiological basis for the natural GH pulse, where endogenous GHRH and ghrelin co-release produces the maximal nocturnal GH surge. The 2:1 Tesamorelin:Ipamorelin ratio reflects the dominant role of GHRH signaling in establishing the somatotroph's overall secretory capacity and the visceral fat-reducing IGF-1 elevation, while Ipamorelin provides the pulse-triggering exocytotic stimulus. The pre-bed fasted administration requirement is critical to the pharmacological rationale: GH is secreted in pulses during slow-wave sleep (SWS), with the largest pulse occurring 60–90 minutes after sleep onset; exogenous GHRH/GHS-R agonism at this window amplifies the endogenous sleep-associated GH pulse rather than creating a pharmacological pulse at an off-physiological time; the fasted state is required because elevated insulin from a recent meal activates somatostatin release from hypothalamic SRIF neurons, which suppresses GH secretion and would blunt the GHRH/ghrelin synergy — the 2-hour fast ensures somatostatin tone is low at injection time. The visceral fat specificity of Tesamorelin is its defining clinical feature and the primary reason for its dominant role in this blend. VAT (visceral adipose tissue — the metabolically active, inflammation-promoting fat depot surrounding the abdominal organs, distinct from subcutaneous fat) expresses higher densities of GH receptors and IGF-1 receptors than subcutaneous adipose; IGF-1 elevation from Tesamorelin-driven GH stimulation produces preferential lipolysis in VAT through hormone-sensitive lipase activation, GH-mediated insulin resistance attenuation in the visceral adipocyte, and direct anti-lipogenic effects in hepatic lipid processing. The FDA Phase III trials for Tesamorelin (EGRIFTA) demonstrated 15–18% visceral fat reduction over 26 weeks in HIV lipodystrophy patients — a degree of VAT reduction that is clinically significant for cardiometabolic risk reduction. In the non-lipodystrophy research context at the standard protocol dose (1.0mg Tesamorelin + 500mcg Ipamorelin daily), the VAT reduction effect is present but context-dependent on baseline VAT burden and GH axis status.

rows.notes: Yields 1.0mg Tesamorelin and 500mcg Ipamorelin. Administer pre-bed on an empty stomach. 5 days on, 2 days off (skip weekends).
Yields 2.0mg Tesamorelin and 1.0mg Ipamorelin. Often split into two 1.5mg doses (Morning fasted and Pre-Bed fasted). 5 days on, 2 days off.

washout: Cycle Length: 8-12 weeks.
4-8 weeks off to prevent pituitary down-regulation.
contraindications: Active malignancy — both Tesamorelin (via IGF-1 elevation) and Ipamorelin (via GH stimulation) increase circulating IGF-1, a potent cellular growth factor with established roles in tumor cell proliferation, survival signaling (PI3K/AKT/mTOR), and angiogenesis; IGF-1 receptor (IGF-1R) overexpression or upregulation is documented in numerous solid tumors; absolute contraindication in all active cancers.

History of rapidly progressive cancer — a history of cancer with documented rapid growth kinetics, IGF-1R expression, or hormonal sensitivity warrants particular caution; the time elapsed since treatment completion and the specific cancer type should be evaluated before initiating any GH axis compound.

Disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis — tumors of the pituitary (pituitary adenoma) or hypothalamus, or prior pituitary surgery or radiation, produce abnormal baseline GH regulation; exogenous GHRH and GHS-R agonism in subjects with hypothalamic-pituitary axis pathology has unpredictable GH secretory effects and requires endocrinological evaluation.
Acromegaly or GH excess states — subjects with pathological GH excess have already elevated IGF-1; further GH axis stimulation is absolutely contraindicated.

Active diabetic retinopathy — GH elevation worsens diabetic retinopathy through IGF-1-mediated retinal neovascularization; subjects with pre-proliferative or proliferative diabetic retinopathy must not use GH secretagogues.

Severe insulin resistance or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes — GH axis stimulation produces transient insulin resistance through GH receptor-mediated inhibition of insulin signaling in peripheral tissue; this is manageable in subjects with well-controlled diabetes but can significantly destabilize glycemic control in severely insulin-resistant subjects.
Carpal tunnel syndrome — GH elevation causes fluid retention and soft tissue edema that worsens carpal tunnel syndrome; a pre-existing carpal tunnel diagnosis requires dose reduction or avoidance.
Known hypersensitivity to Tesamorelin, Ipamorelin, or formulation excipients.

Pregnancy — GH axis stimulation during pregnancy has not been characterized; the GH-IGF-1 axis undergoes significant changes during normal pregnancy and placental GH drives a distinct IGF-1 production pathway; exogenous GH secretagogue activity during this context has not been evaluated.
Pediatric use with open epiphyses — GH axis stimulation in pediatric subjects with open growth plates could produce excess linear bone growth and requires pediatric endocrinological supervision.
sideEffects: Injection site erythema and irritation — Tesamorelin (as the larger 44-amino acid peptide in this blend) is known to produce injection site redness and subcutaneous nodule formation more frequently than Ipamorelin alone; the FDA label for Egrifta (Tesamorelin) specifically lists injection site reactions as the most common adverse effect; rotating injection sites is important.

Joint pain and arthralgia — GH-mediated fluid retention and soft tissue changes produce joint discomfort, particularly in the wrists and ankles; more pronounced at higher doses (Advanced Recomposition protocol at 2.0mg Tesamorelin); typically resolves with dose reduction or cycle cessation.

Water retention and peripheral edema — GH stimulation increases renal sodium retention and antidiuretic hormone sensitivity; manifests as facial puffiness, ankle swelling, and body weight increase without fat gain; common in the first 2–4 weeks; typically attenuates as GH levels equilibrate.

Mild blood sugar fluctuations — GH-induced insulin resistance produces mild fasting glucose elevation; in non-diabetic subjects this typically remains within the normal range but warrants monitoring; more significant at the Advanced Recomposition 3.0mg/day dose.

Carpal tunnel syndrome symptoms — wrist paresthesias, nocturnal hand numbness, and grip weakness secondary to GH-driven soft tissue edema compressing the carpal tunnel; dose-dependent; typically reverses on cycle cessation.

Headache — commonly reported in the first 1–2 weeks; possibly related to GH-mediated intracranial pressure changes or fluid shifts; typically resolves with continued administration as GH levels stabilize.
Mild nausea — occasionally reported particularly with Tesamorelin at initiation; mechanism unclear; typically transient.

Vivid dreams and altered sleep architecture — GH secretion is closely linked to slow-wave sleep; amplifying the nocturnal GH pulse with pre-bed administration frequently produces vivid, highly detailed dreaming; typically reported as neutral to positive but occasionally disruptive in some subjects.

IGF-1 elevation beyond reference range at high doses — the Advanced Recomposition 3.0mg/day dose can produce IGF-1 levels exceeding age-matched reference ranges in GH-responsive subjects; regular IGF-1 monitoring is warranted at this dose level.

records.name: Kisspeptin
records.description: Kisspeptin is an endogenous neuropeptide encoded by the KISS1 gene, acting as the master upstream regulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis through its receptor GPR54 (also known as Kiss1R) — a Gq-coupled GPCR expressed on GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) neurons in the arcuate nucleus and anteroventral periventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus. The identification of kisspeptin as the primary activator of GnRH pulsatility was one of the most significant endocrinological discoveries of the 2000s: loss-of-function mutations in KISS1 or GPR54 produce complete hypothalamic hypogonadism (absence of puberty, complete GnRH/LH/FSH/testosterone suppression) in both mice and humans, definitively establishing kisspeptin as the non-redundant gatekeeper of reproductive axis activation. Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus co-express neurokinin B (NKB) and dynorphin (Dyn) — forming the KNDy (Kisspeptin/Neurokinin B/Dynorphin) neuron network that generates the rhythmic pulsatile GnRH secretion pattern responsible for normal HPG axis function. Kisspeptin receptor activation on GnRH neurons triggers robust, immediate GnRH release, which signals the anterior pituitary to release LH (luteinizing hormone) and FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) — the gonadotropins that drive testicular testosterone production and spermatogenesis in men, and follicular development, ovulation, and estrogen/progesterone production in women. The research application of exogenous kisspeptin is primarily directed at HPG axis restoration and support. In men on long-term exogenous testosterone therapy (TRT), the continuous supraphysiological testosterone signal creates a negative feedback loop that suppresses GnRH pulsatility at the level of kisspeptin neurons themselves — the arcuate KNDy network downregulates in response to the androgen signal, reducing GnRH pulse amplitude and frequency. Kisspeptin administration bypasses this suppression by directly activating GPR54 on GnRH neurons downstream of the testosterone feedback point — restoring GnRH pulsatility and thus LH/FSH release even in the presence of exogenous testosterone. This is the mechanistic basis for kisspeptin's utility in maintaining endogenous LH/FSH signaling during TRT — preserving testicular Leydig cell function, Sertoli cell activity, and spermatogenesis that would otherwise atrophy under continuous gonadotropin suppression. The 3x-weekly dosing protocol mimics the intermittent stimulation required to prevent GPR54 desensitization — continuous kisspeptin exposure downregulates GPR54 just as continuous GnRH agonist exposure (leuprolide, triptorelin) paradoxically suppresses the HPG axis through receptor desensitization. The synergistic compatibility designations for kisspeptin — HCG, gonadorelin, and testagen — reflect complementary activation points across the HPG axis cascade. Kisspeptin acts at the highest level (hypothalamic GnRH neuron activation via GPR54), gonadorelin acts at the second level (pituitary GnRH receptor activation → LH/FSH release), and HCG acts at the third level (direct LH receptor activation at the testicular Leydig cell → testosterone synthesis). These three compounds can be stacked in a hierarchical HPG axis restoration protocol where each compound supports a distinct anatomical node of the axis — providing redundant stimulation that no single compound achieves. The hormone-dependent cancer contraindication (prostate cancer, hormonally-sensitive breast cancer) is absolute: kisspeptin-driven restoration of LH/FSH and resultant sex hormone production directly stimulates androgen receptor-expressing prostate cancer cells and estrogen receptor-expressing breast cancer cells, potentially accelerating tumor growth.

rows.notes: Standard protocol to boost natural testosterone and maintain fertility.

washout: Alternative 1 Washout: Cycle length 8-12 weeks on, 4-6 weeks washout. Washout duration is 1/2 cycle length.
Alternative 2 Washout: Cycle length 4 weeks on, 4 weeks washout.
contraindications: Hormone-dependent prostate cancer — kisspeptin-driven LH/FSH restoration produces testosterone elevation that directly stimulates androgen receptor-expressing prostate cancer cells; absolute contraindication.
Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer — kisspeptin-driven FSH/LH and estrogen restoration in women stimulates estrogen receptor-expressing breast cancer cells; absolute contraindication.

Other androgen-sensitive or estrogen-sensitive malignancies (certain ovarian cancers, endometrial cancer, some testicular cancers) — HPG axis activation in the context of any sex hormone-sensitive tumor is contraindicated.

Concurrent continuous kisspeptin administration exceeding protocol — GPR54 desensitization from uninterrupted kisspeptin exposure paradoxically suppresses HPG axis activity; the intermittent dosing protocol is not merely preferred but mechanistically required.
Central precocious puberty — kisspeptin is a primary driver of pubertal GnRH pulsatility initiation; administration in pediatric subjects with premature puberty would accelerate the condition.
Concurrent GnRH agonist therapy (leuprolide, triptorelin, histrelin) being used for HPG suppression — kisspeptin directly counteracts the intended HPG suppression achieved by these therapies.
Known hypersensitivity to kisspeptin, KISS1 gene-derived peptides, or formulation excipients.
Pregnancy — kisspeptin plays critical roles in placentation, maternal HPG suppression, and fetal development; exogenous kisspeptin during pregnancy has unpredictable and potentially harmful effects.

Active severe hypothalamic or pituitary pathology (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, Sheehan syndrome with no residual pituitary function) — kisspeptin requires intact GnRH neurons and pituitary gonadotroph function to produce its effects; in subjects with destroyed pituitary or hypothalamic architecture kisspeptin will be ineffective and the underlying pathology management takes precedence.
sideEffects: Mood swings and emotional lability — the most commonly reported subjective adverse effect; driven by the acute fluctuations in LH, FSH, testosterone, and estrogen that follow each kisspeptin dose; typically most pronounced in the first 1–2 weeks of a new cycle before hormonal rhythms stabilize.

Testicular discomfort and ache — a direct consequence of increased Leydig cell and Sertoli cell stimulation from restored LH/FSH; the testes experience increased blood flow and metabolic activity; typically mild to moderate; resolves as testicular tissue adapts to the stimulation.

Transient testosterone and estrogen spikes — the LH surge triggered by each kisspeptin dose produces an acute testosterone pulse; in subjects prone to estrogen conversion (aromatase-active), this may produce transient estrogenic effects (water retention, mood changes).
Libido fluctuations — increased libido as testosterone rises; potential libido troughs during the off-days between doses as the acute LH pulse subsides.
Headache — uncommon; possibly related to acute hormonal fluctuations affecting the HPG axis-CNS interaction.
Injection site irritation — mild erythema and tenderness.

GPR54 desensitization with continuous daily use — the primary long-term efficacy concern; daily or continuous administration downregulates GPR54, converting an HPG stimulator into an HPG suppressor; the pulsatile/intermittent dosing protocols are specifically designed to prevent this.
Acne — secondary to testosterone elevation from restored LH stimulation; more pronounced in subjects with androgen-sensitive skin.
Fluid retention — mild; secondary to estrogen elevation from testosterone aromatization.

records.name: KLOW (BPC-157 + TB-500 + KPV + GHK-Cu)
records.description: KLOW is an 80mg co-lyophilized quad-compound total body repair and immune-modulating blend containing BPC-157 (10mg), TB-500 (10mg), KPV (10mg), and GHK-Cu (50mg) — the GLOW blend with the addition of KPV (Lys-Pro-Val), the C-terminal tripeptide of alpha-MSH (alpha-Melanocyte Stimulating Hormone), as an anti-inflammatory and mucosal immune-regulatory fourth component. The standard daily dose of 3.2mg delivers 2.0mg GHK-Cu, 400mcg BPC-157, 400mcg TB-500, and 400mcg KPV — precisely the GLOW blend plus one additional 400mcg KPV dose in the same injection event. KPV's mechanism is fundamentally distinct from the angiogenic (BPC-157), cytoskeletal (TB-500), and matrix gene-regulatory (GHK-Cu) mechanisms of the three GLOW components: KPV acts as an agonist at MC1R (Melanocortin 1 Receptor) and MC3R — alpha-MSH receptor subtypes expressed on immune cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, lymphocytes), intestinal epithelial cells, and skin keratinocytes — producing potent anti-inflammatory activity through NF-κB pathway inhibition, reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokine production (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8), and activation of anti-inflammatory transcriptional programs. KPV's MC receptor agonism in intestinal epithelial cells and gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) produces specific mucosal anti-inflammatory effects that complement BPC-157's cytoprotective GI activity — together addressing both the vascular/structural repair of gut mucosa (BPC-157) and the inflammatory immune regulation of gut-associated tissue (KPV) simultaneously. The designation of KLOW as a "total body repair blend" versus GLOW's "tissue repair and aesthetic blend" reflects the KPV addition's expansion of the protocol's scope from primarily structural tissue repair and aesthetics into systemic and mucosal immune modulation. The subjects most likely to benefit differentially from KLOW over GLOW are those with: active systemic inflammatory burden (elevated CRP, IL-6, TNF-α from chronic lifestyle-related inflammation or post-infectious states), inflammatory bowel conditions (Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, non-specific gut inflammation where KPV's MC3R agonism in the gut epithelium and GALT directly targets the inflamed mucosal surface), skin inflammatory conditions (psoriasis, eczema, dermatitis — where KPV's MC1R agonism in keratinocytes reduces the cutaneous inflammatory cascade), and post-COVID or post-viral inflammatory states where systemic cytokine dysregulation persists. The synergy with Thymosin Alpha-1 and LL-37 places KLOW in the center of a comprehensive immune restoration and antimicrobial defense protocol: KPV modulates the inflammatory cytokine environment; Thymosin Alpha-1 restores T-cell function and Th1 immune competence; LL-37 provides direct antimicrobial defense and bridges innate-adaptive immune signaling. The three together address systemic inflammation (KPV), adaptive immune competence (Thymosin Alpha-1), and innate immune defense (LL-37) — the three principal dimensions of immune system function in a single protocol. The KLOW protocol retains the identical 5-days-on/2-days-off copper safety schedule from GLOW for the same copper accumulation prevention rationale — the KPV addition does not alter the copper safety calculus since KPV is copper-independent in its mechanism. The 8–12 week cycle maximum is similarly copper-driven. The titration protocol (Alternative Titration 1: 2mg→4mg→6mg→4mg over 12 weeks) includes a characteristic peak-and-taper structure at 6mg/day for weeks 5–8 before reducing back to 4mg/day — a cycling approach that maximizes the repair and inflammatory resolution intensity during the peak phase while reducing the cumulative copper load in the taper phase, extending the overall protocol duration relative to a flat-dose 3.2mg/day approach while staying within safe copper accumulation limits.

rows.notes: Yields exactly 2.0mg GHK-Cu, and 400mcg each of BPC-157, TB-500, and KPV. 5 days on, 2 days off (skip weekends).
Yields 250mcg each TB-500, BPC-157, & KPV, plus 1.25mg GHK-Cu.
Yields 500mcg each TB-500, BPC-157, & KPV, plus 2.5mg GHK-Cu.
Yields 750mcg each TB-500, BPC-157, & KPV, plus 3.75mg GHK-Cu.
Yields 500mcg each TB-500, BPC-157, & KPV, plus 2.5mg GHK-Cu.
Yields 375mcg each TB-500, BPC-157, & KPV, plus 1.87mg GHK-Cu.

washout: Cycle Length: 8 to 12 weeks maximum.
Minimum 4 weeks off to allow copper levels to clear.
contraindications: Active cancer — BPC-157's VEGFR2-mediated angiogenic activity and GHK-Cu's comprehensive pro-growth gene program upregulation are absolutely contraindicated in active malignancy for the same reasons as GLOW; KPV's MC receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory activity in the tumor microenvironment is an additional consideration since tumor-associated inflammation suppression could theoretically reduce immune surveillance of the tumor.

Zinc deficiency — GHK-Cu copper competition with zinc absorption applies identically to KLOW as to GLOW; zinc status must be confirmed and repleted before initiating KLOW; concurrent zinc supplementation (15–30mg/day) is required throughout all KLOW cycles.
Wilson's disease — copper metabolism disorder; GHK-Cu copper delivery is absolutely contraindicated.

Active autoimmune disease in acute flare — KPV's MC receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory activity produces immune modulation; in some autoimmune conditions, the NF-κB suppression is beneficial (IBD, psoriasis, skin inflammation); in others (systemic lupus, vasculitis, severe rheumatoid arthritis flare), the interaction between KPV's immune modulation and the existing dysregulated immune response requires medical supervision and monitoring.

Concurrent immunosuppressive therapy (calcineurin inhibitors, biologics for autoimmune disease, post-transplant immunosuppression) — KPV's MC receptor-mediated immune regulation adds an exogenous immunomodulatory layer to subjects already on potent immunosuppressive regimens; the combined immune system activity has not been characterized.
Known hypersensitivity to BPC-157, TB-500, KPV (Lys-Pro-Val), GHK-Cu, or formulation excipients.
Severe hepatic impairment — copper processing limitation applies identically to KLOW as GLOW.
Pregnancy — the combined angiogenic, immune-modulatory (KPV), and copper-delivering activity of KLOW has not been evaluated during pregnancy.
History of copper toxicity — previous copper sensitivity contraindicates the GHK-Cu component.

Active infectious disease requiring antimicrobial management — KPV's NF-κB suppression and pro-inflammatory cytokine reduction could modestly attenuate the acute-phase inflammatory response that is part of the innate immune defense against active infection; KLOW is appropriate for post-infectious repair and maintenance, not concurrent use during active systemic infection.
sideEffects: Injection site redness and welting — more pronounced than GLOW in some subjects; the addition of KPV adds a fourth peptide to the injection bolus and KPV's MC1R activation in local skin can produce mild cutaneous vasodilation at the injection site; typically resolves within 1–2 hours.
Mild fatigue — attributable to the BPC-157/TB-500 dopaminergic modulation component; similar in character and duration to GLOW; typically mild and lasting 1–3 hours post-injection.
Zinc depletion — the same critical monitoring parameter as GLOW; mandatory zinc supplementation throughout all KLOW cycles.
Mild copper accumulation risk — identical to GLOW; the 5-days-on protocol and cycle limits mitigate this risk at standard doses.

Mild pigmentary changes (uncommon) — KPV as an alpha-MSH receptor agonist has very modest melanocyte-stimulating activity compared to full-length alpha-MSH or Melanotan; mild, transient, and far less pronounced than Melanotan-1 or -2; not expected at the 400mcg/day KPV doses in KLOW but represents a theoretical consideration for subjects with existing pigmentation conditions.

Transient blood pressure changes — KPV's vasodilatory activity at MC receptors in vascular endothelium may produce mild transient blood pressure fluctuations in the first days of a cycle; typically self-limiting.
Anhedonia (rare) — same BPC-157 dopaminergic mechanism as GLOW; rare; typically transient.
Mild nausea in first cycle days — occasionally reported with the four-peptide combination; mechanism may involve KPV's area postrema MC receptor interaction; typically resolves within the first week.
Elevated liver enzymes (ALT/AST) — same hepatic copper processing consideration as GLOW; monitor in subjects with pre-existing liver conditions.

records.name: KPV
records.description: KPV (Lys-Pro-Val) is the C-terminal tripeptide fragment of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), specifically representing residues 11–13 of the 13-amino-acid parent peptide. Alpha-MSH is a neuropeptide produced in the hypothalamus and pituitary that mediates a broad spectrum of anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and homeostatic functions through melanocortin receptors (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, MC5R). KPV retains the full anti-inflammatory activity of α-MSH but notably lacks the melanotropic (pigmentation-stimulating) N-terminal acetyl group — meaning it produces no melanin increase or tanning effect that characterizes the full parent molecule or compounds like Melanotan-II. The primary mechanism is inhibition of NF-kB (Nuclear Factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells), the master transcription factor of inflammatory gene expression. By blocking NF-kB translocation to the nucleus, KPV suppresses the production of TNF-alpha, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and other pro-inflammatory cytokines at their transcriptional source. Secondary mechanism activity includes inhibition of the MAPK (p38 and ERK) inflammatory signaling cascades and direct inhibition of activated macrophage and mast cell signaling. One of KPV's most pharmacologically significant properties is its transport via the intestinal PepT1 (SLC15A1) transporter — a proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter normally expressed in the small intestine. In healthy colonic tissue, PepT1 expression is absent or minimal. However, in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis, PepT1 is dramatically upregulated in the colon, creating a natural delivery pathway that concentrates KPV preferentially in the most inflamed colonic tissue. This makes KPV uniquely suited for gut-targeted applications where oral or injectable administration delivers the peptide directly into the cells driving the disease process. In preclinical colitis models (DSS-induced and TNBS-induced), KPV significantly reduced disease activity scores, colonic cytokine expression, and epithelial barrier disruption. PepT1-knockout experiments confirmed this pathway is essential — KPV showed no effect in the absence of the transporter, establishing the molecular mechanism of its gut selectivity. KPV has the most favorable safety profile of any anti-inflammatory compound in this database. It does not suppress systemic immune function in the manner of corticosteroids, NSAIDs, or biological TNF-alpha inhibitors. It does not cause tissue thinning, HPA axis suppression, or metabolic side effects associated with glucocorticoid use. It does not increase infection susceptibility at standard doses. The absence of pigmentation effects removes the melanocortin-axis side effects that accompany full-length α-MSH or MT-II. The primary reason the contraindications list remains thin is that KPV's mechanism is fundamentally modulatory rather than suppressive — it normalizes inflammatory signaling without eliminating it, preserving the acute immune response.

rows.notes: Standard protocol for systemic inflammation or gut repair.
Administer at or near the injury or inflammation site.

washout: Cycle Length: 6-8 weeks.
Washout: 4 weeks off.
Alternative 1 Washout: Cycle length 8 weeks on, 4 weeks washout.
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to KPV, alpha-MSH-derived peptides, or any formulation excipients.

Concurrent use of immunosuppressive biologic agents (TNF-alpha inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors) — additive anti-inflammatory pathway inhibition may push the immune response below the threshold needed for pathogen defense; theoretical but warrants clinical consideration.
Concurrent corticosteroid use — overlapping NF-kB suppression; the additive anti-inflammatory effect may mask warning signs of infection or worsen immune suppression.
Active infections requiring a robust acute immune response — KPV's NF-kB inhibition, while selective, may blunt cytokine response to active bacterial or viral infections at high doses.
Pregnancy — no clinical safety data; melanocortin receptor signaling has developmental implications.
Breastfeeding — no established safety data.
Pediatric use — safety not established.
PepT1-negative intestinal conditions — rare congenital PepT1 deficiency would abolish oral/enteric KPV activity.
sideEffects: Mild injection site redness and irritation — the most commonly reported adverse effect; localized erythema at the subcutaneous administration site; transient; self-resolving.
Mild gastrointestinal discomfort — particularly with oral or higher-dose administration; nausea, loose stools, or abdominal cramping; more common in the first week.
Temporary fatigue — reported in a minority of subjects; likely related to systemic inflammatory modulation during early treatment.
Headache — uncommon; transient.
Skin flushing — rare; mild; may reflect residual melanocortin receptor activity.
Mild dizziness — infrequent; mechanism unclear.
Temporary appetite changes — rare; MC4R activity (which KPV may weakly engage) has minor effects on appetite regulation.

Potential blunting of acute immune response at very high doses — KPV's NF-kB inhibition is dose-dependent; at supraphysiologic doses, the anti-inflammatory effect could theoretically impair the acute phase immune response to active infection.
Allergic reactions to compounding excipients — redness, hives, stinging at injection site; relates to the compounding vehicle rather than KPV itself.

records.name: L-Carnitine (Injectable)
records.description: L-Carnitine is an endogenous quaternary ammonium compound (derived from lysine and methionine) that functions as the essential carrier for long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs) across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Without L-Carnitine, long-chain fatty acids — the primary fuel substrate for aerobic metabolism in skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and the liver — cannot enter the mitochondrial matrix for beta-oxidation. The mechanism is mediated by two transport proteins: carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I) on the outer mitochondrial membrane converts fatty acyl-CoA to fatty acyl-carnitine, which then crosses to the inner membrane; carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT-II) on the inner membrane reconverts the fatty acyl-carnitine back to fatty acyl-CoA inside the matrix, where beta-oxidation generates acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle and ultimately ATP production. L-Carnitine is therefore not a stimulant, a fat burner in the conventional pharmaceutical sense, or a thermogenic — it is a metabolic transport facilitator that ensures fat oxidation capacity is not limited by carnitine availability at the mitochondrial membrane. Oral L-Carnitine has notoriously poor and highly variable bioavailability — approximately 14–18% of an oral dose is absorbed, and much of what is absorbed is catabolized by intestinal microbiota into trimethylamine (TMA), which is oxidized hepatically to TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide). TMAO has been associated with cardiovascular risk in observational studies, making high-dose oral carnitine supplementation a complex risk-benefit calculation. Injectable L-Carnitine bypasses intestinal absorption and hepatic first-pass TMAO production entirely: 100% bioavailability delivers the carnitine directly to systemic circulation, from which it can be taken up by muscle and cardiac tissue without the gut microbiome conversion step. This is the primary clinical rationale for injectable over oral administration, and it is particularly relevant for the cardiometabolic patient population using GLP-1 agonists in this database — these subjects often have altered gut microbiome composition that exaggerates oral carnitine TMAO conversion. The pre-workout dosing with a small carbohydrate source is pharmacologically specific: L-Carnitine uptake by skeletal muscle is insulin-dependent. Without an insulin stimulus, circulating carnitine is poorly taken up by myocytes — it must reach the mitochondrial membrane to perform its function, and GLUT4-type uptake mechanisms require insulin signaling for efficient intramuscular carnitine accumulation. A small carbohydrate dose (20–30g) pre-workout provides a modest insulin spike sufficient to drive carnitine into muscle tissue while avoiding the fat-oxidation-blunting effect of a large carbohydrate load. The injectable form achieves higher peak plasma concentrations than oral, which means the insulin-driven muscle uptake is more efficient. The synergy with AICAR reflects convergent fat oxidation enhancement: AICAR increases the mitochondrial capacity for fat oxidation by upregulating beta-oxidation enzymes and fatty acid transport proteins via AMPK, while L-Carnitine provides the transport molecule required to actually execute the fat oxidation that AICAR's AMPK activation creates the capacity for.

rows.notes: Administer pre-workout with a small carbohydrate source to spike insulin for cellular uptake.

washout: Cycle Length: Indefinite.
Washout: None required.
contraindications: Hypothyroidism (may interfere with thyroid hormone action) — L-Carnitine acts as a functional thyroid hormone antagonist at the receptor level; it inhibits thyroid hormone entry into cell nuclei, reducing gene transactivation by T3 and T4; subjects with hypothyroidism should be aware that L-Carnitine supplementation may worsen hypothyroid symptoms or reduce the effectiveness of levothyroxine therapy.

Concurrent levothyroxine or thyroid hormone therapy — L-Carnitine's peripheral anti-thyroid action may reduce the effectiveness of thyroid replacement therapy; monitor thyroid function if co-administering.

End-stage renal disease (ESRD) without dialysis — L-Carnitine is renally excreted; accumulation to toxic levels is possible in severe renal failure; patients on hemodialysis may actually require carnitine supplementation due to dialytic losses, but administration should be clinically supervised.
Seizure disorder — rare reports of increased seizure frequency in subjects with pre-existing seizure disorders using L-Carnitine supplementation; mechanism not fully characterized; use with caution.
Known hypersensitivity to L-Carnitine or injectable formulation excipients.
Concurrent anticoagulant therapy (warfarin) — case reports suggest L-Carnitine potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin; INR monitoring is warranted if co-administering.

Trimethylaminuria (fish odor syndrome) — subjects with impaired FMO3 enzyme activity cannot efficiently oxidize TMA to TMAO; even injectable carnitine metabolism may produce systemic TMA accumulation and severe body odor.
sideEffects: Fishy body odor (trimethylaminuria-like effect) — the most characteristically reported adverse effect at higher injectable doses; occurs as L-Carnitine metabolism produces trimethylamine as a byproduct; some individuals are poor metabolizers of TMA to TMAO; the odor can be significant and socially notable; injectable routes reduce but do not eliminate this risk compared to oral.

Injection site pain and local reactions — injectable L-Carnitine solutions are often hyperosmolar; subcutaneous administration can cause burning, stinging, and localized irritation; IM injection is sometimes preferred for volume and tolerability reasons.
Nausea and gastrointestinal discomfort — more common with oral forms but reported with high-dose injectable use.
Diarrhea — at high doses; related to systemic carnitine load.
Headache — mild; occasional; mechanism not characterized.
Restlessness or mild insomnia — reported in sensitive individuals at higher doses; carnitine's role in mitochondrial activation may have a mild stimulatory quality in some subjects.
Hypothyroidism worsening — functional anti-thyroid effect in subjects with compromised thyroid function; thyroid-sensitive subjects should monitor thyroid panel.

Elevated TMAO (trimethylamine N-oxide) — cardiovascular risk concern at chronic high doses; the injectable route mitigates but does not entirely eliminate TMAO production; relevance at standard research protocol doses is uncertain.

Muscle weakness in subjects with carnitine-related metabolic disorders — paradoxical; subjects with organic acidemias or other disorders of carnitine metabolism may experience unusual responses to supplementation.

records.name: L-Carnitine (LC500)
records.description: L-Carnitine (product code LC500) is a single-ingredient injectable delivering a high 500mg dose of L-Carnitine per milliliter. It is an amino acid derivative rather than a peptide, and it works through a well-defined metabolic mechanism rather than a hormone receptor, given as a fixed direct dose with no titration. L-Carnitine is a compound the body uses to transport long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane so they can be oxidized for energy. Injectable delivery bypasses the relatively poor and variable absorption of oral carnitine, which allows a much higher effective dose to reach circulation and, in turn, the muscle and other tissues that rely on fatty-acid oxidation. In practice, LC500 is used by people focused on fat metabolism, endurance, and recovery who want a potent, standalone carnitine injection rather than a multi-ingredient blend. It is popular with endurance athletes and physique-focused users because supporting fatty-acid transport can improve the use of fat as a fuel source during training and may support faster recovery and reduced muscle soreness. Many users administer it before cardio or training sessions to prioritize fat oxidation, or in the morning as part of a fat-loss protocol. Because it is a single ingredient at a high dose, it is also frequently stacked alongside MIC-style lipotropic blends by users who want to layer additional carnitine on top of a broader formula. Mechanistically, the value of high-dose injectable carnitine comes from raising tissue carnitine availability well above what diet or oral supplementation reliably achieves, which supports mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, energy production, and clearance of metabolic byproducts from intense exercise. Research also points to a role in supporting blood flow and reducing exercise-induced muscle damage markers. Users should expect endurance and recovery support that builds with consistent use rather than a dramatic acute effect. Timing before training or in the morning is preferred so the mild energizing effect aligns with activity. Injection sites should be rotated, and anyone with seizure history or thyroid concerns should use carnitine only under medical guidance, as it can rarely affect seizure threshold and thyroid hormone action.

rows.notes: Direct-dose L-Carnitine injection with no titration required. A typical protocol is 0.5 to 1 mL (250 to 500mg) administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly 3 to 5 times per week, often before training or in the morning. Rotate injection sites each administration. May be used continuously or stacked with lipotropic blends.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to L-carnitine or any formulation excipient.
Pregnancy or breastfeeding unless directed and supervised by a physician.
Active kidney disease or dialysis unless medically supervised.
History of seizures, as carnitine may lower the seizure threshold in susceptible individuals.
Hypothyroidism managed with medication, without physician oversight, as carnitine can affect thyroid hormone action.
sideEffects: Injection site irritation, redness, warmth, or tenderness.
Fishy body odor at higher intakes.
Nausea or mild gastrointestinal upset.
Increase in energy or restlessness if dosed late in the day.
Headache.

records.name: Libidon
records.description: Libidon is a Khavinson cytomedin — peptide complex A-16 — extracted from prostate gland tissue of young animals, developed as the oral prostatic bioregulator of the Khavinson framework and the commercial cytomedin counterpart to Prostamax (the injectable synthetic tetrapeptide Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp). It delivers a mixture of prostate tissue-derived low-molecular-weight peptides that interact with prostatic epithelial and stromal cells at the transcriptional level, normalizing the gene expression programs governing cell proliferation control, inflammatory cytokine production, androgen receptor sensitivity, and growth factor signaling pathways (EGF, FGF, IGF-1) that maintain prostatic tissue homeostasis. In practical terms, Libidon signals aging prostate cells to restore the regulated, non-inflammatory gene activity of young prostatic tissue — reducing abnormal growth signals that drive benign enlargement, and dampening the chronic inflammatory programs that contribute to prostatitis symptoms. The clinical evidence for Libidon includes a published clinical study from the St. Petersburg Institute documenting statistically significant outcomes in subjects with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and chronic prostatitis. Documented results include reduction in prostate volume on transrectal ultrasound, improvement in urinary flow parameters (peak flow rate, post-void residual reduction), reduction in International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), improvement in quality-of-life domain scores, and reduction in NIH-CPSI pelvic pain subscores in chronic prostatitis subjects. These outcomes span the obstructive (BPH), inflammatory (prostatitis), and functional (urinary flow, symptom score) dimensions of prostate disease, making Libidon one of the more broadly documented prostatic bioregulators in the Khavinson catalog. Libidon's clinical position relative to Prostamax — the injectable synthetic tetrapeptide prostate bioregulator also in this database — is the standard oral/injectable cytomedin-vs-synthetic-peptide trade-off seen across the Khavinson framework: Prostamax delivers the defined single-sequence injectable precision; Libidon delivers the full prostate tissue extract oral convenience. What distinguishes the Libidon/Prostamax pair from other cytomedin/synthetic-peptide pairs in this database is the particular clinical relevance for men's aging health — prostate enlargement and urinary symptom progression are near-universal aspects of male aging, and the PSA monitoring guidance that applies to both compounds positions them specifically within a prostate health maintenance framework rather than purely a longevity intervention. The synergy designation with Testagen (testicular bioregulator) reflects the androgen axis connection: Testagen normalizes the quality of testicular testosterone production; Libidon normalizes the prostate's androgen-regulated tissue program — covering both ends of the male sex steroid axis simultaneously.

rows.notes: Standard intensive course per clinical study protocol. Repeat every 3-6 months. Maintenance: 2 capsules once daily for 10 days every 3 months for ongoing prostate health support.

protocols.label: Alternative Titration 1: BPH Symptom Relief Protocol (Goal — IPSS improvement and urinary flow normalization in subjects with symptomatic BPH)

rows.notes: Intensive dose for significant BPH. Baseline IPSS score, PSA, and peak urinary flow rate before initiating. Run concurrent with Testagen from day 6 for complete androgen axis bioregulator coverage. Repeat IPSS at day 30.

protocols.label: Alternative Titration 2: Chronic Prostatitis/CPPS Protocol (Goal — prostatic inflammatory gene program normalization for Category III-B chronic prostatitis/CPPS; NIH-CPSI score tracking)

Full dose for extended prostatitis course. NIH-CPSI reassessment at day 60. Extended 60-day course appropriate for chronic prostatitis where sustained bioregulator exposure is required for meaningful anti-inflammatory gene program normalization.

rows.notes: Concurrent. Prostamax delivers the Lys-Glu-Asp-Trp prostatic bioregulator signal by injection; Libidon provides the broader prostate cytomedin matrix orally. PSA monitoring throughout. Most complete prostatic bioregulator protocol available.

records.name: Lipo Mino Mix (LMX)
records.description: Lipo Mino Mix (product code LMX) is a well-rounded lipotropic and B-vitamin injection that pairs the classic MIC methylation base with a fuller B-vitamin panel and a solid carnitine dose. It is a vitamin and amino blend rather than a peptide, working through nutritional and metabolic support, and given as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains B6 2mg, Methionine 12.4mg, Inositol 25mg, Choline 25mg, B1 (Thiamine) 50mg, B2 (Riboflavin) 5mg, and Carnitine 125mg. The methionine, inositol, and choline provide the lipotropic fat-transport base, carnitine supports mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, and the B1, B2, and B6 panel supports carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism and cellular energy production. In practice, Lipo Mino Mix is used by people who want a balanced, moderate-strength fat-metabolism and energy injection with a stronger B-vitamin profile than a bare MIC shot. It sits between the entry-level Lipo-C and the higher-potency Fat Blaster in intensity, making it a common everyday choice for users who want reliable lipotropic and energy support without stimulants. It is typically administered in the morning as a standing weekly injection during fat-loss or maintenance phases, and the added thiamine and riboflavin make it appealing to users who want more comprehensive metabolic vitamin support alongside the fat-transport ingredients. Like the other lipotropic blends, it performs best in combination with diet and training. Mechanistically, LMX combines methyl donors (methionine, inositol, choline) and a mitochondrial fatty-acid transporter (carnitine) with the B-vitamins that macronutrient metabolism depends on, so the injection supports both fat mobilization and the conversion of nutrients into cellular energy. Users should expect gradual metabolic and energy support that builds with consistent use. Morning administration is preferred because the carnitine and B-vitamins are mildly energizing and can disrupt sleep if dosed late. Injection sites should be rotated, and the standard liver, kidney, and seizure precautions apply.

rows.notes: Direct-dose balanced lipotropic and B-vitamin injection with no titration required. A typical protocol is 0.5 to 1 mL administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly 2 to 3 times per week, in the morning. Rotate injection sites each administration. Suitable for continuous use during fat-loss or maintenance phases.

records.name: Lipo-C (LC120)
records.description: Lipo-C (product code LC120) is a lipotropic injectable blend built around the classic MIC-style fat-metabolism and methylation support stack. It is a vitamin and amino acid compound rather than a peptide, which means it does not act on a specific hormone receptor and does not require a titration or escalation schedule. Each milliliter of the blend contains Methionine 15mg, Choline Chloride 50mg, Carnitine 50mg, and Dexpanthenol (provitamin B5) 5mg. Methionine is a sulfur-containing essential amino acid that donates methyl groups and supports the liver in processing and exporting fat rather than storing it. Choline works alongside methionine to support hepatic fat transport and helps prevent fat from accumulating in the liver. L-Carnitine transports long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria so they can be oxidized for energy, and Dexpanthenol supports the coenzyme-A pathway that fatty-acid metabolism depends on. In practice, Lipo-C is used as a general lipotropic and metabolic-support injection by people who are already managing calories and training and want additional support for fat metabolism, liver health, and daily energy. Because it is a direct-dose blend, users administer a fixed volume on a consistent weekly cadence rather than working up from a small starting dose. It is commonly run continuously as a standing weekly injection during a fat-loss phase, or cycled in blocks that line up with dieting periods. Many users pair it with a structured training program and adequate protein intake, since the blend supports the metabolic machinery for burning fat but does not by itself create a caloric deficit. It is frequently used as an entry point for people new to injectable metabolic support because the ingredient profile is well understood and the fixed dosing is simple to follow. Mechanistically, the value of Lipo-C comes from combining methyl donors (methionine and choline) with a mitochondrial fatty-acid transporter (carnitine) and a coenzyme-A precursor (B5) in a single injection, so that the liver has both the signal and the raw materials to mobilize and burn fat efficiently. Users should set realistic expectations: this blend is a support tool that works best in the context of diet and exercise, not a standalone fat-loss agent, and results build gradually over weeks of consistent use. Morning administration is generally preferred because the carnitine and B5 content can be mildly stimulating and may interfere with sleep if injected late in the day. Injection sites should be rotated to reduce local irritation, and anyone with liver, kidney, or seizure history should use the blend only under medical supervision.

rows.notes: Direct-dose lipotropic injection with no titration required. A typical protocol is 0.5 to 1 mL administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly 2 to 3 times per week. Administer in the morning to avoid potential sleep disruption from the carnitine and B5 content. Rotate injection sites each administration. May be used continuously alongside diet and training, or in blocks aligned with active fat-loss phases.
