records.name: Lipo-C Fat Blaster (LC526)
records.description: Lipo-C Fat Blaster (product code LC526) is a high-potency lipotropic injection built around a large carnitine dose, a full MIC base, and cellular-energy cofactors, aimed at maximizing fat-metabolism support without stimulants. It is a vitamin and amino acid blend rather than a peptide, delivered as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains L-Carnitine 300mg, Methionine 25mg, Inositol 50mg, Choline 50mg, B12 (Methylcobalamin) 1mg, B6 (Pyridoxine) 50mg, and NADH 50mg. The high carnitine dose drives fatty-acid transport into the mitochondria, the MIC trio (methionine, inositol, choline) provides classic lipotropic fat-mobilization support, B6 and B12 support amino acid and energy metabolism, and NADH supplies a cellular energy cofactor that supports mitochondrial ATP production. In practice, LC526 is used by people who want an aggressive, stimulant-free fat-loss injection with strong metabolic and energy support, making it a good fit for those who are sensitive to stimulants but still want a potent lipotropic shot. The combination of high carnitine plus NADH and a robust B-vitamin panel positions it as an energy-supporting fat metabolism blend suitable for morning use during a cutting phase. It is typically run as a standing 2 to 3 times weekly injection through a fat-loss block, and users who dislike the jittery feel of stimulant blends like LC425 often prefer this formula for a cleaner energy profile. Mechanistically, LC526 combines lipotropic fat transport with cellular energy support: carnitine and the MIC base move and process fat, while B6, B12, and especially NADH support the mitochondrial machinery that turns that fat into usable energy. This positions it as a fat-metabolism blend with a cleaner, non-stimulant energy component. Users should expect gradual, cumulative fat-metabolism and energy benefits rather than an acute stimulant hit. Morning dosing is preferred because the B-vitamin and NADH content can be mildly energizing. Injection sites should be rotated, and standard precautions for liver, kidney, and seizure history apply given the carnitine and choline content.

records.name: Lipo-C Focus (LC425)
records.description: Lipo-C Focus (product code LC425) is a stimulant-enhanced lipotropic injection designed to combine fat-metabolism support with a strong energy and mental-focus component. It is a vitamin and amino blend with added stimulant and cellular-energy ingredients, given as a fixed direct dose rather than a titrated peptide. Each milliliter contains ATP 50mg, Eria Jarensis 50mg, L-Carnitine 200mg, a MIC blend (Methionine 25mg, Inositol 50mg, Choline 50mg), Lidocaine 0.1 percent, and Benzyl Alcohol 2 percent. The high-dose carnitine and MIC base provide lipotropic fat-mobilization support, ATP supplies cellular energy substrate, Eria Jarensis is a stimulant that supports mood, drive, and focus, the lidocaine reduces injection discomfort, and benzyl alcohol acts as a preservative. In practice, LC425 is chosen by users who want a fat-loss injection that also delivers a noticeable pre-workout style lift in energy and mental focus, making it popular as a morning or pre-training shot during aggressive cutting phases. The stimulant content sets it apart from standard lipotropic blends and makes it feel more immediately active. It is typically used by experienced users who tolerate stimulants well and want the combined effect of appetite and energy support with lipotropic fat metabolism. Because of the Eria Jarensis stimulant, this blend is not suited to stimulant-sensitive individuals or anyone dosing later in the day, and it should not be combined with other strong stimulants. Mechanistically, LC425 stacks lipotropic fat transport with a stimulant-driven increase in energy, focus, and drive, plus supplemental ATP intended to support cellular energy availability. The result is a blend meant to feel energizing while supporting fat metabolism during a deficit. Users should expect a clear acute stimulant effect in addition to the gradual lipotropic support, and should treat the stimulant content with respect. This blend must be dosed in the morning only, never late in the day, to avoid disrupting sleep and stacking cardiovascular stimulation. Injection sites should be rotated, stimulant intake from other sources should be reduced on dosing days, and anyone with cardiovascular conditions, high blood pressure, anxiety disorders, or stimulant sensitivity should avoid this blend or use it only under medical supervision.

records.name: Lipo-C with B12 (LC1201)
records.description: Lipo-C with B12 (product code LC1201) is the enhanced version of the standard Lipo-C lipotropic injection, taking the same fat-metabolism and methylation base and adding methylated vitamin B12 for an energy and recovery boost. It is a vitamin and amino acid compound rather than a peptide, so it acts through nutritional and metabolic pathways rather than a hormone receptor, and it is given as a fixed direct dose with no titration. Each milliliter contains Methionine 15mg, Choline Chloride 50mg, Carnitine 50mg, Dexpanthenol (provitamin B5) 5mg, and B12 as Methylcobalamin 1mg. The methionine, choline, carnitine, and B5 provide the classic lipotropic action of supporting the liver in mobilizing and burning fat, while the added methylcobalamin supports red blood cell formation, nervous system function, and cellular energy production through its role in the methylation and Krebs cycle pathways. In practice, LC1201 is chosen by users who want the fat-metabolism support of Lipo-C along with the noticeable energy and mood lift that injectable B12 can provide, especially those who feel fatigued while dieting or who have marginal B12 status. It is used as a standing weekly injection during fat-loss phases, or year-round by people who simply want the metabolic and energy support. The addition of B12 makes this a popular choice for anyone combining a calorie deficit with training, since low energy is one of the most common complaints during a cut and the methylcobalamin helps offset that. Like the base Lipo-C, it works best as a support tool layered on top of good nutrition and consistent activity rather than as a standalone fat burner. Mechanistically, LC1201 pairs methyl donors and a mitochondrial fatty-acid transporter with a methyl-group cofactor (B12), which means the same injection supports both the fat-burning machinery and the broader methylation cycle that governs energy metabolism, homocysteine clearance, and neurological health. Users should expect gradual metabolic support and, in B12-deficient individuals, a more immediate improvement in energy and mental clarity. records.name: Liraglutide
records.description: Liraglutide is the first-generation, once-daily GLP-1 receptor agonist — the compound that proved the entire incretin class was viable for serious weight management before semaglutide existed. It shares 97% structural homology with native human GLP-1 and uses a C16 fatty acid chain to bind albumin in the bloodstream, which slows its clearance and extends its effective half-life to approximately 13 hours. That half-life is why it requires daily injections rather than weekly — it simply does not stay in circulation long enough to sustain receptor activation across a full week. Mechanistically, it works identically to semaglutide: glucose-dependent insulin stimulation, glucagon suppression, delayed gastric emptying, and central appetite suppression via hypothalamic GLP-1 receptors. The difference is purely pharmacokinetic — daily dosing creates a different plasma curve and tolerability dynamic than weekly dosing. Liraglutide was FDA-approved in 2010 as Victoza for type 2 diabetes and in 2014 as Saxenda for chronic weight management, making it one of the longest-running GLP-1 compounds with the deepest long-term safety dataset in the class. The LEADER cardiovascular outcomes trial demonstrated a 13% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk diabetic populations. The SCALE trial program at 3.0mg daily showed approximately 8% mean body weight loss over 56 weeks — lower than what newer weekly agents achieve, but meaningful and well-characterized. Liraglutide also carries one of the strongest evidence bases for cardiovascular risk reduction among all GLP-1 compounds, and its daily dosing profile provides more consistent pharmacodynamic exposure with smaller plasma peaks and troughs than weekly agents. For researchers already familiar with semaglutide, liraglutide represents a step backward in terms of weight loss ceiling and convenience. Its primary relevance in modern research contexts is as a bridge compound for transitioning between weekly agents, as a lower-intensity entry point for subjects highly sensitive to GLP-1 side effects, or as a stacking partner with cagrilintide (the CagriSema combination was directly inspired by the liraglutide + cagrilintide pairing tested in earlier trials). Its main practical drawback is injection site fatigue — daily subcutaneous injections will cycle through sites faster than any weekly protocol, and compliance drops significantly over time compared to once-weekly dosing schedules.

records.name: Livagen
records.description: Livagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala) Khavinson bioregulator derived from liver tissue polypeptide extracts with a uniquely dual mechanism — acting simultaneously on hepatic parenchymal cells (hepatocytes) through the standard organ-specific bioregulator pathway, and on chromatin structure and epigenetic gene regulation at the nuclear level, representing the most fundamentally genomic of all Khavinson bioregulators. The chromatin-level mechanism is what makes Livagen distinctively different from all other bioregulators in this database: Livagen has been demonstrated in the Khavinson research to interact directly with nucleosomal chromatin structure — binding to histone proteins and DNA-histone complexes to influence the compaction state of chromatin in somatic cell nuclei. Aged cells accumulate heterochromatin at specific genomic loci — inappropriate silencing of genes that should remain active in youthful tissue — and this epigenetic silencing contributes directly to the cellular senescence phenotype. Livagen's chromatin-decondensing activity at age-associated heterochromatic loci partially reverses this epigenetic silencing — restoring access of transcription factors to gene promoters that have been inappropriately silenced by aging-associated heterochromatin accumulation. This mechanism is not tissue-specific to the liver: it operates wherever heterochromatin-driven epigenetic gene silencing is disrupting normal cellular function, making Livagen's chromatin bioregulator activity a systemic anti-aging intervention that operates at the most fundamental level of gene expression regulation. The hepatic specificity of Livagen's second mechanism — its organ-targeted bioregulator activity on liver tissue — is explained by the liver's unique metabolic and regenerative biology. Hepatocytes undergo more rounds of DNA replication than most somatic cells (due to the liver's regenerative capacity and the continuous hepatocyte turnover required to replace the 10–20% of hepatocytes lost to apoptosis each year), accumulating DNA damage and replication errors at a higher rate than post-mitotic cells. The combination of Livagen's chromatin-decondensing activity (restoring expression of DNA repair genes silenced by heterochromatin) with its hepatocyte-specific bioregulator activity (normalizing hepatic gene expression programs) creates a compound mechanism specifically relevant to liver aging: restoring the expression of DNA damage response genes that aging hepatocytes have epigenetically silenced, and normalizing the hepatocyte functional programs governing metabolism and detoxification simultaneously. The synergy with Ovagen captures the complementary scope: Ovagen provides the functional hepatocyte metabolic normalization; Livagen provides the genomic stability and DNA repair restoration that allows those hepatocytes to continue functioning reliably over subsequent cell divisions. The systemic chromatin bioregulator activity of Livagen positions it as potentially the most cross-category relevant compound in the Khavinson bioregulator set — its epigenetic mechanism operates at the level that modulates the expression of thousands of genes across multiple tissue types simultaneously. The Khavinson research documented effects of Livagen beyond the liver in aging subjects: improvements in immune cell function (consistent with chromatin decondensation in lymphocytes restoring epigenetically silenced immune gene programs), improvements in cognitive markers (consistent with neuronal chromatin restoration), and broad-spectrum anti-aging biomarker improvements that exceed what would be predicted from a purely hepatic mechanism alone. This systemic epigenetic component makes Livagen a uniquely appropriate anchor compound for comprehensive Khavinson longevity protocols — its chromatin mechanism complements and amplifies the organ-specific bioregulator activities of all other compounds in this category by restoring the gene regulatory access that all bioregulators require to produce their normalizing effects.

Active viral hepatitis with significant liver fibrosis (Metavir F3-F4) — the combination of active viral hepatic injury and chromatin bioregulator activity in severely fibrotic liver has not been characterized.

Decompensated cirrhosis — insufficient viable hepatocyte mass for meaningful hepatic bioregulator response; the coagulopathy and portal hypertension of decompensated cirrhosis create an unfavorable context.

Active systemic DNA damaging chemotherapy — the chromatin decondensation mechanism of Livagen could theoretically interfere with chemotherapy mechanisms that depend on chromatin accessibility for DNA-intercalating drugs or topoisomerase inhibitors.
Known hypersensitivity to Livagen (Lys-Glu-Asp-Ala tetrapeptide) or formulation excipients.

Pregnancy — chromatin-level gene regulatory modulation during embryonic and fetal development — when epigenetic gene programming is at its most active and tightly regulated — has not been evaluated and carries theoretical risk.

Concurrent HDAC inhibitor therapy (vorinostat, romidepsin, valproic acid at chromatin-modifying doses) — the chromatin-modifying mechanisms of Livagen and HDAC inhibitors act on the same epigenetic regulatory machinery and could produce additive or unpredictable chromatin state changes.
Active hematological malignancy — the chromatin-level gene regulatory activity could have unpredictable effects on malignant hematopoietic cell epigenetic programs.
sideEffects: Mild fatigue on initial cycle days — the most commonly reported effect; chromatin decondensation that restores expression of previously silenced gene programs imposes a transient metabolic cost as cells adjust to new transcriptional activity levels; typically resolves by days 3–4.

Mild mood changes — as epigenetically silenced neurological and neuroendocrine gene programs are partially restored, some subjects report subtle mood shifts in the first days of a cycle; typically mild and positive; occasionally disorienting if unexpected.

Mild immune activation — as epigenetically silenced immune gene programs in lymphocytes and macrophages are restored, a mild immune activation response (fatigue, mild myalgia) can occur in the first 2–3 days; similar to the initiation responses of Crystagen and Vilon but typically milder.
Injection site mild reaction — standard subcutaneous peptide response.

Transient mild liver enzyme fluctuation — as hepatocyte gene programs normalize, a brief transient ALT/AST fluctuation is occasionally observed in the first days of a cycle in subjects with pre-existing hepatic stress; self-limiting.

No serious adverse events documented in the Khavinson research literature — Livagen's safety profile across the aging, hepatic disease, and immune research populations studied is clean at standard protocol doses.

Theoretical interaction with epigenetic cancer therapies — the chromatin bioregulator mechanism of Livagen in subjects on DNMT inhibitors (azacitidine, decitabine) or HDAC inhibitors used for cancer treatment creates an interaction potential that has not been characterized; concurrent use requires oncological review.

Potential activation of dormant viral genomes (theoretical) — chromatin decondensation could theoretically restore transcriptional access to integrated viral genomes (HIV provirus, Epstein-Barr, CMV) that are maintained in a latent state through heterochromatic silencing; this is a theoretical concern without documented clinical reports in the Khavinson literature but is mechanistically relevant in immunocompromised subjects.

records.name: LL-37
records.description: LL-37 is the only known human cathelicidin — a 37-amino acid cationic antimicrobial peptide derived from the C-terminal cleavage of the precursor protein hCAP-18 (human cationic antimicrobial protein of 18 kDa). It is constitutively expressed by neutrophils, NK cells, mast cells, monocytes, and epithelial cells of the skin, airways, and gastrointestinal tract, and is dramatically upregulated at sites of infection and inflammation. The name reflects both its length (37 amino acids) and its N-terminal leucine-leucine (LL) motif. As a cationic amphipathic alpha-helix, LL-37 kills pathogens through a fundamentally different mechanism than any conventional antibiotic: it electrostatically binds to the negatively charged lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of gram-negative bacterial outer membranes and the lipoteichoic acid of gram-positive membranes, then inserts into and disrupts the membrane bilayer through detergent-like pore formation and membrane destabilization. This physical membrane disruption mechanism has two critical advantages over enzyme-targeted antibiotics: first, bacteria cannot develop resistance to membrane disruption the way they develop resistance to enzyme inhibitors (mutating the membrane to become positively charged would be lethal to the bacteria itself); second, the same basic mechanism kills bacteria, fungi (disrupting ergosterol-containing membranes), enveloped viruses (disrupting lipid envelopes), and even parasites — making LL-37 a genuinely broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent that no single conventional antibiotic class can match. The immunomodulatory functions of LL-37 extend well beyond direct pathogen killing. At nanomolar concentrations that are sub-lethal to pathogens, LL-37 acts as a potent immunological alarm signal: it binds to FPRL1 (formyl peptide receptor-like 1) on neutrophils and monocytes to drive chemotaxis to infection sites, activates TLR-4 signaling on dendritic cells to initiate adaptive immune priming, promotes mast cell degranulation for inflammatory amplification, and directly stimulates angiogenesis through VEGFR2 activation — the same vascular signaling that promotes wound healing. In the context of biofilm-forming pathogens like Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus MRSA, and Candida species, LL-37's ability to penetrate and disrupt biofilm polysaccharide matrices is particularly relevant: biofilms physically protect bacteria from antibiotic penetration and from phagocytic immune cells, making them among the hardest infection types to eradicate. LL-37's amphipathic helical structure allows it to penetrate biofilm matrices and reach the embedded bacteria in a manner that neither conventional antibiotics nor immune cells can replicate efficiently. The mandatory slow dose escalation protocol for LL-37 is not a precautionary formality — it is the primary safety management strategy for the Jarisch-Herxheimer (JHR) reaction, which is the most practically significant adverse event associated with LL-37 use. The Herxheimer reaction is a systemic inflammatory response triggered by the rapid release of microbial antigens, endotoxins, and inflammatory mediators when LL-37 kills large numbers of pathogens simultaneously — particularly in subjects with high pathogen burdens from chronic Lyme, MRSA, or fungal infections. The severity of the Herxheimer reaction is directly proportional to the pathogen burden and the killing rate, which is why starting at 50mcg (a dose that produces measurable antimicrobial activity but manageable pathogen die-off) and escalating slowly over weeks allows progressive pathogen burden reduction without triggering a catastrophic inflammatory cascade. Subjects with severe chronic infections should have KPV available (for NF-κB-mediated cytokine storm mitigation) and be prepared for significant Herxheimer reactions even at titration doses.

rows.notes: Must titrate up slowly to gauge Herxheimer (pathogen die-off) severity.
Standard therapeutic dose.

contraindications: Active autoimmune disease — LL-37 is a potent immunological alarm signal that activates multiple innate immune pathways simultaneously (TLR-4, FPRL1, mast cell degranulation, neutrophil chemotaxis); in subjects with active autoimmune conditions, this immune activation can trigger severe flares by amplifying the already-dysregulated immune response against self-tissue.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) — LL-37 has been specifically implicated in SLE pathogenesis: endogenous LL-37 forms complexes with self-DNA that activate TLR-9 on plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving the type-I interferon signature that characterizes SLE; exogenous LL-37 administration in SLE subjects could dramatically worsen disease activity.

Psoriasis (active, severe) — LL-37 is a primary initiator of psoriatic inflammation; it forms complexes with self-DNA in psoriatic skin lesions that activate the pDC/TLR-7/9 pathway driving IL-23/IL-17 pathological cascade; LL-37 administration in psoriatic subjects may severely worsen plaques.
Rheumatoid arthritis (active disease) — cathelicidin-mediated immune activation in inflamed joints could precipitate acute synovitis flares.
Organ transplant recipients — immune activation from LL-37 in immunosuppressed transplant recipients may provoke rejection episodes.
Concurrent anticoagulant therapy — LL-37 activates mast cells and platelets; theoretical interaction with anticoagulation warrants monitoring.
Known hypersensitivity to LL-37, cathelicidin-derived peptides, or formulation excipients.

Subjects with a very high established pathogen burden without clinical supervision — the Herxheimer reaction at LL-37 initiation in subjects with severe Lyme, MRSA, or fungal burdens can be medically dangerous; clinical oversight and KPV availability for Herxheimer management is strongly advisable.
Pregnancy — immune activation and cytokine release from LL-37 carry risk in pregnancy; not established as safe.
Breastfeeding — no safety data.

Active inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's, UC) in severe flare — gut epithelial LL-37 dysregulation is already implicated in IBD pathogenesis; systemic exogenous LL-37 during active flare could worsen mucosal inflammation.
sideEffects: Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction (JHR) — the primary, defining, and most clinically significant adverse effect of LL-37 when used for chronic infection; characterized by sudden onset of fever (often 38–40°C), severe chills, intense fatigue, diaphoresis, myalgia, arthralgia, and headache occurring within hours of the first few doses; caused by mass simultaneous pathogen killing releasing endotoxins and microbial antigens faster than the immune system can clear them; severity is proportional to pathogen burden and is the reason for mandatory slow dose escalation.

Intense injection site welts and induration — a consistent and dose-dependent adverse effect; LL-37's cationic amphipathic structure interacts with subcutaneous tissue and activates local mast cells, producing significant local inflammatory welts that can be painful, warm, and raised; more pronounced than virtually any other peptide in this database; site rotation and starting at 50mcg are the primary management strategies.
Severe joint pain (arthralgia) — part of the Herxheimer reaction cascade; may be extreme in Lyme disease subjects as spirochete die-off in joint tissue releases inflammatory mediators.

Profound fatigue — the systemic inflammatory response from Herxheimer reactions consumes significant metabolic resources; profound fatigue lasting 24–72 hours per episode is expected, particularly in early titration.

Fever — Herxheimer reaction fever can reach 39–40°C and be alarming; it is a sign the LL-37 is working but should be monitored; subjects must be able to distinguish Herxheimer fever from infection-worsening fever.
Chills and rigors — accompanies Herxheimer fever; can be intense; warm blankets, hydration, and rest are the management.
Headache — common during Herxheimer reactions; related to systemic cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β).
Autoimmune flare triggering — in subjects with undiagnosed or quiescent autoimmune conditions; LL-37's TLR-9 activation and DNA-complex formation can unmask or worsen autoimmune pathology.
Nausea and gastrointestinal disturbance — less common; part of the systemic inflammatory response during Herxheimer events.

Pro-angiogenic activity — LL-37 stimulates VEGFR2-mediated angiogenesis; in the context of active malignancy this is a theoretical oncological concern; in wound healing contexts it is a therapeutic benefit.
Potential mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) exacerbation — subjects with underlying MCAS may experience severe reactions even at low doses due to LL-37's direct mast cell degranulation activity.

records.name: Matrixyl
records.description: Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, also marketed as palmitoyl pentapeptide-3) is a lipopeptide consisting of a fatty acid (palmitic acid, C16:0) linked to a pentapeptide sequence (Lys-Thr-Thr-Lys-Ser) — the fatty acid moiety dramatically enhancing skin penetration through the stratum corneum compared to unmodified peptides, while the pentapeptide sequence mimics the N-terminal collagen I fragment generated during collagen matrix degradation. This matrikine mechanism is the pharmacological foundation of Matrixyl: when extracellular matrix metalloproteases (MMP-1, MMP-3) degrade type I collagen fibers in the dermis, they release peptide fragments including the procollagen type I N-terminal peptide sequence that Matrixyl mimics. Dermal fibroblasts detect these collagen degradation fragments through cell surface receptors (collagen receptor integrin complexes, particularly α2β1 integrin, and mannose receptor) as a damage signal indicating matrix breakdown — and respond by upregulating collagen synthesis (COL1A1, COL1A2), fibronectin production, and hyaluronic acid synthesis (HAS1, HAS2, HAS3 enzyme upregulation) to repair the perceived matrix damage. Matrixyl exploits this matrikine signaling system: by providing the collagen degradation signal peptide in the absence of actual collagen destruction, it persistently activates the fibroblast collagen synthesis response without requiring ongoing matrix damage — producing a sustained anabolic collagen production signal that counteracts the age-related decline in dermal collagen density (which decreases approximately 1% per year after age 30, with accelerated loss following UV exposure and estrogen decline). The clinical evidence base for Matrixyl is robust relative to cosmetic peptides — it is one of the most studied cosmetic actives with controlled clinical trials rather than only in vitro data. Clinical studies have demonstrated: significant reduction in wrinkle depth (particularly periorbital and perioral wrinkles) measured by skin profilometry, increases in dermal collagen density measured by confocal reflectance microscopy, improvements in skin thickness and firmness as measured by cutometry, and increases in hyaluronic acid content of the dermis measured by ultrasound. These effects emerge over 8–12 weeks of consistent daily application and are maintained with continued use. The effective concentration range (2–8%) establishes the lower bound where clinical efficacy begins and the upper bound where additional skin benefit per unit of peptide diminishes — concentrations below 2% in a carrier serum are unlikely to produce measurable anti-aging effects at the clinical level, while concentrations above 8% do not proportionally increase benefit. The synergy with GHK-Cu operates through complementary matrix remodeling mechanisms: Matrixyl drives fibroblast collagen synthesis through the matrikine receptor pathway; GHK-Cu simultaneously activates matrix metalloprotease (MMP) remodeling activity and fibroblast proliferation through its copper-binding receptor pathway — together producing a coordinated collagen deposition-and-remodeling cycle that produces new organized collagen rather than disorganized collagen deposition. The synergy with SNAP-8 is mechanistically additive from a different angle: Matrixyl addresses the structural collagen matrix of the dermis (the deep scaffolding that determines skin thickness and firmness); SNAP-8 addresses the dynamic muscular wrinkle formation at the dermo-epidermal junction caused by repetitive facial muscle contractions. Structural collagen improvements from Matrixyl improve the substrate that muscle-associated dynamic wrinkles form in; SNAP-8 reduces the muscle contraction intensity that drives those wrinkles. Their combination addresses both the structural collagen deficit (Matrixyl) and the neuromuscular wrinkle formation mechanism (SNAP-8) — a mechanistically complete surface anti-aging approach.

rows.notes: Mix with a carrier facial serum. Use 2% to 8% concentration.

washout: Cycle Length: Indefinite.
Washout: None.
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, palmitic acid, or any carrier vehicle excipients in the formulated product.

Active dermatitis, eczema, or psoriasis in the application area — the integrin and collagen receptor activation that Matrixyl produces in the context of active inflammatory skin disease has not been characterized and could interact with the inflammatory and barrier dysfunction of these conditions.

Open wounds, abrasions, or compromised skin barrier in the application area — Matrixyl should not be applied to broken skin; the enhanced penetration provided by the palmitoyl lipid chain in compromised barrier conditions could produce unintended sub-dermal peptide delivery.
Active rosacea in acute flare — the vasodilatory and cellular activation effects of skin penetration peptides in rosacea-affected skin can exacerbate flushing and erythema during active flares.

Use on mucous membranes or eye area without ophthalmic-tested formulation — standard skin formulations are not evaluated for periocular safety; dedicated eye-area formulations with ophthalmic testing are required for orbital application.
sideEffects: Mild skin irritation and erythema in sensitive individuals — the most commonly reported adverse effect; the palmitoyl lipid chain and carrier vehicle components are more frequent culprits than the peptide itself; patch testing on a small area before full facial application is advisable for subjects with sensitive skin.

Mild tingling or warmth on application — a common transient sensation as the lipopeptide penetrates the stratum corneum; typically subsides within minutes of application and not indicative of irritation.

Comedogenicity potential at high concentrations — palmitic acid (the lipid component) has mild comedogenic potential; subjects with acne-prone skin using formulations with high Matrixyl concentrations (>6%) in an occlusive or heavy carrier base may notice increased pore congestion.

Contact dermatitis (rare) — true contact allergic sensitization to the pentapeptide sequence or palmitic acid; manifests as delayed (48–72 hour) erythema and itch at application sites; requires patch testing confirmation and permanent avoidance.

No systemic adverse effects — topical application with the intact skin barrier limits systemic peptide absorption to negligible levels; Matrixyl is among the safest compounds in this entire database from a systemic safety perspective.

Potential interaction with retinoid-containing formulations — high-dose retinoids (tretinoin) cause significant skin barrier disruption and may increase palmitoyl pentapeptide penetration beyond the dermis; combined use of Matrixyl with prescription retinoids should be separated by at least 20–30 minutes or applied at different times of day.

records.name: Mazdutide
records.description: Mazdutide (also known as IBI362) is a dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist — the world's first compound of this specific class to receive regulatory approval, having been approved in China in 2024 for weight management. Like all GLP-1 agonists, it suppresses appetite, slows gastric emptying, and drives glucose-dependent insulin release. What the glucagon receptor component adds is a distinct thermogenic effect: glucagon receptor activation directly stimulates the liver to oxidize fat, raises basal energy expenditure, and — critically — drives substantial reduction of liver fat content independent of caloric restriction alone. The two receptors work in complementary opposition: GLP-1 prevents the blood sugar spike that isolated glucagon signaling would cause, while glucagon provides the metabolic rate boost and hepatic fat clearing that GLP-1 alone cannot achieve. Mazdutide's most remarkable clinical finding is its effect on liver fat. In exploratory analysis from the Phase 3 GLORY-1 trial, subjects demonstrated an 80.2% reduction in liver fat content — a result that stands out even compared to other next-generation incretins. This makes mazdutide particularly relevant for researchers focused on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), previously called NAFLD or NASH, which is present in a significant portion of individuals with obesity. Beyond hepatic effects, GLORY-1 reported mean body weight reductions of approximately 10–15% across the therapeutic dose range, and emerging research published in The Lancet EBioMedicine (2025) has identified potential cognitive benefits mediated through the same dual GLP-1/glucagon receptor pathways, including improvements in neuroinflammation and insulin resistance in the brain. Compared to survodutide — the other major GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist in this database — mazdutide uses a different molecular scaffold and carries a somewhat more moderate heart rate elevation profile. It is the better-characterized option for hepatic-focused protocols given its direct GLORY-1 liver fat data. For new researchers, it occupies the space between tirzepatide and retatrutide in terms of mechanistic complexity and cardiovascular demand: more aggressive than a pure GLP-1 agonist due to the glucagon component, but without the triple-receptor intensity of retatrutide. Morning dosing is recommended to allow glucagon-driven cardiovascular effects to dissipate before sleep.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Personal or family history of thyroid C-cell tumors.
Active or history of acute pancreatitis.
Pre-existing severe liver disease (cirrhosis, acute hepatic failure) — despite hepatoprotective research data, severe hepatic impairment alters drug metabolism unpredictably.
Severe gastroparesis or clinically significant delayed gastric emptying.
Pre-existing cardiac arrhythmias or clinically significant tachycardia — glucagon receptor activation elevates heart rate.
Type 1 diabetes mellitus.
Diabetic ketoacidosis.

Severe inflammatory bowel disease or active Crohn's disease — GI motility impairment may worsen symptoms.
Planned general anesthesia or elective surgery — delayed gastric emptying raises pulmonary aspiration risk; follow pre-operative fasting protocols.
Concomitant use of insulin or sulfonylureas without dose adjustment — significantly elevated hypoglycemia risk.

End-stage renal disease — safety not established.
Pediatric use — safety and efficacy not established.

Decreased appetite (~29%) — a pharmacological effect that directly contributes to weight loss.
Nausea (~23%) — most common during dose escalation; predominantly mild to moderate.
Vomiting (~14%) — more frequent during escalation phases; generally mild to moderate.
Abdominal pain and cramping.
Constipation.
Abdominal distension and bloating.
Dyspepsia (indigestion).
Gastroparesis — delayed gastric emptying; clinically relevant for surgical anesthesia planning.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) exacerbation.
Fatigue and lethargy — frequently secondary to caloric deficit.
Elevated resting heart rate — mild increases of 2–4 BPM typical; occasional transient supraventricular arrhythmias observed in ECG monitoring during trials.
Headache.
Dizziness.
Hypoglycemia (~10%) — predominantly in subjects on concomitant insulin or sulfonylureas; low risk in non-diabetic monotherapy use.
Acute pancreatitis — theoretical class risk; incidence was low and comparable to placebo in mazdutide trials.
Cholelithiasis (gallstones) — risk increases with rapid weight loss.
Lean body mass reduction — some loss of lean mass accompanies fat loss; long-term implications require further study.
Thyroid C-cell tumor risk — confirmed in rodent models; human risk not established; monitor for neck mass, hoarseness, or dysphagia.
Injection site reactions — redness, swelling, or itching; transient and self-resolving.
Anaphylaxis and angioedema — rare but documented across the incretin class.
Pulmonary aspiration risk under general anesthesia — secondary to delayed gastric emptying.
Rapid weight regain upon discontinuation — expected without sustained lifestyle intervention.

records.name: Melanotan I
records.description: Melanotan I (afamelanotide) is a synthetic linear tridecapeptide analog of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH) — the endogenous 13-amino acid peptide cleaved from proopiomelanocortin (POMC) — in which methionine at position 4 is replaced with norvaline to substantially increase metabolic stability and extend the half-life from minutes (endogenous α-MSH) to approximately 24 hours (afamelanotide). This single substitution transforms a rapidly degraded endogenous peptide into a clinically viable drug. Melanotan I acts primarily on the MC1R (melanocortin-1 receptor) expressed on melanocytes throughout the skin — the receptor that governs melanin synthesis in response to UV radiation. MC1R activation by afamelanotide triggers the intracellular cAMP/PKA cascade that activates microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), which transcriptionally upregulates tyrosinase — the rate-limiting enzyme for eumelanin (brown-black melanin) synthesis. The result is dramatically accelerated eumelanogenesis: skin darkening that is 10–20 fold faster than UV alone, with eumelanin providing broad-spectrum UV photoprotection (SPF equivalent of approximately 15–20) across UVA and UVB wavelengths. The key distinction from Melanotan II is receptor selectivity: afamelanotide has high affinity for MC1R and minimal activity at MC4R (the hypothalamic receptor driving sexual arousal and nausea), which is why MT-I produces robust tanning without the spontaneous erections, libido amplification, and severe nausea that characterize MT-II use. The clinical development of Melanotan I under the name afamelanotide has produced one of the most robust regulatory approval records of any peptide in Category VII. It is approved as Scenesse (16mg subcutaneous implant) by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) — a rare genetic disorder in which deficiency of ferrochelatase produces extreme sun hypersensitivity and pain from porphyrin accumulation in the skin upon any UV exposure. In EPP patients, a single subcutaneous implant releasing afamelanotide over 60 days provides dramatic protection against phototoxic reactions, extending tolerated sun exposure time from minutes to hours. This approval establishes the highest-quality regulatory evidence for MT-I's MC1R-mediated photoprotective mechanism. In the research context, MT-I is used for cosmetic tanning — the same eumelanin-induction mechanism operating in normal skin to produce sustained darkening without the EPP disease context. The requirement for UV exposure to activate the tanning response reflects the fact that MC1R activation initiates the melanin synthesis cascade but UV light is required to transfer melanin granules from melanocytes to keratinocytes (melanin transfer requires UV-triggered keratinocyte signaling) — without UV, the melanin is produced but not distributed throughout the epidermis. The history of melanoma contraindication for all MC1R-targeted compounds requires clear mechanistic explanation. MC1R activation drives melanocyte proliferation and differentiation alongside melanin synthesis — the same cellular processes that, in cells with existing oncogenic mutations (BRAF V600E, NRAS, CDK4), could accelerate malignant transformation or progression. Afamelanotide at the molecular level activates the same signaling cascades (cAMP/MITF/tyrosinase/melanocyte proliferation) that are amplified in melanoma pathogenesis. While there is no direct clinical evidence that MT-I causes melanoma in people without prior melanocytic mutations, the biological plausibility of accelerating subclinical melanoma is sufficient to make any personal or family history of melanoma, dysplastic nevus syndrome, or multiple atypical moles an absolute contraindication. The interaction with BPC-157 designated in the compatibility as synergistic reflects BPC-157's angiogenic and skin repair properties complementing MT-I's melanocyte-activating photoprotection — BPC-157 supports the dermal vasculature and wound healing context while MT-I provides the photoprotective melanin.

Once desired tan is reached.

contraindications: Personal or family history of melanoma — MC1R activation drives melanocyte proliferation and MITF-mediated transcriptional programs that overlap with melanoma pathogenesis; any existing oncogenic mutation in melanocytes could be accelerated; absolute contraindication.

History of any skin cancer (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma) — while non-melanocytic skin cancers do not involve MC1R-driven pathways directly, the history indicates a compromised UV-protection/DNA repair phenotype where additional melanocyte stimulation is inadvisable.

Dysplastic nevus syndrome or multiple atypical moles — the presence of numerous atypical melanocytic lesions with existing dysplastic changes represents the highest pre-malignant risk context for MC1R agonism; absolute contraindication.
BRAF V600E mutation carrier or known melanocytic oncogenic mutations — any confirmed oncogenic mutation in melanocyte lineage cells makes MC1R-driven proliferation stimulation dangerous.

Concurrent use with Melanotan II — MT-I and MT-II share MC1R activity as their pigmentation mechanism; co-administration produces additive/redundant MC1R stimulation without proportional additional benefit while combining the side effect profiles of both; these compounds are contraindicated together.
Known hypersensitivity to afamelanotide, alpha-MSH-derived peptides, or formulation excipients.
Pregnancy — melanocyte stimulation and the hormonal context of pregnancy interaction are not established as safe.
Breastfeeding — no safety data.
Active or recent immunosuppression — MC1R has immunomodulatory activity; interaction with immunosuppressed states is not fully characterized.
sideEffects: Darkening of existing moles, nevi, and freckles — the most commonly observed and predictable effect; MC1R activation drives eumelanin production in all existing melanocytic lesions proportionally to their baseline MC1R expression; most pronounced in fair-skinned individuals with numerous existing moles; all moles should be photographed and monitored for atypical changes.
Mild flushing — MC4R is minimally activated by MT-I at standard doses but not completely absent; mild transient flushing occurs in a minority of subjects particularly at higher loading doses.

Mild nausea — rare and dose-dependent; the near-absence of nausea compared to Melanotan II is the defining pharmacological advantage of MT-I's MC1R selectivity; only occurs at high doses that produce some MC4R spillover.

New nevus formation — afamelanotide has been associated in clinical EPP trials with the formation of new melanocytic nevi (moles); this is a direct consequence of MC1R-driven melanocyte proliferation and differentiation; all new lesions should be evaluated by a dermatologist.
Injection site reactions — mild erythema, tenderness, and bruising at the subcutaneous injection site.
Headache — uncommon; mild; mechanism not fully characterized; more likely at higher loading doses.

Skin hyperpigmentation beyond intended areas — areas of existing hyperpigmentation (scars, sun spots, birthmarks) may darken disproportionately as their melanocyte density responds to systemic MC1R agonism.

Spontaneous erections (rare, dose-dependent) — at doses above 1.5–2mg, some MC4R activation does occur; spontaneous erections have been reported at higher MT-I doses though far less frequently than with MT-II.
Transient appetite suppression — minimal MC4R hypothalamic activity may produce mild anorexigenic effects at higher doses.

records.name: Melanotan II
records.description: Melanotan II is a synthetic cyclic analog of alpha-MSH in which the linear tridecapeptide backbone of native α-MSH is cyclized into a lactam ring structure through a Asp-Lys bridge — a modification that dramatically increases binding affinity across all melanocortin receptor subtypes (MC1R through MC5R) compared to both native α-MSH and Melanotan I. Developed at the University of Arizona in the 1980s-90s by Victor Hruby and colleagues who were originally pursuing an afamelanotide analog with enhanced sun protection, MT-II was unexpectedly found to produce intense spontaneous erections and sexual arousal in male subjects — a serendipitous discovery that redirected research toward what ultimately became PT-141 (bremelanotide), the MC4R-selective fragment. MT-II itself was never developed into an approved pharmaceutical due to its broad receptor activity and side effect profile, but remains the highest-potency melanocortin agonist available for research use. The dual MC1R/MC4R activity that defines MT-II's pharmacological character means every dose simultaneously drives melanin production (MC1R on melanocytes) and activates the hypothalamic arousal, nausea, appetite suppression, and cardiovascular circuits (MC4R in the CNS). Unlike MT-I where MC4R activation is minimal at normal doses, MT-II's cyclic structure produces substantial MC4R activity at every melanogenic dose — making the sexual arousal, nausea, and flushing effects not manageable side effects but expected pharmacological consequences of each injection. The potency differential between MT-II and MT-I is the central pharmacological fact that governs all MT-II protocol design. MT-II achieves equivalent or superior melanogenic effect to MT-I at 250–500mcg versus MT-I's 1000–2000mcg loading doses — reflecting approximately 4–8 fold greater potency at MC1R per microgram administered. This potency amplification applies equally to the MC4R-mediated effects: nausea at 250mcg MT-II is equivalent in magnitude to nausea at doses of MT-I that would require significantly exceeding standard protocols. The pre-bed administration during loading is specifically designed to sleep through the acute nausea and arousal onset window — the first 2–4 hours post-injection when MC4R receptor activation is at peak intensity. By the time the subject wakes, the most intense MC4R effects have subsided while the MC1R melanogenic cascade (which operates on a slower transcriptional timescale) continues over the subsequent 24 hours. The micro-dosing protocol (100mcg/day) was empirically developed to find the threshold below which MC4R-mediated nausea and spontaneous erections are sub-threshold while maintaining progressive melanogenic accumulation through sustained low-level MC1R stimulation. The contraindication with Melanotan I is mechanistic and absolute: MT-I and MT-II both activate MC1R as their shared pigmentation mechanism — concurrent use produces redundant, additive MC1R agonism without proportional additional tanning benefit while stacking the cardiovascular, nausea, and MC4R-mediated side effects of both compounds. The melanoma contraindication applies with even greater force to MT-II than MT-I given MT-II's broader melanocortin receptor activity — MC5R activation in particular has been documented in some melanoma cell lines, and the cyclic structure's higher binding affinity means a greater per-molecule oncogenic acceleration risk in cells carrying melanocytic mutations. The association of spontaneous darkening of melanocytic lesions, new nevus formation, and rare melanoma cases in MT-II users in post-market surveillance data — while not establishing direct causation — makes the melanoma history contraindication among the most conservatively enforced in Category VII.

records.name: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor)
records.description: MGF (Mechano Growth Factor) is a splice variant of IGF-1 — meaning it is generated from the same IGF-1 gene as standard IGF-1, but produced through alternative RNA splicing that creates a distinct peptide with a unique E-domain at its C-terminus. In the body, MGF is produced locally in muscle tissue in response to mechanical stress and micro-damage from resistance training. Its primary biological role is as a first-responder muscle repair signal: when muscle fibers are damaged by exercise, MGF is released locally to activate satellite cells (muscle stem cells) that proliferate and fuse to repair and expand existing muscle fibers. This is the mechanism by which resistance training stimulates long-term muscle growth — MGF is the molecular trigger for satellite cell activation and hyperplasia (creation of new muscle fibers), not just hypertrophy (enlargement of existing ones). The non-pegylated form of MGF used in this database has an extremely short half-life — approximately 5–7 minutes in the bloodstream before the E-domain is cleaved and the peptide is inactivated. This is why the administration protocol for MGF is fundamentally different from every other compound in this database: it must be injected directly into the trained muscle, bilaterally, immediately post-workout — typically within 15–30 minutes of the training stimulus while the local anabolic signaling window is still open. Subcutaneous injection in the abdomen for systemic effect is possible but largely ineffective due to the extremely short half-life — the peptide is degraded before it can reach muscle tissue in meaningful concentrations. The localized IM injection approach exploits the short half-life as an advantage, concentrating the satellite cell proliferation signal precisely in the trained tissue. The synergy with IGF-1 LR3 is well-characterized: MGF activates satellite cells (proliferation signal), while IGF-1 LR3 drives those activated satellite cells through differentiation and fusion with existing muscle fibers (differentiation signal). Running them sequentially — MGF post-workout, IGF-1 LR3 on rest days — harnesses both phases of the muscle repair cycle. BPC-157 adds connective tissue repair to the same stack, making it a comprehensive tissue recovery protocol. The 4–6 week cycle limit exists because extended satellite cell activation beyond this window may produce organizational abnormalities in muscle fiber architecture rather than continued productive hyperplasia.

Together, the blend targets mitochondrial dysfunction from three separate angles: repair of existing mitochondria, construction of new mitochondrial capacity, and protection of stressed cells during the repair process. From a performance and optimization standpoint, MITO-3 is positioned for age-related energy decline, chronic fatigue patterns, post-illness mitochondrial recovery, metabolic dysfunction, exercise-performance support, insulin-resistance states, and neuro-mitochondrial stress. records.name: MK-677 (Ibutamoren)
records.description: MK-677 (ibutamoren) is a non-peptide, orally active GH secretagogue — the only compound in this database that stimulates the GH axis without requiring subcutaneous injection. It is a small molecule ghrelin mimetic that binds and activates GHS-R1a (the ghrelin receptor) with high selectivity, producing sustained elevations of both GH and IGF-1 that persist for 24 hours following a single daily dose. Unlike the peptide GHRPs (ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6) which produce sharp GH pulses that clear within hours, MK-677's oral bioavailability and long half-life (~24 hours) create a continuous hormonal elevation rather than pulsatile bursts. This means it does not mimic natural GH pulse physiology but instead maintains a steady IGF-1 plateau — with the attendant advantages of consistent anabolic and recovery signaling and the disadvantages of sustained rather than physiologic GH exposure. MK-677 was developed by Merck and advanced through multiple Phase 2 clinical trials primarily in elderly populations for applications including GH deficiency, hip fracture recovery, and muscle wasting. The trials confirmed its efficacy — sustained 40–60% increases in IGF-1 from baseline, improvements in lean body mass, bone mineral density, and sleep architecture (particularly REM and slow-wave sleep) — but clinical development was ultimately discontinued after a cardiac safety signal emerged. In the Adunsky et al. hip fracture recovery trial, the ibutamoren group showed a 6.5% rate of congestive heart failure versus 1.7% in the placebo group, leading to early trial termination. This signal was concentrated in elderly patients with underlying cardiac vulnerability, but it has become the defining safety concern for this compound and the reason it never progressed to Phase 3. In the research community, MK-677 occupies a practical niche that injectable GHRPs do not: it requires no reconstitution, no injection, and no fasting window management, making compliance dramatically easier for long-duration protocols (16–24 week cycles). Pre-bed dosing is standard because GH naturally peaks during deep sleep, and mitigating daytime lethargy from the GH-ghrelin effect is easier when the dose is taken at night. The 5-days-on/2-days-off cycling protocol was developed specifically to preserve insulin sensitivity, which is the most common metabolic complication with continuous daily use — blood glucose should be monitored throughout any cycle, and subjects with pre-diabetic glucose tolerance should not use this compound.

records.name: MOTS-c
records.description: MOTS-c (Mitochondrial Open Reading Frame of the 12S rRNA type-c) is a 16-amino acid micropeptide encoded not in nuclear DNA but within the mitochondrial genome itself — specifically in the 12S ribosomal RNA gene. This makes MOTS-c one of only a handful of known mitochondria-encoded peptides (mitochondrial-derived peptides, or MDPs), alongside Humanin and the SHLP family. As a retrograde signal — a message sent from the mitochondria to the nucleus and to systemic tissues — MOTS-c functions as a metabolic stress sensor and adaptive regulator. Its primary molecular target is AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase), the cellular "fuel gauge" that is activated by energetic stress (high AMP:ATP ratio). MOTS-c activates AMPK through both direct binding and via modulation of the folate cycle-AICAR pathway: during cellular stress, MOTS-c inhibits the folate cycle, leading to AICAR accumulation, which is itself an endogenous AMPK activator (explaining the direct synergy between MOTS-c and AICAR in the compatibility matrix). AMPK activation cascades into increased fatty acid oxidation, upregulation of glucose transporter GLUT4 expression on muscle cells, suppression of mTORC1 (anti-anabolic but pro-longevity), PGC-1α induction for mitochondrial biogenesis, and activation of antioxidant defense programs. The "exercise in a bottle" characterization in the original description is not marketing language — it reflects the actual findings of the research that defined MOTS-c. Studies by Lee et al. (2015) demonstrated that exogenous MOTS-c administration in mice on a high-fat diet completely prevented diet-induced insulin resistance and obesity — without changes in food intake — through the activation of the same metabolic programs that exercise activates. Subsequent research has extended this to aging-associated metabolic decline: endogenous MOTS-c levels decline with age, and this decline correlates with reduced exercise capacity, impaired glucose metabolism, and increased adiposity in aging humans. In a 2021 clinical study, intravenous MOTS-c administration improved insulin sensitivity and reduced visceral fat in a small human pilot. MOTS-c also demonstrates nuclear translocation under stress conditions — entering the nucleus and altering gene expression directly in addition to its cytoplasmic AMPK signaling, giving it a gene regulatory dimension that most metabolic peptides lack. The pre-workout dosing mandate is functionally important. MOTS-c's AMPK activation drives the body into a high-fat-oxidation, glucose-sparing metabolic state — the same state that physical exercise creates. When this metabolic switch occurs in the fasted state without a corresponding energy demand (exercise), the AMPK activation drives aggressive glucose uptake by muscle tissue and accelerated fat mobilization without the glycogen replenishment that exercise provides, which can produce symptomatic hypoglycemia. Co-administering MOTS-c 30–45 minutes before physical training provides the metabolic demand that matches and channels the AMPK-driven energy program productively, prevents hypoglycemia by consuming the mobilized energy substrate, and amplifies the training adaptation signal through convergent AMPK stimulation from both the exercise and the peptide.

IGF-1 LR3 provides the downstream anabolic layer by supporting IGF-1-mediated protein synthesis, nitrogen retention, anti-catabolism, and PI3K/AKT-driven tissue growth signaling. Together, PEG-MGF opens the repair and growth window, while IGF-1 LR3 drives the anabolic construction phase that follows. From a performance and optimization standpoint, Muscle Architect is positioned for post-training hypertrophy support, muscle repair, recovery from mechanical overload, lean-mass retention during cutting phases, post-injury muscle rebuilding, and advanced physique development. This is a subcutaneous-only blend because systemic IGF-1R and satellite-cell access are required. Intranasal administration is not supported. records.name: NAD+
records.description: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is a critical coenzyme found in every living cell that serves as the essential electron carrier for cellular respiration and the primary substrate for a family of NAD+-consuming enzymes that regulate DNA repair, inflammation, and longevity. In its oxidized form (NAD+), it accepts electrons from metabolic substrates in glycolysis and the TCA cycle, becoming NADH, which then delivers electrons to Complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain to drive ATP synthesis. Beyond its role in energy metabolism, NAD+ is the required substrate for three enzymatic families with profound health implications: Sirtuins (SIRT1–7) — NAD+-dependent deacetylases that regulate mitochondrial biogenesis (SIRT1/PGC-1α), inflammation (SIRT3), genomic stability (SIRT6), and caloric restriction mimicry; PARPs (poly-ADP-ribose polymerases) — NAD+-consuming DNA repair enzymes that consume massive quantities of NAD+ in response to DNA damage, potentially depleting the cellular pool; and CD38/CD157 — NAD+glycohydrolases that consume NAD+ in calcium signaling cascades and whose activity increases dramatically with age and inflammation. The core aging hypothesis is straightforward: NAD+ levels decline 40–50% between the ages of 40 and 60 in most human tissues, depleting the substrate supply for sirtuins and DNA repair machinery at the same time that PARP and CD38 activity increase due to accumulated DNA damage and chronic inflammation — a catastrophic positive feedback loop that accelerates aging physiology. Injectable NAD+ bypasses the biosynthetic pathways entirely and delivers the oxidized coenzyme directly to the bloodstream, from which it is taken up by tissues. This distinguishes it from oral NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR) which must first be converted enzymatically to NAD+ inside cells — a conversion that may be rate-limited in older or metabolically compromised tissues. The clinical and research evidence for NAD+ supplementation is the most substantial of any compound in the longevity section of this database. Human studies using IV or subcutaneous NAD+ have demonstrated improved cognitive clarity, elevated mood and motivational state, reduction in chronic fatigue, improved sleep quality, and measurable increases in blood NAD+ levels and PBMC NAD+ concentration. The anti-addiction and neurological restoration applications derive from NAD+s role as a cofactor for the enzymatic machinery of neurotransmitter synthesis and neuronal energy metabolism — depleted NAD+ in reward circuit neurons is associated with reduced dopamine synthesis capacity, which contributes to anhedonia, craving, and post-stimulant crash phenotypes. The notorious injection site pain of NAD+ is mechanistically distinct from the copper peptide pain of GHK-Cu. NAD+ at therapeutic concentrations is an osmotically active molecule that creates a transient osmotic gradient in subcutaneous tissue upon injection, simultaneously triggering adenosine receptor-mediated pain signaling through the purine pathway. The burning and cramping experienced with too-rapid injection are dose rate-dependent — injecting slowly over several minutes dramatically reduces the pain intensity. Chest tightness or nausea that occurs with rapid injection is a vagal response to the rapid NAD+ pulse rather than a pharmacotoxic event, and resolves immediately upon slowing the injection rate. The morning dosing requirement is specifically designed to capitalize on the circadian activity patterns of the sirtuin and PARP enzymes, which have peak activity in the early waking hours and are most responsive to NAD+ substrate availability in the first half of the day.

records.name: NeuroSync
records.description: NeuroSync is a neuroregulatory peptide blend combining Semax, Selank, and Oxytocin into a single coordinated cognitive, emotional, and social-performance support system. The blend is structured around a 10mg Semax, 10mg Selank, and 1mg Oxytocin ratio, allowing each 2.1mg of total blend to yield approximately 1mg Semax, 1mg Selank, and 100mcg Oxytocin. Semax provides the cognitive and neurotrophic backbone of the formulation through support of BDNF-related signaling, dopaminergic tone, executive function, alertness, and mental endurance. Selank adds the anxiolytic and mood-regulatory layer through GABAergic, serotonergic, and stress-buffering pathways, helping reduce excessive mental noise without creating the heavy sedation associated with stronger calming agents. Oxytocin provides the social and emotional modulation component, supporting emotional openness, trust signaling, interpersonal ease, and parasympathetic tone. Together, these pathways create a blend designed for calm focus rather than stimulation, sedation, or emotional flattening. From a performance and optimization standpoint, NeuroSync functions as a state-control peptide blend for users seeking improved clarity, reduced stress reactivity, better communication, social confidence, and higher emotional bandwidth. Intranasal administration is best suited for fast-onset cognitive, social, and event-based use, while subcutaneous administration is better positioned for longer-cycle neuroplasticity, burnout recovery, and sustained emotional regulation. The blend may appeal to executives, entrepreneurs, clinicians, public speakers, high-stress professionals, and users who need mental sharpness without sympathetic overdrive. Because the three peptides operate through complementary signaling systems rather than redundant pathways, NeuroSync is positioned as a broad-spectrum neurobehavioral blend rather than a simple nootropic stack. Its defining effect profile is clear, calm, connected cognition.

records.name: Ovagen
records.description: Ovagen is a synthetic tripeptide (Ile-Glu-Pro) Khavinson bioregulator derived from liver tissue polypeptide extracts — identified as the bioactive core sequence responsible for the hepatoprotective, hepatocyte regenerative, and liver function-normalizing activity of the native hepatic tissue extract. The liver is the metabolic hub of the body, performing over 500 distinct functions including: glucose and glycogen metabolism, lipid synthesis and transport, protein synthesis (albumin, clotting factors, acute phase proteins), bile acid synthesis and secretion, detoxification of endogenous metabolites and xenobiotics through Phase I (CYP450) and Phase II (conjugation) enzymes, iron storage and metabolism, immune function through Kupffer cell activity, and regulation of systemic hormone metabolism. Hepatocytes — the primary liver parenchymal cells comprising approximately 70–80% of liver volume — are uniquely capable of regeneration: a healthy liver can regenerate its full mass from as little as 30% remaining tissue. However, this regenerative capacity is progressively impaired by age-related hepatocyte senescence, accumulated oxidative DNA damage, lipid peroxidation, chronic low-level inflammatory signals from gut microbiome-derived endotoxin, and the progressive replacement of functional hepatocytes with fibrotic tissue that characterizes non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MAFLD) and aging-related hepatic fibrosis. Ovagen acts as a bioregulator at the hepatocyte level — normalizing the gene expression programs governing hepatocyte survival, regenerative proliferation, detoxification enzyme expression (CYP450 isoforms, UGTs, GSTs), mitochondrial respiratory chain function, and lipid metabolism — restoring the homeostatic hepatic phenotype that aging and metabolic stress have disrupted. The hepatic metabolism context makes Ovagen the Khavinson bioregulator with the broadest secondary implications for the rest of the stack in this database. Because virtually every compound in Categories I–VIII is hepatically metabolized to some degree, optimizing hepatocyte CYP450 expression and mitochondrial function through Ovagen has the potential to normalize the pharmacokinetic handling of co-administered peptides and other agents. The synergy designation with Livagen is complementary in a tissue-level sense: Ovagen targets hepatocyte parenchymal function (the metabolic working cells of the liver), while Livagen targets the liver's DNA repair and genome stability programs — Ovagen improves the hepatocyte metabolic machinery while Livagen protects the genomic integrity that allows those hepatocytes to continue functioning without accumulating replicative errors. Together they address both the functional and the genomic stability dimensions of hepatic aging simultaneously. In subjects with existing metabolic liver disease (NAFLD, elevated AST/ALT), Ovagen cycles represent the most directly relevant Khavinson intervention available — combining hepatoprotection, anti-fibrotic bioregulator activity, and normalization of lipid and glucose metabolism at the hepatocyte gene program level. The clinical research evidence for Ovagen in the Khavinson literature demonstrates measurable improvements in hepatic function markers following standard protocol cycles. Documented outcomes include: reduction in serum ALT and AST in subjects with elevated baseline transaminases, improvement in hepatic steatosis scores by ultrasound in NAFLD subjects, normalization of serum albumin levels in subjects with mild hepatic synthetic dysfunction, reduction in gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) — a sensitive marker of hepatic oxidative stress and alcohol-related hepatocyte damage, and improvements in hepatic metabolic efficiency markers including bilirubin clearance and glucose-insulin homeostasis. The practical application in the context of this database is particularly significant for subjects running multi-compound peptide stacks: Ovagen cycles before and during intensive peptide protocols are logically positioned to optimize hepatic clearance capacity for the co-administered compounds, ensure adequate albumin production for protein binding of hepatically-cleared peptides, and protect hepatocytes from any additional metabolic burden imposed by a complex concurrent stack.

records.name: Oxytocin
records.description: Oxytocin is an endogenous nonapeptide (Cys-Tyr-Ile-Gln-Asn-Cys-Pro-Leu-Gly-NH₂) synthesized in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and supraoptic nucleus (SON) of the hypothalamus and released both peripherally into circulation from the posterior pituitary and centrally within the brain through direct axonal and dendritic release from oxytocinergic neurons. The peripheral and central pools are pharmacologically distinct: circulating oxytocin produces the hormonal effects on uterine smooth muscle contraction, mammary gland milk ejection, and cardiovascular regulation; centrally released oxytocin acts as a neuromodulator at Gq-coupled oxytocin receptors (OXTR) in the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, ventral tegmental area, prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and brainstem — producing the social, emotional, and behavioral effects that gave oxytocin its popular designation as the "love hormone." Mechanistically, OXTR activation in the amygdala reduces fear and threat responses by dampening the basolateral amygdala's alarm circuitry while facilitating social reward processing in the nucleus accumbens through dopaminergic interaction — a dual anxiolytic/prosocial mechanism that is functionally distinct from both GABA-A anxiolytics (which produce sedation) and melanocortin-based compounds. OXTR activation in the hypothalamus and brainstem also modulates the HPA stress axis, reducing cortisol release in response to psychosocial stressors — providing a direct hormonal anti-stress effect beyond the behavioral changes. The neuroscience of oxytocin's social bonding function reveals a significantly more complex pharmacological profile than the "love hormone" simplification suggests. Oxytocin does not uniformly increase positive social behavior — it is better characterized as a social salience amplifier: it increases the emotional and motivational significance of social cues, which in secure social contexts produces trust, bonding, and generosity, but in threatening social contexts can increase in-group favoritism, out-group hostility, and vigilance toward threatening individuals. This contextual dependency is mechanistically important for the research protocol application: oxytocin's prosocial and anxiolytic effects are most reliably produced in genuinely safe, positive social contexts — using it in high-stress or threatening interpersonal contexts may amplify negative social emotions rather than attenuate them. The sexual enhancement application of oxytocin is mediated through OXTR in the nucleus accumbens and ventral striatum enhancing the reward salience of sexual stimuli and physical touch, and through direct peripheral effects in genital tissue (smooth muscle and sensory nerve ending modulation) that increase sensitivity and climax intensity. The synergy with PT-141 is mechanistically layered: PT-141 drives central arousal via MC4R while oxytocin amplifies the social reward, emotional bonding, and peripheral sensitivity components of the sexual experience. The cyclical protocol (12 weeks on, 6-week washout) reflects the neuromodulatory adaptation that occurs with sustained exogenous oxytocin exposure. Chronic exogenous OXTR activation produces receptor downregulation and reduced sensitivity of endogenous oxytocinergic circuits — the natural oxytocin release from social bonding, physical touch, and orgasm becomes progressively less effective as OXTR density decreases. The 6-week washout allows OXTR upregulation back to baseline, restoring the normal physiological responsiveness of the endogenous oxytocin system. The most important contraindication — pregnancy — is critical because oxytocin is the pharmacological agent used clinically to induce and augment uterine contractions during labor; exogenous oxytocin in pregnancy at any dose above physiological carries risk of premature uterine contractions, placental insufficiency, and preterm labor.

sideEffects: Mild lethargy and fatigue after effects wear off — the most commonly reported adverse effect; as the acute OXTR activation resolves, a mild parasympathetic-dominant "afterglow" state can transition to fatigue; typically 2–4 hours post-dose.

Increased anxiety in high-threat contexts — oxytocin's social salience amplification can worsen anxiety or hostility responses in subjects exposed to threatening social stimuli during acute OXTR activation; context-dependency is the defining pharmacological nuance of oxytocin's behavioral effects.

records.name: P021
records.description: P021 (also known as P21) is a synthetic tetrapeptide derived from the CNTF (Ciliary Neurotrophic Factor) binding domain — specifically designed to act as a small, BBB-permeable peptide mimetic of CNTF that activates downstream neurotrophic signaling without engaging the JAK/STAT3 pathway that mediates CNTF's adverse inflammatory side effects. CNTF is a potent neurotrophic factor for motor neurons, hippocampal neurons, and retinal ganglion cells, but as a large protein it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and its systemic administration produces dose-limiting inflammatory side effects. P021 was engineered at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging by researchers including Bhanu Bhanu and colleagues to capture CNTF's neurotrophic benefits in a small, BBB-permeable peptide form. The result is a compound that activates BDNF gene transcription, CREB phosphorylation, and TrkB receptor signaling in hippocampal and cortical neurons — the same downstream pathways that CNTF activates via its cognate receptor — while completely avoiding the JAK/STAT3-mediated inflammatory cascade that limits clinical CNTF use. Critically, P021 has been shown in animal models of Alzheimer's disease to reduce tau hyperphosphorylation (a primary driver of neurofibrillary tangle formation) by upregulating PP2A (protein phosphatase 2A), the phosphatase that normally dephosphorylates tau at pathological sites — providing a mechanistic rationale for P021 that goes beyond general neurotrophic support into direct targeting of Alzheimer's pathology. The neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and memory enhancement research profile of P021 is among the most compelling in the neuropeptide space. In transgenic mouse models of Alzheimer's disease, P021 administration improved Morris water maze performance (spatial memory), reduced amyloid plaque burden, reduced tau phosphorylation at multiple pathological epitopes, and increased hippocampal neurogenesis (measured by BrdU/DCX co-labeling of new neurons). In normal aging animals, P021 reversed age-related declines in dendritic spine density, synaptic protein expression, and hippocampal BDNF levels — suggesting applicability to physiological aging-associated cognitive decline as well as frank neurodegenerative pathology. The CREB activation mechanism is particularly important for memory: CREB-mediated transcription is the molecular switch that converts short-term synaptic potentiation into the new protein synthesis required for long-term memory consolidation. By driving CREB phosphorylation in hippocampal and cortical circuits, P021 directly facilitates the cellular mechanism of memory formation at the transcriptional level. P021 occupies a distinct mechanistic niche within Category V that is complementary to but non-redundant with the other neural compounds. Semax and Adamax drive BDNF transcription through ACTH-derived MC4R and TrkB agonism; Cerebrolysin delivers exogenous neurotrophic peptide fragments; P021 specifically targets the CNTF receptor domain to drive BDNF/CREB signaling while simultaneously addressing tau pathology through PP2A upregulation — a mechanism none of the other Category V compounds provide. This makes P021 particularly valuable in stacks targeting age-related neurodegeneration, post-inflammatory cognitive dysfunction, or any context where tau pathology (rather than just amyloid or synaptic loss) is a mechanistic concern. The range of titration protocols reflects the spectrum from general cognitive enhancement (100–500mcg/day) to aggressive neurodegenerative and TBI recovery applications (up to 2mg/day), with the taper phases in each protocol reflecting the importance of gradual CREB/TrkB downregulation management rather than abrupt cessation.
