records.name: Tri-Heal
records.description: Tri-Heal is a multi-domain regenerative peptide blend combining BPC-157, TB-500, and KPV into a single coordinated recovery and inflammatory modulation system. Rather than targeting only one aspect of tissue dysfunction, the blend simultaneously addresses structural repair, cellular migration, vascular support, immune regulation, and inflammatory suppression. BPC-157 primarily drives angiogenesis, tendon and ligament recovery, gastrointestinal repair, nitric oxide modulation, and fibroblast activation. TB-500 expands systemic healing capacity through actin regulation and enhanced cellular mobility, allowing repair mechanisms to distribute more efficiently throughout injured or inflamed tissues. KPV provides the immunomodulatory backbone of the blend, suppressing excessive inflammatory cytokine signaling, mast-cell activation, and chronic inflammatory cascades that often impair or delay tissue recovery. Together, these mechanisms create a synergistic environment that supports faster healing while reducing the inflammatory burden that commonly limits regenerative outcomes. From a performance and optimization standpoint, Tri-Heal functions as both a recovery accelerator and a systemic resilience enhancer. Athletes and high-performance users often utilize the blend to improve recovery capacity, reduce downtime between training sessions, enhance connective tissue durability, and mitigate chronic inflammation associated with repetitive stress. Individuals recovering from surgery or long-standing injury may benefit from improved mobility, reduced discomfort, faster tissue normalization, and enhanced healing consistency. Because the three peptides operate through complementary rather than redundant pathways, the blend often produces effects that feel substantially stronger and more comprehensive than equivalent standalone dosing strategies. This layered regenerative architecture is what makes Tri-Heal particularly appealing as a broad-spectrum recovery platform rather than simply another injury-repair peptide stack.

records.name: Ventfort
records.description: Ventfort is a Khavinson cytomedin — peptide complex A-3 — extracted from vascular tissue of young animals, developed as the oral vascular endothelial bioregulator of the Khavinson framework. The vascular endothelium is the single cell layer lining every blood vessel in the body, and it does far more than passive containment — it actively regulates vessel tone through nitric oxide production, controls clotting through thrombomodulin and tPA expression, governs inflammatory cell adhesion through ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, and directs angiogenesis through VEGF signaling. Ventfort delivers a multi-peptide vascular tissue extract that interacts with endothelial cell nuclear receptors to normalize the gene expression programs governing these functions — in plain terms, it signals aging, dysfunctional endothelial cells to restore the protective, anti-inflammatory, vasodilatory phenotype they had when young. The clinical evidence for Ventfort is among the better-documented in the oral cytomedin class. A published 49-patient clinical trial demonstrated a 30% reduction in total cholesterol over a treatment course, improvement in endothelium-dependent vasodilation measured by flow-mediated dilation on brachial artery ultrasound, reduction in intima-media thickness progression, normalization of lipid peroxidation markers, and reduction in inflammatory adhesion molecule expression in vascular endothelium. These outcomes span the metabolic (lipids), structural (IMT), and functional (vasodilation) dimensions of vascular health — consistent with restoration of normal endothelial gene programs rather than a single-mechanism pharmacological effect. Ventfort's position relative to Vesugen — the injectable synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) vascular bioregulator also in this database — follows the same oral/injectable cytomedin-vs-synthetic-peptide pattern seen across all the Khavinson pairs. Vesugen delivers the defined single-sequence injectable precision; Ventfort delivers the full vascular tissue extract oral convenience. What makes Ventfort particularly notable is Professor Khavinson's specific recommendation to combine it with Svetinorm (the liver cytomedin) as a paired metabolic-cardiovascular protocol — reflecting the hepatic-endothelial metabolic axis where liver output of lipids and glucose directly loads the vascular wall, and vascular endothelial health in turn determines the metabolic efficiency of hepatic blood supply.

records.name: Vesugen
records.description: Vesugen is a synthetic tripeptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) Khavinson bioregulator developed as the defined bioactive core of vascular tissue polypeptide extracts, representing the smallest peptide sequence that retains the vascular endothelial cell regulatory activity of the original tissue-derived extract. The vascular endothelium — the single-cell-layer lining of all blood vessels — is the most functionally critical interface in the cardiovascular system: it regulates vascular tone through nitric oxide (NO) and endothelin production, controls coagulation through thrombomodulin, von Willebrand factor, and tissue plasminogen activator expression, mediates inflammatory cell trafficking through ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and E-selectin regulation, and governs angiogenesis through VEGF and angiopoietin signaling. Endothelial dysfunction — the loss of these homeostatic endothelial properties through oxidative stress, inflammatory injury, and replicative senescence of endothelial cells — is the foundational pathological event in atherosclerosis, hypertension, and age-related vascular disease. Vesugen acts as a bioregulator at the endothelial cell level, interacting with endothelial cell surface receptors and transcription factors to normalize endothelial gene expression programs that have drifted from their youthful homeostatic state through aging and cumulative vascular stress. This mechanism is categorically different from compounds that address vascular function through NO donors, vasodilators, or anticoagulants — Vesugen targets the upstream gene regulatory machinery that governs all endothelial functions simultaneously, providing a broad-spectrum endothelial restoration rather than a single-pathway vascular effect. The research evidence for Vesugen in the Khavinson literature demonstrates effects across multiple dimensions of vascular function. Studies in aging animal models and human clinical series showed Vesugen administration producing: reduction in vascular wall thickening and intima-media thickness (a surrogate measure of atherosclerotic burden), improved endothelium-dependent vasodilation (reflecting restored nitric oxide signaling capacity), normalization of lipid metabolism and reduced lipid peroxidation products in vascular tissue, and reduction in markers of vascular inflammation. In the context of this database, the synergy designation with Cardiogen is mechanistically logical: Vesugen restores the vascular endothelial function of the blood vessel wall while Cardiogen restores the cardiomyocyte function of the cardiac muscle — addressing the two primary tissue compartments of the cardiovascular system simultaneously. A subject with age-related cardiovascular decline benefits from both endothelial (Vesugen) and myocardial (Cardiogen) bioregulator support as complementary interventions targeting different cell types within the same organ system. The 8-week gradual titration protocol is the most conservative approach and may be preferred for subjects with significant existing cardiovascular disease where rapid endothelial remodeling could produce hemodynamic changes. The absence of established contraindications in the original database entry reflects the excellent safety profile observed in the Khavinson research cohorts — but this absence of documented contraindications should be understood in context: the research was conducted primarily in elderly subjects with cardiovascular risk factors where vascular bioregulator therapy was clearly indicated. The theoretical considerations for subjects on anticoagulation therapy deserve specific attention: if Vesugen normalizes endothelial coagulation regulation (restoring thrombomodulin and tissue plasminogen activator expression that were reduced in dysfunctional endothelium), this could produce modest changes in coagulation parameters that interact with anticoagulant drug dosing. The interaction is not documented as clinically significant in the Khavinson literature, but coagulation monitoring is prudent in anticoagulated subjects beginning a Vesugen cycle.

records.name: Vilon
records.description: Vilon is a synthetic dipeptide (Lys-Glu) developed by Vladimir Khavinson as the minimized bioactive core of thymus gland polypeptide extracts — the result of systematic fractionation work that identified the smallest peptide sequence retaining the full immunoregulatory bioregulator activity of the thymic extract epithalamin-family compounds. As a dipeptide, Vilon is the simplest and most bioavailable of all Khavinson bioregulators: at two amino acids it is below the threshold where proteolytic degradation becomes a significant pharmacokinetic challenge, allowing it to reach target tissues intact even without the modified amino acid chemistry required for larger peptides. Vilon's primary mechanism operates through the thymus — the central lymphoid organ responsible for T-cell maturation, selection, and export into the peripheral immune system. The thymus undergoes progressive involution beginning in adolescence and reaching near-complete functional atrophy by the fifth and sixth decades of life — a process called thymic involution that is one of the most consistent and well-documented biological features of immunosenescence. Thymic involution reduces naive T-cell output, narrows the T-cell receptor repertoire, and produces the aging-associated immune phenotype: reduced adaptive immune competence, impaired response to novel antigens, reduced vaccine efficacy, and increased susceptibility to infection, cancer, and autoimmune dysregulation. Vilon acts as a thymic bioregulator by interacting with thymocyte cell surface receptors and intracellular signaling cascades that govern thymopoiesis — the maturation of T-cell progenitors into functional T-cells — partially restoring the declining thymopoietic activity of the involuted thymus in aging subjects. The mechanistic distinction between Vilon and Thymalin (another Khavinson thymic compound in this database) is one of scope and origin: Thymalin is a broader polypeptide complex derived from bovine thymus that contains multiple bioactive peptide sequences acting across various aspects of thymic function and immune-endocrine cross-regulation; Vilon is a defined single dipeptide representing the most potent and specific thymopoietic signal within that complex. In the Khavinson research literature, Vilon demonstrated the ability to: normalize CD4+/CD8+ T-cell ratios in immunosenescent subjects, increase interleukin-2 (IL-2) production and T-cell proliferative responses to mitogenic stimulation, reduce aberrant pro-inflammatory cytokine production from senescent immune cells, and partially restore delayed-type hypersensitivity responses — a clinical measure of T-cell mediated immunity that declines characteristically with age. The immune restoration produced by Vilon is not immunostimulation in the non-specific sense (which would be contraindicated in autoimmune subjects) but rather immune normalization — moving dysregulated aging immune phenotypes back toward the functional balance of younger immune systems. This normalizing rather than simply stimulating mechanism is the fundamental characteristic of all Khavinson bioregulators across their respective target organs. The synergistic designations for Vilon — Epithalon, Thymosin Alpha-1, Thymalin, and Crystagen — reflect the multi-level immune and aging restoration strategy of the comprehensive Khavinson protocol. Vilon restores thymopoiesis and T-cell output. Thymalin provides broader thymic hormone signaling. Thymosin Alpha-1 enhances T-cell activation and Th1 cytokine profiles for infectious and oncological immune defense. Epithalon addresses the upstream pineal-melatonin-immune axis that modulates thymic function through the neuroimmune network. Crystagen supports the bone marrow hematopoietic compartment that supplies the T-cell progenitors that Vilon-restored thymic function requires. Together these compounds create a hierarchical immune rejuvenation stack spanning from the bone marrow progenitor source through thymic maturation to peripheral T-cell activation — the most complete immunosenescence intervention framework in this database.
